item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on fame and success: Don't crown yourself king | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"如厕悖论"：谦卑的生理学基础

Khabib 用了一个看似粗俗、实则极其精妙的论证："我们连去厕所这件事都控制不了，还谈什么控制人生？" 这不是随口一说的比喻，而是一个隐藏的哲学装置——他把"谦卑"从道德教条降维成了生理事实。

有趣的是，这与斯多葛派的 Marcus Aurelius 在《沉思录》里的做法惊人一致：这位罗马皇帝在权力顶峰时反复提醒自己"你吃的是死去动物的尸体，喝的是发酵的葡萄汁"。两个相隔 1800 年、语言不通、宗教不同的人，都发现了同一个反自恋的技术——用身体的原始性去戳破自我的膨胀。 当谦卑不再是"我选择谦卑"（这本身就是骄傲），而是"我的膀胱不允许我不谦卑"，它就变得不可反驳。

二、双人格开关：为什么"最谦卑的人"往往是最狠的竞争者

访谈中最反直觉的一段是他描述的"心理边界"：一侧是谦卑的人，另一侧是要"清除对手"的战士。大多数人以为强者就是"一直强"，弱者就是"一直弱"，但 Khabib 揭示的是一种可切换的双模态系统。

这让我想到一个跨领域的映射——外科医生的心理结构。顶级外科医生在病房里对家属温柔至极，但握起手术刀的瞬间必须能在人体上做出"违反日常道德直觉"的切割。他们同样需要这道"心理边界"。换句话说，Khabib 的心智架构不是格斗独有的，而是所有"高风险执行者"共享的操作系统：日常态的低自我 + 任务态的高侵略性。

更出人意料的是：恰恰是"日常态的低自我"保护了"任务态的高侵略性"不失控。一个 24 小时都想"称王"的人，会把每次买咖啡排队都变成战场，能量会散掉；而 Khabib 把王者模式锁进"八角笼"这个具体场景里，日常释放的能量为零，因此比赛时的浓度是 100%。谦卑不是侵略性的对立面，而是它的电池。

三、隐藏的"父亲协议"：为什么他从未真正为观众战斗

大多数关于名声的讨论会假设：冠军需要抵抗观众的爱慕，以免迷失。但 Khabib 的自述里藏着一个更深的结构——他从一开始就没把观众放进方程式里。他战斗的对象一直只有一个人：他的父亲 Abdulmanap。

这产生了一个反常识的推论：他之所以能免疫全球千万粉丝的爱，不是因为他"抵抗"了这份爱，而是因为这份爱在他的心理坐标系里根本不占位。 他的成就不是给世界的表演，而是父子之间的一封长信。当父亲成为唯一的观众，其他所有观众就自动变成了背景噪音。

这里有一个极冷门的跨领域连接——Bach 在乐谱手稿上写 "S.D.G."（Soli Deo Gloria，"荣耀独归于神"）。Bach 一生写了上千部作品，却不为国王、不为公众、只为一位"唯一的听众"而写。这种"单一听众结构"是防止创造者被大众反馈系统腐蚀的终极算法。 Khabib 的父亲就是他的 S.D.G.。理解这一点，你会突然明白：他不是"没有被名声改变"，而是他的整个成功从一开始就被建立在一个名声无法进入的房间里。

📝 转录文本

名声的重量

Lex： When it comes to you, I see that everyone here just loves you. Even early on in your career, millions of people loved you. That is also a tough thing to deal with because maybe you start believing it. Yeah, and you can lose yourself in all of it.

So, is it all in the mind? I mean, what actually goes on in a champion's head? In yours, when you sat alone thinking about your life — who am I really? And what do I do to keep being a champion, or to become one?

不要给自己加冕

Khabib： Well, first of all, from the very beginning, if you realize that what you're chasing isn't the most important thing in life, then it gets easier for you.

And then, you know, there are some people whose, let's say, ultimate goal is to be successful, powerful, and to make it big. At the end of the day, after all, we are not really such big, important people. And like I believe it's wrong to just crown yourself king. Because, to put it bluntly, if we're being honest here — [sighs] — we can't even control the basic need to go to the restroom.

Maybe to some — yeah, to some people, this will probably seem a bit crude, but we all go to the restroom. Excuse my language. If we can't control even this, so what can we actually control in this life?

同一个坟墓

Look how many people we know. How many great people have left this earth. It doesn't really matter how big, strong, or famous you are, how wealthy you are, champion or no champion. Either way, they put us all in the exact same grave, you know, 2 m down — or like a meter or a meter and a half. Different confessions, different religions, they bury people in different ways.

So, I actually believe that every single person should have this realization that we are just not some kind of big, important people here who just decide and get to control everything. We don't get to do that. [sighs]

父亲，唯一的观众

In my case, I was raised under the guidance of my father. My father was a coach. And my goal was always to become — to prove to my father that out of everyone, even though he trains many other people, he trains everyone. I mean, I'm also here. I can show him. He doesn't have to look very far. I'm right there.

And under his guidance, I can become a champion. I looked up to him and followed his example. Trained hard, and it was like, you know, a kind of a challenge to prove to him that: look, I am right here, father, and everything you teach, I will take it all in zealously, worthily. I'll follow your program, do it right, and I will become a champion.

And that was exactly the kind of goal I had — to prove it first and foremost to my father, and secondly to the entire world, that I can become the best wrestler or fighter. But I never thought of being crowned king after I became a champion. I was never going to walk around like, "Look how cool I am." That was never in my head. And I'm really glad that the almighty protected me from all of that, because many people end up in a bad place if they act like that.

内心的两道边界

Lex： This is a profound wisdom — not thinking about being crowned. But even if you don't, a fire should burn within you driving you to become a champion, right? As you said, hundreds of thousands, millions of people want to be a champion, but only one can be.

Khabib： Yeah, but that is actually about you confronting your opponent. You've got to put a barrier inside your mind where, on one side, you're a humble person, but on the other side you're different — because you have a goal, your goal.

Of course, you should still follow a code of honor. You should be a man, a righteous man, and know what you can and cannot do. You should always do that.

But in the end, your opponent is the person who wants to stop your dream. So here, the boundaries expand just a little bit. Right here, you're already not playing humble. Right here, you just step out and you want to clear your opponent out of your way, and that's it. Because your goal is to be the best in the world, and they are blocking you. Excuse me, but in this situation, there's no way you can act all humble.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [a16z] Inside Stripe's AI Strategy with Will Gaybrick
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏的悖论：Stripe 正在把"卖铲子"倒过来做

大多数人看这场对话，会说"Stripe 又发布了很多产品"。但真正颠覆性的模式是：Stripe 正在把自己从"卖铲子的人"变成"淘金者的孵化器"——而且是内部孵化。

注意 Will 说的那句被大多数人忽略的话：Metronome 的 CEO 现在在 Stripe 领导 billing，Privy、Bridge、Lemon Squeezy 的创始人各自领导一个新版图。Stripe 正在做的不是收购公司，而是收购"创始人型大脑"，然后把公司当作培养皿把他们放回野外。这与 Google/Meta 的收购逻辑（收购团队+产品并入体系）完全相反——Stripe 是收购团队+把体系拆散给团队。

跨领域连接：这其实是好莱坞制片厂制度在软件公司的复活。1930 年代 MGM 让导演拥有"制片人式的独立王国"，用工作室的资源但保留创作决策权。AI 让工程师变成"一人导演"后，Stripe 复活了这个模型——这也解释了为什么他们叫内部工具"Minions"（小黄人）：一个导演 + 一群可编排的执行体。

二、令人意外的观察：Stripe 的最大瓶颈已经从"写代码"变成了"卖代码"

Will 说了一句真正重要但很容易被略过的话：

"我们合并的代码比去年多得多，这在压迫每一个系统——如何把新功能塞进销售系统？如何塞进定价页面？我们训练销售人员的速度跟不上产品上市的速度。"

这是一个惊人的信号：软件公司的"最慢一环"正在从工程转移到 GTM（市场化）。过去 30 年，engineering 一直是稀缺资源，sales、marketing、legal 是"支持职能"。现在反过来了——工程侧的产能是 30x（Minions 每周从 1200 PR 变成 7000 PR），但销售培训、定价页面更新、合规审查这些"人的带宽"成了新瓶颈。

跨领域连接：这跟制造业的"瓶颈迁移"定律（Goldratt 的 Theory of Constraints）一模一样。当你解开一个瓶颈，瓶颈会立刻移到下一个环节——但很多公司会继续在原瓶颈上加速投入（"雇更多工程师"），完全没意识到问题已经搬家了。未来 18 个月，最先意识到这个迁移的 CEO 会赢，因为他们会把 AI 投入砸向 GTM 而不是 engineering。

三、隐藏的哲学转向：从"检查点开发"到"注射成型开发"

Will 用了一个绝妙但被随口带过的类比：AI 编程 = 注射成型（injection molding）。这不是修辞，是范式声明。

传统软件开发像手工木工——每个 PR 是一个手作品，需要迭代、雕琢、review。注射成型的核心是：你只做一次模具（templates + agents.md + patterns），然后按下按钮，产品源源不断地流出来。这就是为什么他们说"你不再进 planning mode，你只说'go do it'"——因为一旦模具做好，规划环节就消失了。

出人意料的推论：如果这个类比成立，那么软件公司的资产负债表要重写了。传统 SaaS 公司的价值在于"已经写好的代码"（存量）。注射成型公司的价值在于"模具的质量"（元资产）。Stripe 真正在积累的不是代码库，而是"agents 能理解的金融基础设施抽象"这个模具集。

跨领域连接：这也解释了为什么"稳定币 + 微支付 + 代理商务"必然会一起爆发。当生产的边际成本趋近于零，交易的边际成本必须也趋近于零，否则整个系统会在结算层堵死。这是热力学第二定律在经济系统里的体现——你不能让生产端流速是结算端的 100 倍，能量必然会在瓶颈处耗散成摩擦。Tempo（Stripe 的专用支付区块链）不是"又一条链"，是这个新物理定律逼出来的流速匹配器。

四、一个反直觉的预测

Will 说 "check out pages will go away"——这被当作 UX 演进。但真正的震撼是他后面那句几乎没被讨论的话："agent 可以直接从 espn.com 抓数据填 NCAA bracket"。

如果代理是主要用户，那么整个 SEO 产业、广告产业、UI 设计产业的底层假设都会崩塌——因为这些行业都假设"人类眼球在浏览"。代理不看广告，不被字体和配色说服，不点"limited time offer"。"品牌溢价"这个持续 100 年的商业概念，在代理商务里可能不存在——只剩下 API 契约、价格、延迟、准确率。

这才是 Stripe 押注 agentic commerce 真正的 endgame：不是让代理更方便地购买，而是重新定义"什么叫购买决策"。

Stripe Minions：一次性、单发的 Agent PR

We created something called Stripe Minions, which we've blogged about a little bit. The reason for that is that Minions are one-shot. You give it a prompt and it's going to build it, and then it's going to go through CI/CD and all of testing, and then you're going to review it. So you're not going to iterate, not go into planning mode. You're just going to say "this is what I want, go do it."

We think that's kind of where the world is going. It's the one-shot or the glorified REPL loop where you're just letting the agent be super super powerful.

We blogged about Minions I think in January/February, and they were doing 1,200 PRs per week. Last week, I think 7,000 PRs came from Minions. And about 30% of our PRs in that week came from Minions.

That sort of developer tooling — and then the internal processes just get out of the way and make the tools amazing. And that's how we're going to go fast.

Jevons Paradox

It's almost trite in tech circles now, but the Jevons paradox: as assets become more productive, you don't want less, you want more.

And it is very much the case for us when it comes to engineers. Our engineers are just magnificently more productive.

I mentioned earlier just making Stripe a platform for founders — internal platform for founders — going forward. You could say, well, because engineers are so productive there'll just be fewer engineers in the world. And I just really don't believe that. That's not what we're seeing at all.

There was a narrative 9 months ago about SaaS platforms, and how vertical platforms were all going to struggle. Our new SaaS platform cohort is 103% larger in 2026 than it was in 2025. So people are just saying "well, there's so many spaces that need a SaaS platform, I'm building it faster and faster and faster."

So I think there will be more software engineers in the world. We will need fewer of them to do the things we're already doing.

缺失的 Primitives：MPP 与 402

We created with Tempo the machine payments protocol so that services can indicate what needs to be paid and how you can pay for it. That's a primitive — we think machines will want to buy from other machines.

There's really a question of what should checkout look like for agents. It's still sort of an open question. Browser automation is getting better, so maybe agents should just be crawling through checkout forms and filling them out. I think there's still a lot of open questions.

That's the skeuomorphic version. There's going to be a native version.

B2B Agentic Commerce：Stripe Projects

One of the places we are the most excited about agentic commerce actually is B2B. So we launched Stripe Projects. Stripe Projects is a way to scaffold apps — that's the narrow definition of it. But the most exciting thing that Stripe Projects is, is a way to provision B2B services agentically.

So you can go — an agent can go adopt Vercel for hosting, and they can do it without you needing to go to vercel.com and do anything.

This has actually informed our investment thesis in a few investments recently that are developer tools. And we say, okay, assume that the agents are going to be the shoppers in the future. Is this the one that the agents will want to pick?

Exactly. That's a very good framework. An agent can go adopt Browserbase.

Demo：Browserbase 填 NCAA Bracket

We actually had a really great demo a while back at Stripe where we used Browserbase live via an agent to fill out an NCAA bracket. Which I thought was awesome because I have three brothers and we all love sports, but I'm always too busy to engage in the family pools. It was so cool to just watch the agent pick up a Browserbase session and fire up espn.com and do a bit of research and just fill it out.

How'd it do?

I don't actually know — I don't think we ever ran the evals on it.

I suspect probably as good as human.

Probably better.

So I do think agents adopting B2B or B2C services that are more utilitarian will be very popular. And so today again, as a primitive, we're just trying to make it easier for agents to adopt services.

But the sociology will continue to evolve. The long-running tasks are not — I don't know that we've figured out exactly how to do them on the consumer side. It's not there yet.

消费者场景：Micro-Consumption

I was trying the other day — I was using Claude Code to try to compose a song for my niece's birthday.

Oh, yeah.

It was pretty cool. In the past without Suno, I just definitely wouldn't have done that. With Suno I might do that. You might do it with a Higgsfield as well — we're talking about them earlier.

But I'm not sure that I want to go create a $10.99 or $9.99-a-month account with them. I just want the micro-consumption for that.

Along with the actual commerce primitives, I think there's these micro-consumption APIs that need to start to exist. Browserbase we're talking about — they're leaning into it. But I'm very bullish on all these services standing up sort of not necessarily anonymous but just ephemeral or one-time consumption.

I think that will really unlock agent commerce too. Because then you won't have to say "well, I need to pay these guys 10 bucks a month, and these guys 10 bucks a month, and these accounts and all this stuff." Just use the service and pay.

"Agent, do this. Discover the services. Your budget is $15. Go."

My 10-year-old has been creating rap songs, so I'm very familiar with all of these services. And by the way, the quality is actually pretty good, and he posts them on Spotify. But the execution maybe is not quite as good — the lyrics are very good from AI, and the music itself is pretty good. So I would welcome that.

微支付（Microtransactions）为什么这次会成？

One of the critical things that you just said is this concept of micropayments or microtransactions. This has been something that has been talked about probably since the advent of the internet — why do you think now it could work?

Well, agents really increase human agency. I guess it almost sounds redundant. But talking about these applications — composing a song for your niece, filling out your NCAA bracket, whatever else — it's really hard to do without agency. They take a lot of time. You're creating all these different accounts.

I'm just very bullish on services leaning into saying "you can use me ephemerally, you can use me in a lightweight way." And to make that work, you're just going to need to support microtransactions.

The case against microtransactions has always been: well, you're trying to consume content, and if you're trying to sell an article, you're always going to be squeezed between the subscriber business model and the free business model.

You want to capture the excess as part of the subscriber. That's the business model. Or you do it with ads — and they're one or the other is better than what you're doing.

I think that was probably true in the past. But as you give agents more complex tasks, you want them to be these little hummingbirds going around the internet — just slurping up a little data here, pulling it over here, some very transient ephemeral storage, doing a little compute over here. You don't want the individual human to have to think about what they're using. You want these services to be secure — but you don't want them to create accounts everywhere. So I think microtransactions will just be necessary for that economy to exist — the agentic economy.

Stablecoins 是解锁微支付的关键

And then on the flip side, they're now eminently possible because of stablecoins. Stablecoins are today relatively inorganic — if you're a human, you have to jump through a bunch of hoops. But if you just give an agent a budget, they can easily take dollars, move into stables, or just use or share a stored balance and find a way to check out. They don't mind the back-and-forth of stables.

I totally agree with that. We've seen that transition happen in a lot of software business models today — the predominant business model of selling subscriptions and seats. We've now seen a shift to consumption, and there's probably analogies where the consumers are better off because they can get access to more stuff, and then the businesses can access more people which they otherwise couldn't access with a subscription service. So my hope is that that does come into play.

Stablecoins：更优的全球货币基础设施

On the topic of stablecoins — we've covered how you guys build software, how you move so fast in an AI development world. We've talked about the idea of agentic commerce. Talk about stablecoins. Like you said, there's a lot of friction in the process today. But state of the stablecoin market and what you see the opportunity to be for the next call it five years.

I'm an infrastructure nerd, so I always will go there first. Stablecoins are just a better platform for moving money than exists otherwise.

Better for a couple reasons. There are certain countries that have rolled out really good payment systems. Most of them are nationalized — UPI in India. It's interesting when you look at these economies, the percentage of sub-$5 payments in India on UPI is I think something like 86%, whereas in the US on cards I think it's single-digit %.

There's some good, cheap, fast payment schemes that are nationalized. Pix, another one in Brazil, which has grown meteorically.

But you need a Schelling point for the global economy. Just: what can we all agree on? That's where crypto rails solve this political problem — this platform works everywhere.

If we just all used it, the global financial system would work better, be faster, be cheaper. So if we all went to sleep tonight and woke up tomorrow and we all held stables, it would just be a better global —

Less friction and less cost in the economy.

Exactly. Now that might be one of those "should work this way, may never work this way" problems. And so we are sort of resolutely focused on trying to change that.

We talked earlier about Stripe Treasury, and we decided to make stablecoins native to Stripe Treasury. So you can just hold a balance in stables just like you hold a balance in USD or EUR or GBP.

The opportunity for stables is just faster money movement, cheaper money movement, and more global money movement. Right now you can be a Stripe user in — I can't remember what the exact number is — but around 60 countries in fiat. But you can be a Stripe user in stablecoins in I think about 150 countries.

So just bringing more people into the online economy in a way that allows them to transact with the AI companies. As the software economy gets more and more global, bringing more people into it is more and more valuable. You can build a powerful AI company with two engineers in Thailand just as well as you can do it in the US, or as well as you can do it in Brazil.

For stables, for us, it is higher performance, more global.

I like the position that you guys are in as it relates to stablecoins, just because — talk about meeting the market where it is — people don't want to cut over full wholesale and just drop all their fiat and move over to stablecoins. The relationships that you have and the comprehensive offering that you have allows for adoption to happen at the pace that the enterprises want to adopt at, or startups.

And all of this works when you really lean into it. Félix Peña — Félix, I think, is what they're called now — which started as a remittance company between the US and Mexico and now has other corridors as well. They built it on stables, and a few years in, they're now between 5 and 10% of remittances along that corridor, which is the largest remittance corridor in the world.

It's amazing.

You think about how long it takes companies to move fiat money efficiently — how long it took initially for the Wises of the world to do this, let alone the Western Unions before it. These are great companies, but to get to 5 to 10% in just a few years is amazing.

Tempo：为支付而生的区块链

I'd love to have you talk a little bit about Tempo. Obviously it's a big important project that you guys are in the center of. Talk about where that is and what the aspirations for it are.

I'll just play the infrastructure nerd card again for a second. There are great blockchains, and I think there was no obvious need for another blockchain outside of payments.

There's a whole lot of reasons why a payments-specific blockchain can work really well:

  • Privacy — because blockchains are generally public, and you can sort of reverse-engineer what's happening on blockchains. So I want to make sure that privacy is a first-class primitive.
  • Throughput — making sure that throughput is never sacrificed. Blockchains are disproportionately used for trading, and so when you see massive trading events happen, you'll typically see performance degrade a lot.
  • Transaction fees — finding a way to create a blockchain where the transaction fee is never going to spike because other blockchains have floating gas fees. Capability is important.

The project there is just saying: how do we move money as efficiently, consistently and cheaply as possible? Still in the early stages of building out, getting a lot of great traction, working with companies like DoorDash. Making it the default but not only blockchain in Stripe. Feeling very optimistic about it.

Token 经济：钱与算力的边界正在融化

Last topic I would love to cover with you is the token economy. It sounds a little buzzwordy, but you guys are — I think over two trillion of volume now. I think you and I would probably share the belief that the token economy is going to be one of the biggest things we've ever seen. What do you think is the state of play for accessing tokens? Obviously there's a lot of work that gets done in first-party applications today. But what do you think is the future state of how we all access models and tokens?

Well, I love — I've always loved the word "token." The reason is that it just sounds like an approximation of money.

And increasingly that's just what it is, right? We talked earlier about free trial abuse, multi-accounting, and the attacks that we're seeing against users who have platforms that are general-purpose token consumers. You can do just about anything with tokens on Cursor. You can do just about anything with tokens on Replit.

The attacks against these users are very sophisticated. They're very reminiscent of what we see in terms of people trying to steal money from Stripe users.

And so there's this blurring that you see between tokens and dollars.

For us, we think about wanting to help users move money, store money, send money safely, compliantly, and so on. We now feel this mandate to do the same thing on tokens — to protect our users in the same way.

Over time I think this is only going to happen more. We talk about some of these long-running agentic tasks — a lot of them will replace services, and you'll just be able to say "close my books." And I used to pay a human in dollars for that. Now I pay fewer humans, or a human, or in tokens, because they're augmented by agents.

So we just want to make sure that moving between tokens and dollars is as seamless and safe as moving between dollars and euros. We're at the beginning of this journey, but we think it's going to be a big part of the future of Stripe.

It's super exciting. And personally speaking, I think you guys have a real right to play a role there because of the relationship that you have with so many companies since inception all the way through to enterprise, as you said.

And it's funny — we're always a little bit careful internally about talking about rights, and so we talk about mandates.

Win, and then win it again.

Exactly. We have a mandate to help users with this. And so that's why we're really leaning into it.

Spend Management：Token 使用的产品化

We're also focusing even more on spend management for our customers. They're using Stripe Treasury, they're thinking a lot about how much they're spending and how to reduce their spending, how their spending ties through to revenue. And a lot of token usage is actually in product.

You see two different types of token usage: 1. Opex management side — using tokens to build things. 2. Product efficacy side — how good is my token-oriented or token-driven product? How should I shift between different models to make it the most effective?

So we're really thinking about how do we help users on both of these.

Certainly in the latter, this position as an orchestration layer that helps you effectively get the most out of tokens — and you also maintain some form of control — I think has never been more top-of-mind than it is right now.

Absolutely. And it's interesting because there's a hypothesis that software will be severely commoditized. And it's plausible. I think we're either in the singularity or creeping towards the singularity, and it's very hard to estimate what a future looks like where models are recursively generating models and so on.

But we are seeing the exact opposite right now — software creation is exploding.

Customers are monetizing faster than ever. We talked about our 2026 cohort growing 50% larger and growing faster than the '25 cohort, that one being 70% larger and growing faster than the '24 cohort. So more software being created, being adopted faster than ever before. And then more Stripe products are being adopted than ever before. 11 Labs is using 14 Stripe products — sort of wish it were 11 in a way, but actually I'm glad it's 14.

Just make it 22. He got really close with Matty and he does everything in denominations of 11. So you got to shoot for 22.

Exactly. And there's a lot more to software than just building. There's the expertise about how abstractions should thread through your entire business, and keeping those up to date — and you have turnover inside of your company, and so you build a system internally and then it starts to degrade, and that person leaves the company and the expertise goes away.

So we think about just how can we help companies across their entire revenue stack — manage cash, manage revenue, close the books faster, grow faster, globalize faster. That opportunity, I think, is just larger than it ever was before.

尾声：Taste 如何在 AI 时代规模化？

In closing, I wanted to just get your take — and this is, I don't want to get too deep into the role of humans versus AI — but one of the things that Stripe has always been universally recognized for and appreciated for, I think, is your taste. It sounds funny because you're an infrastructure company, but I think it's generally agreed upon. How do you continue to uphold that at such a large scale and with so much of the work that you're doing now being done by AI?

It's interesting how much the word "taste" is being used right now. It's sort of hard sometimes to — the cynical view is that it's how we're all justifying our future value. That no one actually has taste, and it's just we're all reproducing machines of things that we had previously perceived. Suddenly my fingers are no longer as useful, but this nebulous notion of taste is — and models will never have taste, and so on — which is probably just not true.

Yeah, I agree with you on that.

But to your question — product quality is really really core to our culture and to our identity. And it's for a few reasons.

  • User lens: We want users to have amazing tools that are carefully crafted, that can make them go faster, enjoy the journey of building a company that much more. It's not an easy journey. But if you have tools that are surprisingly great, it feels that much better.
  • It's just more fun: You look at what you created with your team and you're like, "wow, that looks amazing." Versus you kind of janked this thing together and it barely works, and it just isn't as fun to go through the slog — the long nights, the long weekends — to build it.

两件事：Tops-Down + Use the Product

The single thing I would say for scaling — actually two things:

  1. It has to be tops-down. You just have to say it 1000% over and over and over again. Like the company strategy of "when the startups, win them again" — talk about quality and talk about it again.
  2. Use the product — and make it easy to use the product.

类比：航空模拟与英伟达的芯片仿真

In aviation, simulation is so important. You can't just say "I hope the jet works." You have to prove to yourself that it does before you ever fly it.

Or Nvidia — when they really hit escape velocity was when they went from needing to wait for the fab to give them the chips to try the chips, to actually simulate chip performance.

So we actually invest a lot in simulating the usage of products.

You can point to an account and say "give me something that looks like that." But make it completely PII-free, randomize the growth rates so I don't actually know how big they are — but just the day-to-day problems that they face, the ups and downs of their business, the seasonality, give me a sense of that. And then make it feel live, so that I feel like I'm receiving disputes from customers and refunds are happening. Of course these aren't real disputes, they're not real refunds — but just give me the experience that the user is having, so I can really live in it and use that with my team.

So you have the mandate to use the product. We really ask our EMs to lead this because they're the ones who control the resources and they're the ones who can say "wow, this does not feel good, it needs to get fixed. So our next sprint is going to be elevating quality."

And the other side — how do you give people the tools to do it more easily?

Scaling taste for us is culture, and the shibboleths, and then the daily rhythms of just using the products and stepping into these issues.

That's awesome. Will, this is so fun to talk to you about all these topics — obviously covering how you're building so much product inside Stripe, which is super unique and right on the cutting edge, and the future of how we engage in agent commerce and stablecoins. One of the things that I think you guys have said is: how do we ensure that we build the next Stripe inside of Stripe? I love that in closing. I really appreciate the time.

Thank you. Great to be here.

item.description:
## 一、隐藏的悖论：Stripe 正在把"卖铲子"倒过来做
大多数人看这场对话，会说"Stripe 又发布了很多产品"。但真正颠覆性的模式是：**Stripe 正在把自己从"卖铲子的人"变成"淘金者的孵化器"**——而且是内部孵化。
注意 Will 说的那句被大多数人忽略的话：Metronome 的 CEO 现在在 Stripe 领导 billing，Privy、Bridge、Lemon Squeezy 的创始人各自领导一个新版图。**Stripe 正在做的不是收购公司，而是收购"创始人型大脑"，然后把公司当作培养皿把他们放回野外**。这与 Google/Meta 的收购逻辑（收购团队+产品并入体系）完全相反——Stripe 是收购团队+**把体系拆散给团队**。
跨领域连接：这其实是**好莱坞制片厂制度**在软件公司的复活。1930 年代 MGM 让导演拥有"制片人式的独立王国"，用工作室的资源但保留创作决策权。AI 让工程师变成"一人导演"后，Stripe 复活了这个模型——这也解释了为什么他们叫内部工具"Minions"（小黄人）：一个导演 + 一群可编排的执行体。

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on genius of Javier Mendez as a coach | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的教练天才藏在"拒绝"里，而非"能力"里

大多数人评价教练，看的是他"能教什么"。但 Khabib 描述 Javier Mendez 的方式里，藏着一个反直觉的真相：Javier 的伟大恰恰体现在他愿意说"不"的地方——他不愿意角落里指导那些没有跟他完整走过训练营的选手。

这看似傲慢，实则是一种极度诚实的自我校准：我不知道你在第三、第四、第五回合里会怎么塌方，所以我不能替你承担那个决策。Khabib 花了将近十年才真正理解这句话——一个真正意义上的"教练资产"，不是他掌握的技术库，而是他对一个具体的人在极限状态下会如何反应的私密知识。

这是一个让人意外的观察：顶级教练的核心竞争力不是"教"，而是"看"。Khabib 反复强调 Javier 从 2012 年至今 14 年，几乎没有缺席过任何一次陪练。这意味着 Javier 真正卖的不是技术，而是连续性的观察记录——他脑子里储存着每个选手在几百次陪练中细微的状态漂移。

二、"深水区"隐喻：一个跨领域的通用原理

Khabib 用了一个惊人的词——"deep waters（深水区）"。他说自己现在也不愿意去指导没跟他一起训练的选手，因为"我不知道他能潜多深"。

这个隐喻的力量在于它跨领域适用：

  • 外科医生几乎不接手别人术前评估过的病人上手术台——不是能力问题，是信息断层问题。
  • 巴菲特和芒格的"能力圈"理论，本质上是同一个原则：我只在我完整了解其历史行为的对象上下注。
  • 心理治疗师行业有类似的伦理：不为没有建立长期关系的来访者做危机干预。
  • 特种部队的营救行动里，最优先考虑的不是敌情，而是队友的"已知反应模式"。

也就是说，Javier 教给 Khabib 的其实不是一个 MMA 技巧，而是一切高风险专业领域的元原则：不要在你没有充分校准过的系统上做全押决策。

三、传承的真正介质：不是招式，而是"未被理解的一句话"

这段对话里最动人的结构，是一个延时理解的闭环：2016 年 Javier 说了一句话，Khabib 当时"没懂"；十年后 Khabib 自己成了那个角色，才突然理解，并用几乎相同的语言复述出来。

这里有个反常识的洞见：真正深刻的师承，靠的不是被理解的教导，而是被记住却暂时无法理解的教导。那些当时你觉得"莫名其妙"的话，反而是种子——因为它们不能被立刻消化，就在意识里持续发酵，最终在生活给你相同处境的那一刻自动解压缩。

这也解释了一个跨领域的现象：为什么禅宗的"公案"、犹太教的"塔木德"、乃至中国师徒制里"话头"式的教诲，都倾向于不解释。因为过早的解释会杀死时间维度上的理解。Javier 只说了一句"我不喜欢指导没跟我准备过的人"，没有展开、没有教学，就转身走了。这句话在 Khabib 心里潜伏了近十年，然后才活过来。

啊哈时刻：Khabib 现在描述的 Javier，其实已经是"Khabib 版本的 Javier"——他描述的不是 Javier 客观是什么，而是他花了十年才在自己身上长出来的那部分 Javier。真正的教练从不留下学生，只留下未来某天会显影的自己。

📝 转录文本

领导者的位置：面对一群顶尖但迥异的运动员

Lex: Now, you're in this new position as a leader, and you're looking at all these athletes — these young guys who are already at the very top of the world. And I think they're all very different from one another psychologically, physically, and stylistically. What can you say as a coach? I know you're not a coach, but as a leader — how do you figure out what each person needs? Like now, we were watching Umar prepare.

Khabib: Yeah.

Lex: That each person needs something different.

因材施教：一种方法无法套用所有人

Khabib: Yes, everyone is different. Different styles, different mentalities, and different mindsets, different approaches to fight week and to preparation as a whole. But you have to adapt to all of it. Here, you can't just take one approach.

Let's say we take my approach and apply it to everyone else — to Usman, Islam, and Umar. It doesn't work like that. Everyone needs their own approach. I knew them since they were nobody, and I know them now when they are the best. So, you have to treat each one differently.

Javier Mendez 的加入：从选手到教练的过渡

I'm very lucky to have Javier Mendez. He's been by my side since 2012. And when I became a coach after I finished my career, he was there with me as a coach. I switched from being a fighter to a coaching role. My father was no longer with us, and together with Javier Mendez, we've been guiding them for these last 6 years.

And his experience helps me tremendously. Because there is no coach, no MMA coach with the kind of results Javier Mendez has, you know. So many champions, double champions, UFC fighters. So many people have trained under him. From Frank Shamrock all the way to Islam Makhachev. So many fighters have trained under him. Which makes things very easy for me. Because I have Javier Mendez by my side. And he can help me with so many things.

Javier 的天才究竟在哪里

Lex: What do you think is the secret behind Javier's genius? Why is he such a great coach for so many different athletes?

Khabib: It's the mental side of things. I'm not going to say he's one of the best at holding pads or anything like that. But his understanding of MMA itself, his approach to training camp, to the whole preparation process, to sparring inside the cage.

I'm not talking about those sparring sessions with 50 people in the gym and everyone is sparring with each other. For example, when I was preparing for a five-round fight, he would always bring in two or three high-level opponents, constantly rotating in fresh sparring partners. And he would watch and analyze.

十四年不缺席：一种近乎苛刻的在场

I don't remember him ever missing a single sparring session since 2012. Can you imagine? 14 years have gone by. And right now, we're in training camp. He's there for every training session, morning and evening. He's at every sparring session, watching everyone, coaching them, giving advice, guiding them.

He's incredibly dedicated to what he does. He's either all in or he steps away completely. He never shows up and gives only 50%.

一次让 Khabib 十年后才懂的对话

I remember one situation. Abubakar was getting ready to fight in WSOF. And I had another student fighting there as well. Abubakar went through the entire preparation with us, but the other guy didn't. When we got there, I told the coach:

"Coach, can you work his corner with me, too?"

He said:

"You know, Khabib, I haven't seen his preparation. I don't know what he's capable of. He didn't train under me. But since you're asking, I'll do it. But for the future, remember — I don't really like to corner guys I haven't prepared."

I didn't understand him then, but now I do. This was 2016 or maybe 2017. I don't want to be wrong. And now I understand.

十年后的复述：我终于成了那个人

Now when people ask me, I'm like:

"I didn't prepare you. I don't know how ready you are. I'm not ready to go in there and give all my energy to someone who didn't go through camp with me."

Now I understand that. At that time, I told the coach, "Can you come out and corner him with me?" He said, "No problem." We went out there. Abubakar had won his fight, and the other guy's fight ended in a draw. But that's not really what I'm getting at.

I've come to the point where if I haven't trained someone for two, three, or four months, I don't like to corner them — because they didn't go through a full training camp, and I don't know how they'll respond in the third, fourth, or fifth round. I don't know how he prepared. I don't know how ready he is to go into those deep waters. That's why I try not to corner just anyone. I learned that from Javier.

深水区：你必须知道他能潜多深

Lex: So you need to know he can go into those deep waters.

Khabib: How deep he can go. I need to know exactly what he's capable of.

Lex: Hey.

大多数人评价教练，看的是他"能教什么"。但 Khabib 描述 Javier Mendez 的方式里，藏着一个反直觉的真相：**Javier 的伟大恰恰体现在他愿意说"不"的地方**——他不愿意角落里指导那些没有跟他完整走过训练营的选手。
这看似傲慢，实则是一种极度诚实的自我校准：**我不知道你在第三、第四、第五回合里会怎么塌方，所以我不能替你承担那个决策**。Khabib 花了将近十年才真正理解这句话——一个真正意义上的"教练资产"，不是他掌握的技术库，而是他对一个具体的人在极限状态下会如何反应的**私密知识**。

item.title: [Lex Clips] A fighter's toughest enemy: The trap of money and fame | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：冠军的"真正对手"不是别人，而是自己达成目标的那一刻

大多数人以为格斗手最艰难的时刻是拳台上的对决——但 Khabib 揭示了一个更隐秘的战场：登顶的瞬间就是崩塌的开始。这里有一个几乎被所有励志叙事忽略的心理机制——"目标真空"。一个人用二十年把自己塑造成"追逐者"的形状，当追逐的对象消失，这个形状本身就失去了容器。他不是败给了对手，而是败给了"没有对手"这件事本身。

这让我想到一个跨领域的对照：登山者死于下山，而非登顶。喜马拉雅的统计数据显示，绝大多数事故发生在从峰顶返回的路上——因为大脑在达成目标后会释放大量多巴胺，警觉性骤降。冠军的"分心因素"——合同、飞行、拍摄——本质上就是心理层面的"下山路"。身体还在山上，注意力已经在山下。

隐藏的系统性真相：Khabib 的"厕所哲学"是一种反脆弱的身份锚

他说的那段"我们连上厕所都控制不了"看似粗俗，其实是整个访谈里最精密的心理防御机制。这是一个身份层级的降维——他人为地把自我拉回到"生物性人类"这个最底层，让冠军身份无法在其之上建立傲慢的上层建筑。

有意思的跨领域连接：这与斯多葛派的"memento mori"（记住你终将死亡）、佛教的"不净观"、甚至硅谷 CEO 用"未来自传体记忆"做决策的方法结构完全一致——都是通过引入一个更大的时间尺度或更低的存在层级，来消解当下身份的膨胀。Khabib 不是一个宗教化的例外，他实际上无意间演示了一种普适的抗傲慢算法：你越是能随时把自己缩回到最基础的存在，你在最高处就越稳定。

最反常规的洞见：谦逊与凶猛不是矛盾，而是同一套操作系统的两个模式

一般人以为"做人要谦逊 vs 竞技要凶猛"是道德困境——Khabib 提供了一个更精妙的架构：在心里画一道边界。这不是虚伪，也不是双重人格，而是一种上下文切换的心智协议。

这里藏着一个跨领域的深层模式，与顶级外科医生高度相似：手术台外温和克制，手术台上冷酷决断——他们不是"变了个人"，而是明确了每种模式的适用边界。反观许多失败的冠军（无论是拳手、创业者还是艺术家），他们的问题恰恰是边界渗透：把台上的凶猛带回家庭，把家庭的柔软带上赛场。

而 Khabib 那句"对手是想阻止你梦想的人，所以此刻边界稍微扩张一下"——这是把攻击性重新定义为一种功能性工具，而不是人格特征。这种"工具化的攻击性"或许才是所有长期高水平表演者的共同秘密：他们不是天生凶猛的人在假装温柔，而是天生温柔的人学会了精准地调用凶猛。

📝 转录文本

冠军的真正考验：登顶之后

Lex： You mentioned money and we were just talking about comfort because right now there are so many champions. They win so much. Things are going so well. How much harder is it to stay a champion when the money and the fame start coming in? When all that stuff starts showing up?

Khabib： Well, those are all distracting things. When you become a champion, there's a massive amount of attention on you. Sometimes it's contracts. Sometimes you end up having to fly a lot. You start getting busy with things. And little by little you begin to miss your workouts. You miss one, you miss two, you miss three. [sighs] And all of that takes a toll.

And the person who used to train with such a drive with a hunger to be the best, as soon as they actually become the best, they just don't know what to do next. And they live their whole life just to become — uh — stay on the top.

Lex： Mhm.

Khabib： As soon as they get there, what are they supposed to do? That's it. They already made it. They've reached their goal, and there are just so many distracting factors. Money, flights, you know, meetings, contracts, video shoots — there are just so many distracting factors. And so if a person doesn't know how to handle all of this, then that person comes down from the top real fast.

And I'm saying this based on my own experience, from what I've seen all around me — with the ones who came before me and back then when I was training with my father, his students who went on to become world champions, just how they finished their careers and so on. And it's what I saw from — uh — from my own observations of other types of sports, how they came back down.

As far as I've learned, this is a very delicate moment. If a person climbing all the way to the top, if they can handle all of that, that already shows they have an incredibly serious mindset. Reaching the championship and staying there — reaching it is one thing, but staying a champion, that's totally different. It's incredibly tough.

从业余到职业：一层比一层更难

Lex： You're saying that even on a local level, once you become a champion, that's already the tough moment? Because a lot of people who start winning, like you said, they stop fighting, they quit doing MMA and switch over to fitness. They find themselves that comfort, but holding on to it is hard even on a local level. Every single time you become more and more of a champion. You won the championship. You keep winning more and more, and every time it gets harder.

Khabib： Yes. And it depends on the person's goals. If you want to become an amateur champion just to prove something to yourself, that's one thing. But if you view amateur sports as a springboard to jump right into professional sports and become a champion among professionals, that's a whole different thing.

There are different paths: - First, you build an amateur career just to get into the pros and go even further from there. - Second, after you've made it into the pros, you become a champion. - Third, after you become a champion, you have to stay there.

Not everyone has what it takes. It is incredibly tough. If you look at the numbers, you can literally count these champions on one hand. How many of them are there? Maybe 15, 20, 30 people. Let's say 50 over the last 30 years. And how many have tried?

For example, 50 achieved it over 30 years, over 35 years — uh — of MMA combat sports. But how many tried? Hundreds of thousands. And look at that number. Such a tiny amount actually reach the end goal.

So for you to actually make it into this tiny list, you really have to be like — uh — just a truly unique — uh — person and a fighter and, and, you know, a student and a person who can accept guidance from a coach, who when they are being guided, discard the cons and take only the pros.

But there are people who take criticism very hard and very negatively and are very sensitive, let's say, when they take criticism —

Lex： Mhm.

Khabib： — from [clears throat] uh a mentor. [sighs and gasps] So it all has to click. And some accept criticism at the very beginning, but then once they become champions, it's hard for them to take it.

Lex： Mhm.

成功之前，人不知道自己是谁

Khabib： It happens differently. A man sometimes doesn't even know what he is capable of. Sometimes he just can't really understand himself until he achieves success or becomes famous, wealthy and powerful. That is exactly when he discovers his true qualities.

When he is limited in something — in money, in power, in everything that success eventually brings him — he doesn't really know how he's going to act in this new role. Doesn't know how he'll behave once he becomes big, famous, and a champion. Nobody knows.

Some people say and wish, "Oh, if only I'd made it like that, I would do things this way." I think it's better if people don't throw around such big words. Because you never know how you'll carry yourself once you actually get there. You know, it's such a delicate thing — getting up there and still remaining human.

Lex： When it comes to you, I see that everyone here just loves you. Even early on in your career, millions of people loved you. That is also a tough thing to deal with because maybe you start believing it.

Khabib： Yeah. And you can lose yourself in all of it.

Lex： So, is it all in the mind? I mean, what actually goes on in a champion's head — in yours — when you sat alone thinking about your life? Who am I really? And what do I do to keep being a champion or to become one?

冠军的心内独白：我们并非什么大人物

Khabib： Well, first of all, from the very beginning, if you realize that what you're chasing isn't the most important thing in life, then it gets easier for you. And then, you know, there are some people whose — let's say — ultimate goal is to be successful, powerful, and to make it big.

At the end of the day, after all, we are not really such big important people. And like, I believe it's wrong to just crown yourself king. Because uh [sighs and gasps] uh, if we put it — to put it bluntly, if we're being honest here — we can't even control the basic need to go to the restroom. Maybe to some — yeah, to some people this will probably seem a bit crude — but we all go to the restroom, excuse my language. If we can't control even this, so what can we actually control in this life?

Look how many people we know, how many great people have left this earth. It doesn't really matter how — like — big, strong, or famous you are, how wealthy you are, champion or no champion, either way they put us all in the exact same grave, you know, 2 m down, or like a meter or a meter and a half. Different confessions, different religions, they bury people in different ways.

So, I actually believe that every single person should have this realization that we are just not some kind of big important people here who just decide and get to control everything. We don't get to do that.

父亲的凝视：一个私人化的动力源

In my case, I was raised under the guidance of my father. My father was a coach, and uh, my goal was always to become — to prove to my father that out of everyone — even though he trains many other people, he trains everyone, I mean — I'm also here. I can show him he doesn't have to look very far. I'm right there.

And under his guidance, I can become a champion. I looked up to him and followed his example, trained hard, and it was like, you know [sighs and gasps], a kind of a challenge — to prove to him that: look, I am right here, father, and everything you teach, I will take it all in zealously, worthily. I'll follow your program, do it right, and I will become a champion.

And that was exactly the kind of goal I had — to prove it first and foremost to my father, and secondly to the entire world, that I can become the best wrestler or fighter. But I never thought of being crowned king after I became a champion. I was never going to walk around like "look how cool I am." That was never in my head. And I'm really glad that the Almighty protected me from all of that, because many people end up in a bad place if they act like that.

谦逊与凶猛：心中的那道边界

Lex： This is a profound wisdom — not thinking about being crowned. But even if you don't, a fire should burn within you driving you to become a champion. Right, as you said, hundreds of thousands, millions of people want to be a champion, but only one can be.

Khabib： Yeah. But that is actually about you confronting your opponent. You've got to put a barrier inside your mind where on one side you're a humble person, but on the other side you're different, because you have a goal — your goal.

Of course, you should still follow a code of honor. You should be a man, a righteous man, and know what you can and cannot do. You should always do that.

But in the end, your opponent is the person who wants to stop your dream. So here the boundaries expand just a little bit. Right here you're already not playing humble. Right here you just step out and you want to clear [gasps] your opponent out of your way, and that's it. Because your goal is to be the best in the world, and they are blocking you. Excuse me, but in this situation, there's no way you can act all humble.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib explains why Dagestan produces so many champions | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"匮乏经济学"的反直觉真相：稀缺不是限制，而是过滤器

大多数人读到"70人共用一个冷水澡"，会得出"艰苦锻造冠军"这种俗套结论。但哈比布真正说的是更微妙的东西——匮乏的核心功能不是磨砺身体，而是筛选动机。

他反问了一个关键问题："一个富爸爸会强迫自己的孩子每天带着淤青回家吗？富家子弟自己会愿意吗？"这句话戳穿了"苦难塑造冠军"的浪漫化叙事。真相是：匮乏创造了一个动机自筛选系统——只有那些饥饿到愿意承受非理性痛苦的人才会留下。达吉斯坦不是"生产"冠军，而是在源头就淘汰了所有不够饿的人。

这与硅谷创业圈的一个悖论惊人一致：斯坦福 MBA 的创业成功率远低于辍学者。不是因为教育有害，而是退路越多，穿越"死亡谷"的意愿越低。风投界甚至有个反向指标——如果创始人有 Plan B，就不投。达吉斯坦体系与之同构。

二、跨领域的意外连接：达吉斯坦 = 摔跤界的维也纳咖啡馆

哈比布提到达吉斯坦有 40-50 个格斗馆、密集的教练网络、清晰的晋升阶梯（村 → 达吉斯坦 → 北高加索 → 俄罗斯 → 世界）。他把这归因于"传统"和"教练体系"。

但这里藏着一个更深的模式，这不是体育现象，而是"知识密集集群"现象。它精确复现了： - 19 世纪末维也纳咖啡馆——弗洛伊德、维特根斯坦、马勒在同一个几公里半径内相互撞击，催生现代思想 - 佛罗伦萨美第奇圈——达芬奇、米开朗基罗、波提切利在同一条街上竞争 - 贝尔实验室的走廊效应——晶体管、信息论、Unix 都诞生于同一栋楼

关键机制不是"训练"，而是"局部竞争密度"。哈比布说"每个位置都有 10-15 个高水平摔跤手"——这意味着每天日常训练的强度，等于其他地方的全国锦标赛。这就是"地板即天花板"效应：当你的训练伙伴的水平已经是别人的上限，你的日常就是别人的极限。

更令人意外的是：父亲的角色不是"传授技术"，而是"制造知识溢出"。当阿卜杜勒马纳普成名后，他的哲学被媒体传播，其他隐藏的教练获得了"合法性上升通道"——这解释了为什么冠军往往成群出现，而非孤立涌现。冠军不是被制造的，是被"氛围"传染的。

三、地缘史诗与身体记忆：一个你可能没意识到的模式

哈比布用了一大段讲达吉斯坦的历史——可萨汗国、阿拉伯哈里发、波斯、蒙古、帖木儿、俄罗斯帝国轮番碾过这片土地。表面看这是"民族性格论"的老调。

但注意他透露的一个奇怪细节：帖木儿的大军停在山下没有上去。为什么？因为"骑兵和补给上不去冷山"。这个地理事实催生了一个惊人的社会分层——

低地被反复征服 → 高地保持独立。这创造了一种独特的文化基因：同一民族内部既有"被殖民的记忆"又有"未被征服的骄傲"。这种张力比单纯的"战斗民族"叙事深刻得多。

而这里有个跨领域的意外映射：这与瑞士为什么产出了不成比例的私人银行家、精密制造和永久中立完全同构——都是"山地屏障 + 低地贸易通道"的产物。达吉斯坦的"Babul Abwab"（门之门）与瑞士的阿尔卑斯山口在功能上是同一个地缘结构。

所以哈比布真正遗传的不是"暴力基因"，而是一种"边界感"——知道什么可以让步（低地贸易），什么绝不让步（山地身份）。这恰恰是顶级 MMA 选手比赛中最关键的判断：什么时候可以承受伤害推进，什么时候必须绝对防守。他的战术风格里，藏着他祖先 1500 年的地缘政治学。

有一个让我出乎意料的收尾观察：哈比布说"过去我没真正感觉到（历史），但随着时间流逝，你开始以全新的眼光看它"。这暗示了一件事——冠军不是从小就意识到自己是冠军的，而是在成为冠军之后，才回溯性地读懂了自己身上的历史。身份认同是果，不是因。

📝 转录文本

传奇的健身房：斯巴达式的条件

Lex： So that gym back in Dagistan where you trained is legendary for its Spartan conditions. There was just one shower for 70 people, only cold water. And yet this humble little gym managed to raise more than 20 world champions, including several UFC champions. Can you try to explain or maybe reflect on what factors in that gym, those training sessions, that life in Dagasthan created so many champions?

Khabib： Sure. So, we're talking about the gym, the one located in Mahagekala. And Mahachkala, for the people who don't know, it's the capital of Dagistan. This was back around the years from 2000 to 2010 and even later on. In 2019, we opened up a big gym, a major facility that is still functioning to this day.

But before 2019, we all actually trained in that gym where there was practically nothing. It was just a school gym with nothing but muts, a single punching bag, one climbing rope, and a kind of indoor basketball court.

从村庄到马哈奇卡拉：父亲的家庭健身房

And if we go even further back before 2000, before we moved to Mahachkala, we lived in a village. In the village, we had a gym right inside our house. My father, he built a gym at home and he was training all the local village kids right there.

And uh there were times back when I was a child, let's say when I was maybe 6 or 7 years old, I would occasionally wake up to the sound of uh people training, doing their drills right there in the gym. You know, like with judo or freestyle when they're drilling, one guy throwing another. Those are my first conscious memories. I was maybe 5, 6, 7 years old at that time.

So my father set up this gym in the village and trained local kids, including me, my older brother, and all our close and distant relatives, anyone who wanted to come. A lot of kids came to him.

Lex： So you would wake up and there are these sounds.

Khabib： Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You hear the hitting, the throwing over and over and my father's voice, how he's shouting, giving instructions, pushing someone, coaching, teaching. I lived with those sounds, but that was in the village.

And later when we moved to Makkcala, well, you couldn't say the gym there was wow either. They were only muts. And of course, the most valuable thing an athlete can have, a coach, my father. So, he trained us there. And to be honest, until I uh let's say until I became a champion and had big success, we never had a good big gym where we could, you know, all take a shower together at the same time after training. We always had just one shower for everyone. No proper amenities.

舒适是否是冠军的敌人？

Lex： So your life story began in the mountains of Dagistan and Sildi then Kiraova and then Mahachkala and in all these situations there are very interesting stories but one of the things I heard you say is that the best results are born out of the worst conditions. What can you say about that philosophically? Is it correct to say that comfort is kind of the enemy for champions?

Khabib： It depends on the sport. For example, let's say in football you have to have conditions. You can't really play if there is practically no field. Of course, you can play in the dirt and it happens sometimes. You can start there, but when you are 10 or 12 years old, you already have to be at a certain level. You must have conditions.

But if we look at our sport, then what is the most important thing? The coach. You also need sparring partners who will uh push you in the gym as they say, right? And you need the mats. Our sport is not expensive. You just buy your wrestling shoes, singlets, shorts, a t-shirt, and if there's a mat, you wrestle, you become a champion, you fight.

But when you live too well, let's say, you know, you're never in need. For example, you were born into a wealthy family and you already have everything. Would that same wealthy father, would he force you to do such a brutal sport? A sport where you come home every day with injuries, uh where you come home with an exhausted body, you come home with bruises, would he really do that? That's the question.

And the kid himself who lives a life of luxury, would he even want to do this? When we look at it statistically, the answer is no. This is where you need that hunger. You have to be in a position where you are truly in need.

巴西的足球，达吉斯坦的摔跤：文化与体系

Lex： And it's interesting that there's a psychological side to this as well that you need a tough situation to create champions. But what's really interesting is how Dagistan has produced so many wrestling champions. You mentioned football. Let's look at other countries. Why has Brazil produced so many great football players? Why does Argentina have so many football players? Of course, you have Germany, France, and all that.

Khabib： European.

Lex： Yeah. The whole European side, but those are completely different cultures.

Khabib： Yes. Well, in Brazil, their strength is in their numbers. How many people do they have? The population is huge. More than 200 million. And people really love it there. It's a huge tradition because you know without a real love for this sport, you can never achieve any success. You truly have to love what you are doing. So they have the tradition and they have the love for it. And that is why they play for all the top clubs. Well, I think they just win by numbers.

Lex： Yeah, that's a powerful aspect of their culture. How much people, how much the whole nation loves to play football. And if you add to that a system that creates strong teams, that's how you can produce so many football legends.

Khabib： Yes, take Dagasthan for example. We love football. I just know how much people in Dagasan love football. Yes, we have wrestlers, fighters. There are many of us. But for football players, there is no ecosystem like that. Not so well organized where a kid can, for example, play at school then go to some academy then get noticed there and then get picked up by a club. We don't have that system.

It's just kids running on the streets playing on the streets following football. Let's say playing on PlayStation. There is no system. There is no selection process where kids can go and show themselves so they can be noticed and get signed. I think Brazil and other countries and of course Europe, they have it. So yeah, we have big problems with football.

However, in our sports where you can wrestle, where you can fight, in that sense we have a system. For example, the gyms, you know, in Makashkala, let's say for combat sports — I'm not even counting like freestyle wrestling or other styles — there may be 40 or 50 gyms for combat sports and all are full.

If you win in Dagasan, you move on to the North Caucases level, then to the Russian nationals. If you're champion of Russia, you go to the worlds. In amateurs, they notice you and you make a name for yourself. There is a certain ladder here. But in many other sports here in Dagistan, we don't have such a well structured ladder for people to climb.

一间健身房为何能产出如此多冠军？

Lex： Can we look at this philosophically again? I mean, you've seen so many wrestlers, fighters. Why exactly were these gyms creating so many champions? I'm just honestly curious because it's rare in any sport. One gym or a small number of gyms creating so many champions.

Khabib： Well, first important factor is the competition level is incredibly high. You come to the gym and in every spot you have good wrestlers, 10 or 15 guys right there and the coaches are great.

You know, it so happened that my father broke through in the media and then I became a champion and the other guys became champions too and my father's philosophy it really resonated and he became known for it. Yeah. But there are coaches in Dagistan that not many people know about. They are known locally but they are very good and actually they have the knowledge, they have the approach, they have the philosophy, they could also be at the same level as my father was. I believe there are really quite a few of them.

教练传承的谱系：从 1950 年代说起

In terms of the coaching, I think Dagistan was extremely lucky. It probably goes back to the 1950s when wrestling really took off here. Starting with Ali Ali, our legendary wrestler, a five-time world champion who went to the Olympics three times.

That's where it started with his generation. There was Zagalav Abdul Beov, Ali Alf. Those are the well-known names. I mean those guys are famous, but there were so many other less-known wrestlers who later on after they retired, they all became great coaches themselves.

And these coaches, they raised a very large number of guys who are really good at wrestling. And then some of those coaches, they kind of switched over to fighting — let's say to grappling, to MMA — and they started coaching in combat sombo as well. And uh it just kept going like that, you know, it was moving forward step by step. And so we have a huge number of really great coaches. I believe this is one of the uh single most important keys to the success of Dagistani wrestlers and fighters — the coaching staff of Dagistan.

技术还是苦练？还是文化？

Lex： Is it more about technique or is it really just about serious incredibly hard work?

Khabib： Well, you have to look at the traditions because generally it's just the way it is in Dagistan. Everyone wrestles. Everyone fights. It's part of our culture. You know yourself. Fighting is like 50% wrestling.

Every parent wants their children to wrestle to be physically strong. Our approach to kids is that a child must be strong. They must be able to stand up for themselves, for their family. It's something that has traditionally always been in every single one of our clans, every family, every village. It's just in our blood.

千年历史的印记：门之门与高加索山脉

Lex： I mean, it's worth pointing out, and you've actually written about this, that this isn't just a recent thing. It's been going on for hundreds of years.

Khabib： Yes, that's right. These lands, Dagistan specifically, have seen powerful armies sweep through time and time again. Because of that, people here have always had to fight to survive, refusing to back down, refusing to give up their land or lose their identity, their homes, their villages here, their families and land.

If we look back a thousand years in history, maybe 500 years, there was the Kazar Kaganate, the Arabic caliphate, then the Iranian Empire — or the Persian Empire, I should say. Then uh the Russian Empire, Timour passed through there, the Mongols.

And if we look at the geographical location of Dagistan, for those who don't know, the Caucasus range runs across the whole region like a wall. And then it slopes down right where the Caspian lands are. So you've got the sea on the right, the mountains on the left, and the Caspian lowlands right here.

And uh there was a city there that's still standing today. It's one of the oldest cities in the world, not just in Russia. It's Derbent. It used to be called Babul Abuab. It means the gate of gates. Very major trade routes went through there. Very large armies passed through and it was bound to leave a mark on the people.

三十种语言的土地：文化的沉淀

Uh we have so many languages, more than 30 different languages, and people just don't understand each other. Take Islam and me. We have different languages, come from different backgrounds. Islam is L and I'm A. When we talk it's not like it's a dialect. We don't understand each other at all. But since Islam has been with us for nearly 25 years, he actually picked up some A over time.

But anyway, the deep history of the region — it all left its mark. It created many different languages and traditions. Basically, of course, Islam is our primary religion, but Dagistan has actually absorbed a lot of cultures and faiths. Even our food culture, it is incredibly rich. We have European and Asian and Caucasian, our own unique cuisine.

So on the people, on the people themselves, the last 1500 years of history have left a huge mark. If you're into history and you start reading about Dagistan, I think you'll get completely immersed and be amazed by what a unique place it is.

高地人的独立：帖木儿为何止步

So all of this left a huge mark. Look at the terrain. It's a coastal plane and then the mountains rise up. For instance, take someone like Timur. When he passed through with a huge army, he stayed in the Dagastan lands but never went up into the mountains. Why? Because you've got hundreds of thousands of troops, soldiers traveling with horses and supplies. If they had started going up into the mountains where it's cold and there are no roads, it would have been too tough for them.

So, the Highlanders somehow managed to stay independent. Uh, but the lands, the Caspian lands of Dagistan, they kept changing hands. Massive empires would roll in and all of that left a mark on the people.

The gate of the gates, Babul Abwab — historians wrote about it, say a thousand or 500 years ago. Great historians from various countries. People have written so much about Dagistan. It went by different names back then but they wrote a ton about this exact region. Many people, many empires invaded our land.

血液中的历史与身份

Lex： So, do you feel that inside you in your blood, your heart, like all of this history?

Khabib： Well, in the past, it's not like I really felt it. I knew Dagistan's history. But maybe with time, you start to see it in a whole new light. Every year, you change a bit on a mental and psychological level.

Now I understand. I really do. You cannot just um be born physically and mentally strong. Your environment shapes you no matter what, where you grew up, how you grew up, the conditions, and who you had around you. And after all, genetics are also a part of who you are. So when you add all this up, yeah, I just feel like all of this has come together inside me.

被遗忘的英雄与伊玛目沙米尔

Lex： It's interesting because in sports, we know many of the names of the great fighters and wrestlers. Yet, when it comes to war, there are so many people who fought, heroes, truly great warriors. Some we know by name, but most of them will never actually know and will never know. You write about Imam Shamil that he's an important figure for this region and a hero as well.

Khabib： Well, Imam Shamil, he was known for resisting an empire as huge as Russia. Dagistan is so small and he had so few people with him. How did he get famous? He got famous because he held out for a very long time. He didn't just resist for a couple of years. He was like a regular fighter, let's say a soldier for 10 years, and then when he became the leader, he went on for another 25 years.

So 35 years of his conscious life he spent fighting not just some random empire but what was then, if not the most powerful, definitely one of the strongest empires of that era. And that is what made him famous.

And so there are villages in Dagistan that deeply honor the memory of particular warriors who came from their villages, from their clan, from their ethnic group. But in world history, they're barely known. Like take Shamil — he's a leader, right, so everybody knows him. But there are plenty of heroes who've been forgotten. But yeah, their own people remember.

## 一、"匮乏经济学"的反直觉真相：稀缺不是限制，而是过滤器
大多数人读到"70人共用一个冷水澡"，会得出"艰苦锻造冠军"这种俗套结论。但哈比布真正说的是更微妙的东西——**匮乏的核心功能不是磨砺身体，而是筛选动机**。
他反问了一个关键问题："一个富爸爸会强迫自己的孩子每天带着淤青回家吗？富家子弟自己会愿意吗？"这句话戳穿了"苦难塑造冠军"的浪漫化叙事。真相是：**匮乏创造了一个动机自筛选系统**——只有那些饥饿到愿意承受非理性痛苦的人才会留下。达吉斯坦不是"生产"冠军，而是**在源头就淘汰了所有不够饿的人**。
这与硅谷创业圈的一个悖论惊人一致：斯坦福 MBA 的创业成功率远低于辍学者。不是因为教育有害，而是**退路越多，穿越"死亡谷"的意愿越低**。风投界甚至有个反向指标——如果创始人有 Plan B，就不投。达吉斯坦体系与之同构。
## 二、跨领域的意外连接：达吉斯坦 = 摔跤界的维也纳咖啡馆
哈比布提到达吉斯坦有 40-50 个格斗馆、密集的教练网络、清晰的晋升阶梯（村 → 达吉斯坦 → 北高加索 → 俄罗斯 → 世界）。他把这归因于"传统"和"教练体系"。

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] AI Risk Might Be Manageable Yet Still Be Mismanaged - Ryan Greenblatt
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"中间地带"：不是失控，而是"管得住却管不好"

大多数关于 AI 风险的讨论陷入了二元对立——要么是"AI 觉醒并终结人类"，要么是"一切都会没事"。Greenblatt 却撕开了一个几乎没人正视的第三条道路：问题在技术上完全可解，却在制度上被系统性搞砸。这是一个令人不适的洞察，因为它把风险从"技术未知"转移到了"人性已知"——而后者恰恰是我们最没办法通过研究突破来解决的部分。

一个让人意外的暗线是：他描述的"警告信号频率下降但严重性上升"的模式，恰好是反向的黑天鹅演化路径——不是罕见冲击变常见，而是常见小事故被驯化成罕见大灾难的伪装。这在系统性上比传统的"崩溃前夕"更危险，因为下降的频率会给决策者提供"我们在改善"的错觉。

二、跨领域连接：AI 治理的"COVID 同构"

Greenblatt 主动把 AI 风险与 COVID 类比，但他的类比其实比他说的更深。真正同构的不是病毒和 AI，而是"可管理的复杂问题遇上功能失调的社会响应机制"这个结构。可以进一步扩展到： - 2008 金融危机：风险模型知道尾部风险存在，但激励结构让所有人假装不知道 - 福岛核事故：技术上可预见的海啸高度，被组织政治覆盖 - 波音 737 MAX：MCAS 系统的问题工程师早已提出，被商业竞争压过

这些案例都指向一个更深的模式：在竞争压力下，"过拟合式修补"（overfitting fix）会系统性地击败"根因修复"，因为前者可测量、可展示、可用于季度汇报，而后者是隐形的、慢的、政治上不讨好的。AI 对齐领域正在重演这个古老剧本。

三、更颠覆的观察：透明度赤字才是"元风险"

表面上看，这段对话是在谈 reward hacking 和对齐。但真正的核心命题被 Greenblatt 悄悄埋在中间——"当前的公开透明度不足以支撑一场关于 reward hacking 是否被真正解决的公共讨论"。

这是一个隐藏的元层级问题：即便技术上有解，社会也没有认知基础设施去区分"真解"和"伪解"。这意味着 AI 安全的关键瓶颈可能不在实验室，而在认识论基础设施（epistemic infrastructure）——独立审计、公开评估基准、跨组织的科学共识机制。

一个反常识的推论：推动 AI 安全的最有效行动，可能不是研究新的对齐算法，而是建立让"我们真的解决了吗"这个问题可以被公开辩论的机制。这把 AI 安全从工程问题重新定义成了新闻业问题、监管问题、科学社会学问题——一个我们过去两百年一直在处理但从未处理好的老问题。

也就是说：AI 可能不会因为它的智能超过我们而毁掉我们，而是因为它的复杂度超过我们的集体制度性理解能力——而这个门槛，可能已经被跨过了。

📝 转录文本

灾难先于接管：警告信号的悖论

Before you take over the world, you cause damage on the scale of billions and tens of billions and hundreds of billions of dollars, and even people die, etc. And we — this does not lead to a solving of the alignment or shutting down AI development altogether.

I just feel like before the takeover happens, society is just like, "Holy [ __ ]. The AI just like killed a thousand people in order to increase quarterly profits," you know, or something like that.

But maybe this is too much hope — that we can at that point be like, "Okay, we have to solve alignment before we keep [going]. And we have to make sure we know that this thing will not happen again before we keep going."

Yeah, yeah, yeah.

场景一：地缘竞赛下的"管理但不解决"

So, I think it's plausible that what will happen is: we'll see a bunch of crazy, like, reward hacking warning shots of increasing severity. People be like, "Look, we need actual assurance that this problem is going to be solved — and solved in a way where you're not just papering over it. You're actually solving the underlying problem."

And then the question is going to be like: how costly will that actually be? How much will competitive pressures make it hard to do that?

So, a situation you could imagine is: both the US and China are like, "Whoa, we have these crazy reward hacking incidents. We basically know that we haven't remediated them in a way that actually would solve the underlying problem and will durably solve it, but we're in this insane geopolitical race, and it's kind of unclear whether the current situation will lead to a takeover. The arguments are kind of complicated. And also, the incidents — you know, they go down in frequency but increase in severity. Like, we could basically manage it. It's pretty bad. Ideally, we'd fix it, but, you know, it is what it is."

And then basically, we continue until a really late regime, and then takeover happens. That's, I think, one possibility.

场景二：过拟合式修复——你以为解决了

Another possibility is that it is remediated in a way that doesn't actually solve the underlying problem, but does reduce a bunch of the incidents in the wild — basically by overfitting. Or things analogous to overfitting. Like, you would just overfit.

You solved it, but you haven't actually —

You think you solved it, but you haven't actually solved it.

And I think that in that case, the thing we need is a really good scientific understanding of: "Did we actually solve it?"

透明度赤字：公共讨论的缺席

And unfortunately, I think that currently, the amount of public transparency into the development practices of AI companies are not sufficient to answer very basic questions about, you know: How are they solving issues with reward hacking? Are they overfitting? What's going on there?

And so I think we would just need a better — I think the current situation is, I would say, not really tenable to a regime where there's a thriving public discourse about whether or not reward hacking is being solved in a durable way.

Yeah.

And so I think we would need to move into a somewhat different world for me to feel good about that situation.

Right.

平庸之道：本可管理，却被搞砸

But it's not impossible for me to imagine this, and I think it's pretty plausible that we end up in a world where sort of really mundane [ __ ] is sufficient. Where it's just like: you spend a bunch of time fixing these problems. You put in a bunch of effort. You actually check that you've remediated reasonably. You have a bunch of evals. You are iterating reasonably well on these problems. And you actually have the sufficient transparency that the outside world can check.

And then in practice, that would be sufficient — but it just would be kind of expensive. It would slow things down. It would put some sand in the gears. It would require companies to do somewhat costly things. It would maybe require various targeted government interventions.

And then we just don't do that because the situation is a rushed [ __ ] show.

COVID 类比：可控问题的失控响应

It's just so easy for me to imagine the situation being totally manageable, but brutally mismanaged in practice — in the same way as, like, maybe COVID could have been avoided in the first place if the Chinese response to COVID was less of a cover-up and more of a pandemic response.

Yeah.

And similarly, I could imagine a world where the US response to COVID was way more functional. But just — sometimes the response to societal problems is extremely dysfunctional.

Yeah, yeah. If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Lex Clips] MMA vs street fighting - Khabib explains the difference | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、看不见的"相变点"：规则消失的瞬间，胜负逻辑完全反转

Khabib 那句话是整段故事的灵魂——"无论摔跤手多强，仰面朝天就是摔跤的终点，但那却是 MMA 的起点。"

这不是格斗心得，这是一句系统论的公理。同一个物理姿态（后背着地），在两个规则体系中被赋予了完全相反的估值符号：摔跤里那是 -1（判负），巴西柔术里那是 +1（进攻位）。当两个系统的边界重叠时，一方的"绝招"会以 1:1 的比例转换成对方的"送分动作"。

有意思的是，那位重量级更大、地区冠军级别的对手，他做对了每一件事——shot in、lift、take down——每一步都是摔跤教科书的完美执行。恰恰是他技术越娴熟，交付进 triangle 的路径就越顺滑。他不是败给了技术欠缺，而是败给了"过度专精"。

二、跨域连接：这是网络安全里最经典的失败模式

这一幕在其他领域反复上演，只是穿了别的马甲：

  • 金融：让市场效率最大化的量化算法，也是导致 2010 闪崩的加速器。
  • 网络安全：企业越自动化的防御机制，越是攻击者的杠杆点——SolarWinds 就是把"更新系统"武器化。
  • 生物学：抗生素越有效，耐药菌的选择压力越强。
  • 组织管理：越擅长执行既定流程的团队，遭遇范式转移时越难转身。

"某个封闭系统里的顶级选手"，几乎必然是"系统边界打开时的最大受害者"。这不是意外，是数学。你的所有优势都是在旧规则下累积的，当规则消失，累积得越多，失重得越彻底。

三、真正让人意外的观察：他承认自己"可视化"错了

绝大多数冠军谈起 visualization 都是神话叙事——"我早就看见了自己胜利的画面"。Khabib 在这里做了一件极其罕见的事：他坦白他清清楚楚地预演了兄弟输掉的场景，甚至已经在想着自己要下场替他打——然后现实完全反转。

这才是那一天的真正礼物。不是兄弟赢了，而是他的世界模型崩了。

在贝叶斯认知的意义上，Khabib 遇到的是一次高信息量的"预测失败"——先验概率被现实猛烈打脸。庸人的反应是把它当作 outlier 忽略掉；天才的反应是立刻问："我的模型哪里错了？"14 岁的 Khabib 用了不到一天时间：回家、告诉父亲、要求切换训练体系。这个更新速度，比triangle 本身更能预示他日后的统治力。

顺便说一句，值得留意的还有他父亲的回应——不是"好，你去练 MMA"，也不是"不行，继续摔跤"，而是"叠加，不是替换"：三天摔跤打底，三天格斗拓展。这与技术领域里最成功的架构迁移策略（strangler fig pattern）、以及职业转型里"T 型人才"的形成路径完全同构。真正强大的转型从不推倒重来，而是在旧地基上做维度扩展。

四、彩蛋：那场大雨

留意 Khabib 反复强调"下着大雨、一场倾盆大雨"。这个细节看似闲笔，却在潜意识层面强化了整段叙事的隐喻——规则消失的地方，天气都在提醒你：欢迎来到没有屋顶的世界。擂台是干燥的、有边界的、有裁判的。而街头，是湿的、开放的、只有后果的。他人生真正的转折，恰好发生在这两个世界的物理交界处。

📝 转录文本

The Question: Street vs. Sport

Lex: What is your understanding of the difference between the street fight and sports?

Khabib: There is a very big difference. I saw many fights where, if you put those same guys into sparring — in wrestling, MMA or combat — one guy could beat the other very easily. But the street is completely different. There are no rules, no referees, no points. You just fight there. And it's totally different.

The Turning Point (2002–2003)

I can say I actually had a major turning point in my life — let's say the one that, in terms of psychology, really changed my whole attitude towards MMA.

Back in 2002, 2003, my father kept me in wrestling. He trained MMA, combat sambo, but wanted me to stay in wrestling. My cousin, who was older than me by a couple of months, was training with my father. His freestyle wrestling was weak. So my father sent him to me, to the place where I was training. It was called the School of Higher Sports Mastery — the local guys from the city know this place.

The Conflict in the Gym

He came to practice and got into it with a guy in our gym who was heavier, maybe one class heavier. This guy was the best in his weight, winning Dagestan and the city too. So they got into a conflict. They were arguing.

My brother had just joined. He was new to our freestyle wrestling gym, right? But I knew the other guy well. They paired up and they got into it. Well, that's my brother, right? So the guy goes, "Let's meet up after." And they agreed, as we say, to step outside after the training.

The Fight in the Rain

I remember it was raining heavily. A real downpour. The guy brought his brother. I came with mine. We went outside and they started fighting one-on-one.

I remember he shot in, lifted, and took him down. Abdul Rahman — my brother — threw up a triangle, and he choked him out.

When we went out, I was thinking Abdul Rahman will lose to this guy. I even visualized it happening — the whole thing — like this guy beats him, and then I start fighting. Well, I'm not going there for my brother to lose. In my head, I was getting into a fight. But he threw him, locked up in a triangle.

For the first time, I saw with my own eyes how someone chokes another person with a triangle and they lose consciousness. Wow. They fought. He put him to sleep. We had to pull them apart — me and other guys.

Fight's over. Abdul Rahman won.

The Realization on the Way Home

And on the way home, I'm like, "Abdul Rahman, wow, you impress me." I came home and immediately told my father. I said — that was in 2002 or 3, if I'm not mistaken, I am 14 years old — I said: "I'm switching to combat sambo."

I said, "What Abdul Rahman did — the one he choked out — he's not just anyone in the gym. He's one of the best wrestlers, but he couldn't do anything."

The Father's Verdict

My father said: "You'll go to wrestling, but you'll come to me. I'll teach you. You'll learn techniques here, and so on. But I want you to gain wrestling skills."

I started going 3 days to train with my father, 3 days to wrestling.

Where Wrestling Ends, MMA Begins

And at that moment, I realized that no matter how strong the wrestler is, lying on the back is where wrestling normally ends. But MMA only begins there. And I was like — I thought — I need this. I need this mixed style. I realized this was for me.

I started going to my father's trainings. Despite that, he didn't let me — he didn't want me to do fighting. I think most people don't know this. My father wanted me to do freestyle wrestling or judo. But in my head, I already had this mixed style.

The Amateur Journey

I always wanted to compete. I was already getting tapes to watch. I always wanted to compete where there are no rules — where I could fully use my skills, maximum freedom. Yes: judo, freestyle, grappling, jiu-jitsu. More people knew jiu-jitsu than grappling.

After that, I switched, and from there my journey slowly started — which I had already begun. That's when I started the amateur journey. Then, when I started getting good results as an amateur, I realized that I can switch to pro and achieve success — symbol in combat.
