item.description:
## 一、看不见的"相变点"：规则消失的瞬间，胜负逻辑完全反转
Khabib 那句话是整段故事的灵魂——"无论摔跤手多强，仰面朝天就是摔跤的终点，但那却是 MMA 的起点。"
这不是格斗心得，这是一句**系统论的公理**。同一个物理姿态（后背着地），在两个规则体系中被赋予了**完全相反的估值符号**：摔跤里那是 -1（判负），巴西柔术里那是 +1（进攻位）。当两个系统的边界重叠时，一方的"绝招"会以 1:1 的比例转换成对方的"送分动作"。
有意思的是，那位重量级更大、地区冠军级别的对手，他做对了每一件事——shot in、lift、take down——每一步都是摔跤教科书的完美执行。**恰恰是他技术越娴熟，交付进 triangle 的路径就越顺滑。**他不是败给了技术欠缺，而是败给了"过度专精"。
## 二、跨域连接：这是网络安全里最经典的失败模式
这一幕在其他领域反复上演，只是穿了别的马甲：
- **金融**：让市场效率最大化的量化算法，也是导致 2010 闪崩的加速器。 - **网络安全**：企业越自动化的防御机制，越是攻击者的杠杆点——SolarWinds 就是把

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on retiring: I will never feel that rush again | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"预先怀念"：冠军的时间感是倒着走的

最反直觉的一点在于——Khabib 不是在退役之后才开始怀念，而是在最后一战正在进行的当下就已经在怀念它。这打破了普通人对"体验"的线性理解：我们以为先经历、再回忆、最后思念，但顶级运动员的时间轴是折叠的。他在出拳的那一刻，同时在场上、在记忆里、在告别中。

这其实是一种"预知性哀悼" (anticipatory grief)——通常出现在临终关怀病房里，家属知道亲人时日无多时的心理状态。Khabib 把这种通常属于死亡语境的心理机制，带进了竞技场。八角笼在那个夜晚不是运动场，而是一场提前进行的葬礼。这也解释了为什么他退役后如此坦然——真正的告别，早在铃声响起之前就已经完成了。

二、"能再来一份吗？"：食堂隐喻里藏着现代人的根本焦虑

Khabib 用了一个极其朴素、几乎有点滑稽的比喻——冠军的巅峰体验就像食堂里问"能再来一份吗？"，服务员说不行。这个比喻的天才之处在于，它把神圣的、史诗级的巅峰时刻，拉平到了日常琐碎的层面。

跨领域联想一下：这与神经科学中的"多巴胺基线漂移"惊人地吻合——大脑对峰值刺激会迅速重设基线，你上一次的高峰会成为下一次的起点，永远追不回同一种"第一次"。也与佛教的"无常"、与心理学家 Daniel Kahneman 的"体验自我 vs 记忆自我"理论形成呼应：你以为你在追求幸福，其实你在追求的是一个不可重复的神经化学事件。

而更深一层的洞察是：现代消费主义正是建立在"能再来一份"的幻觉之上——广告、社交媒体、成就系统都在承诺"下一个"能复现"上一个"的感觉。Khabib 作为一个宗教信仰虔诚的战士，反而在最资本主义化的体育（UFC）里参透了这个骗局：造物主没有把人类设计成能持续快乐的动物。

三、"次日清晨"才是真正的对手——运动员从未在擂台上被击败

最容易被忽略的一段是他描述登冠后第二天的场景：打包行李、飞回家、大家庆祝、然后所有人都散了。这段话里没有任何戏剧性，却是全篇最残酷的一段。

一个隐藏的系统性真相是：Khabib 描述的不是"退役综合症"，而是所有目标驱动型人生的结构性缺陷。这个模式在跨领域里反复出现： - 登山者登顶珠峰后的"高山抑郁" - 创业者IPO 敲钟后的空虚 - 博士生答辩通过后的"PhD blues" - NASA 阿波罗宇航员登月归来后的中年危机

它们共享同一个结构：你把整个自我压缩成一个"到达点"，而到达之后，那个自我就没地方去了。

而 Khabib 意外给出的解药藏在他的用词里——他反复说"每一个动作、每一个瞬间，我都在深处感受它"。这暗示了一个悖论：只有当你在过程中就已经在告别时，你才真正拥有过它。那些第二天感到空虚的人，恰恰是在过程中忘记感受、只顾追逐结果的人。运动员训练一生追求那个瞬间，但真正救赎他们的，不是抵达瞬间，而是在瞬间里同时经历"拥有"和"失去"的能力——这是竞技场教给他的禅。

📝 转录文本

场上就已开始的告别

And I heard or maybe read somewhere that you said you were already starting to miss it while the fight was still going on.

Yeah. Inside the octagon. I knew it would never happen again. I stepped in there and I just took it all in. I was fighting and just every single moment, every moment, every single move, I felt it deep down. And in my head, I already knew this was the final run. Everything I'd been doing my entire life, it all came down to this, that competitive rush. I'll never feel that anywhere else. I knew deep down this was my last fight.

只属于那一夜的感觉

What kind of feelings were those?

I've never felt anything like that again. Those feelings could only be experienced right there on that exact day, that very evening with that opponent inside that cage. I've never had them before that night and never had them since. And I don't think I'll ever be able to feel that way again.

I think Bouvisar said that these feelings — standing on the podium becoming an Olympic champion — you only feel them in that moment when they announce you. You step onto the podium. That's it. They announced you. You won. You live. That's it. You only feel them there. You don't feel them anywhere else. And athletes live for those feelings. They train their whole lives for them.

一生中只有一两次的巅峰

Do you ever think about that? That in our lives, if we're lucky, we only get maybe one or two moments like that — at that uh that absolute peak.

Yes. Yes. Yes. Very rarely. It's so rare.

幸福是什么？——短暂的感受

What is happiness really? The way I see it is when you experience certain feelings for a very short time. You can't be constantly happy — like you achieve something and then you're happy for years. It just doesn't work that way. The Almighty didn't build us that way.

You get there even when you become a champion and you fully feel that moment. You win, and then you wake up the next morning and that's it. Is that all I worked for? There's nothing more like that.

"能再来一份吗？"——食堂里的隐喻

You know, like — can I have seconds? You can't have seconds. It's like in our cafeteria. Can I have seconds?

So — well, you become champion. You win. Then you wake up the next day. That's it. Your daily routine continues. It doesn't end. You've already got different things going on, different problems, other tasks now. And you're like, it all went by so fast.

冠军的第二天清晨

Then you wake up the next day, pack your bags, head to the airport, fly out, land back home, everyone's celebrating, and just like that, the next day, everyone's gone. That's it.

item.title: [GoldRepublic Global] Francis Hunt: Japan's Debt Crisis Could Send Silver to $330
item.dc:creator: GoldRepublic Global
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、日本不是"东方的孤岛"，而是美元帝国的隐藏心脏起搏器

大多数投资者把日本国债当作一个"太平洋另一端的地方新闻"，但 Francis 揭示的真相是反直觉的：美国霸权的强度上限，是由日本能否维持其债券市场决定的。这就像一个人的心脏节律器藏在陌生人的胸腔里——你的生命体征取决于一个你从不关心的人。

这里有一个让人意外的观察：日本从二战后就从未完全恢复财政主权（Prof Werner 的论点）。也就是说，我们今天看到的"日美金融联动"，本质上是 1945 年那份投降协议在 81 年后仍在收取的复利。Bessant 出面为日元"喊话"不是外交礼节，而是债主对自家抵押品的紧急护理——因为如果日元继续贬值、JGB 收益率继续冲高，日本将被迫抛售美债，Hotel California 的"永远无法真正退房"规则就会当场破产。

二、"加州旅馆效应"——市值幻觉是这个时代最大的定价谎言

Francis 讲了一个跨领域的绝妙类比：美国国债市场 = Richard Hart 的 Hex 微币盘。这个 Hex 代币用"锁仓 555 天"的话术让持币者变成永久买方、消灭卖方，从而把市值撑到 770 亿。而 24 万亿美元的美债市场本质上运行着同样的机制——只不过锁仓的"话术"叫地缘政治、swap line、以及"你敢卖我就冻结市场"。

这里有一个跨领域连接值得深思：加州教师退休基金曾想卖掉自己借出去的 1.2 万亿国债，结果被回复"我们给你一个借款额度吧"。这在心理学上叫斯德哥尔摩综合症的债权版本——你借出去的钱，反过来要以求助者的姿态才能拿回一部分。同样的模式在 CV-19 的健康叙事、次贷危机的银行救助、乃至 AI 军备竞赛中的"太大而不能倒"逻辑中不断重演。这不是金融现象，这是一种通用的权力语法：制造不对称的进出门。

三、被忽视的隐藏关联：AI 泡沫、保险业、和你的宠物医疗

Francis 抛出了一个几乎没人在讨论、但极其锋利的推演链：Nvidia 借 5000 亿 → 保险公司被诱导买入私募债 → 私募债爆雷 → 保险公司无法赔付你的车险宠物险 → 保险业被迫救助 → 全民买单。

这意味着：你为宠物买的医疗险，正在悄悄成为 AI 军备竞赛的抵押品。这是"太大而不能倒"逻辑的最新变种——过去是通过住房抵押贷款绑架社会，现在是通过 AI 的"存在主义焦虑"（"打不赢中国我们就完了"）来把整个保险资产负债表绑架进去。

四、Pyrrhic Victory——白银 330 美元不是致富预言，而是文明降级的读数

这是全场最反直觉的观点：Francis 预测的"金银比跌破 10、白银冲 330、黄金再加一个零"不是白银的胜利，而是记账单位的死亡。金银比从来不是金属的比值，而是"人类信任度"的温度计——当它跌破 10，说明人类对法币的信任正在归零。

跨领域连接：这与生物学上的"极端热梯度反应"有相似之处——当环境剧变，最简单、最古老、最不依赖复杂系统的生命形式反而胜出（例如冰河期的苔藓，或大灭绝后的蟑螂）。黄金和白银是货币宇宙里的苔藓和蟑螂——它们赢，不是因为它们进化了，而是因为周围复杂精妙的信用生态崩溃了。

所以 Francis 才说"要咬住下唇，不要为我们的欢呼太大声"。这句话你可能一带而过，但它其实是整场访谈最重要的一句情绪指令：真正的资本保全者，未来将不得不学会在他人的废墟上安静地富有。这是一种前所未有的心理挑战——你以为在打投资的仗，其实要打的是道德姿态的仗。

五、一个被埋在末尾的关键信号：南非白金矿的股权正在被"提前拿到剧本的人"扫货

BlackRock 又买入 5% Impala Platinum；Zelensky 及其背后的富豪集团掌握 Northam Platinum 的控股权益；南部非洲提供全球 80% 白金供应。这不是"投资组合多元化"这么简单——这是同一批人在为"下一次商品级稀缺事件"提前占位。当稀有金属的产地被少数具有情报优势的资本吸收，其价格发现机制事实上已经在正式行情启动前就完成了。

你可以问自己一个不舒服的问题：如果 BlackRock 正在悄悄买白金，而你在等 CPI 数据决定买不买白银——那你和他们的信息时差是几年？

📝 转录文本

开场：全球金融体系的"手拉手"结构

Particularly if you're talking about the hegemony, which is the US. They're only as strong as the Japanese can hold their game together. Because if Japan collapses, they will be a forced seller of treasuries. At some point they'd have to let them either sell to stop them from collapsing, or they would just freeze the treasury markets and say no one can sell.

It's ring-a-ring-a-rosies, a pocket full of posies, a tissue, a tissue, we all fall down. So we've all got our hands in the other guys' pockets and we're dancing and skipping around. We're all intertwined. The weakest heart to fall, they will drag the other down by scale. That's what part of the subprime crisis on the bank.

Is there a more bullish macro chart? Not for me, anywhere in the world. So if you ask me the question, are you still silver bullish? 100%. And we've also said beyond the 333, we are expecting a four-digit and a single gold-silver ratio for at least one day. One moment in time, you will fall through the 10. I just have no idea what capital will be doing, but I imagine it'll be doing something pretty interesting, too. And gold, wow.

主持人开场

Welcome to the Microscopic Podcast presented by Gold Republic. My name is Alexander Onuf, I'm your host, and today I have the great honor of welcoming back Francis Hunt, the market sniper. And today is the 12th of August, 2026. Welcome back, Francis. Good to see you.

Thank you for having me back. Glad to be here.

Francis, the last time we spoke was around May, I think. And there's a lot of recurring topics that are pretty obvious. One of them is now plastered all over the headlines, on prints, online, TV, wherever you want to see this. But this is nothing new to you. Since I know you, you've been covering this, and this has been a couple of years, but I think you've covered this since maybe 2020, and I'm talking here about the Japanese bond crisis, the carry trades, the yen, and you've been my — I think for my side at least I can say — the most consistent commentator on this.

We had an interview I think that was in April of last year 2025 if I'm mistaken, or July, sorry, July. And we talked about this almost the whole episode and this was one of the least watched interviews with you. And I was quite surprised. I was like, well, how is this possible? This is such an important topic, but it doesn't get the attention it deserves. So let me maybe start with this. How would you then resume maybe for someone who hasn't been following this since some time in a very short condensed way if possible, what this is all about and why it matters so much and why it's not covered as much as it should?

为什么西方听众忽视日本

Yeah, so the minute we talk about Japan, it feels for most — we're dictated by the Western world. Our audience is English language speaking, which means the predominance is Northern Hemisphere. And if you talk about investable people, you're going to have to say, I mean, my YouTube channel will be about 53% US. Then there'll be probably half that will be my UK audience, and then each time half again, you know, you throw in Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and maybe a tiny bit of South Africa.

So that's our audience group audience group, and we're actually talking about the West when we talk about Japan, but it's of course far far East and very much removed. And most people have never traveled even to Japan, so it has no consciousness — sense of consciousness. And people also forget that it was the second largest economy after the US for a very, very long time before the full emergence of China. And you know, the whole history of World War II and all of that, it's very well interwoven into Western society.

It never got its fiscal freedom back after the surrender of World War II. It is not a sovereign on all matters state anymore. That comes out of Prof Werner who we were lucky enough to interview. I know you've been looking to get a hold of him. And it comes out of history in essence.

中短期展望：黄金在区间震荡

So that's short-term what's happening. You're probably more interested in, "Okay, hotshot, what happened next if you're claiming you've played it so well?" Well, this time we have. We don't always get it right. I think you're going to remain in range for the rest of this year unless — so there's wild card over here.

But broadly, once you do this, a lot of people that just think you go straight back to melt up bull. The circumstances that were here are not recreated immediately here. We are back some when we were much earlier in the run. You've had a reset of retail. There's a lot of really angry paid off people. I see it in my YouTube comments that only started buying metals somewhere up here and got destroyed on the waves of selling, you know? We all assume people are smart and watching our channels and getting in at the right times, not advisory, you know, all usual stuff and know what a stop loss is and do that. No, there's a lot of people that are just careering in like a casino.

So this freshened up the precious metals for me in terms of soft hands being eliminated to a large degree. There's not much retail involvement. I think if you talk to most of the bullion dealers, the big buying is central banks and institutions. Retail is not way straight back to all-time highs that were probably happening in January of this year, as they were getting their Christmas bonuses. I don't think that's where we are. So I think we drift up a little and then we might — it depending on the wild card of a demand destroying event.

AI 资本狂潮与"太大而不能倒"

Because I do feel, you know, Nvidia's borrowing 500 billion, you know, a 6 trillion — is it 5 or 6 trillion? I can't even keep up. It's getting so big so fast. It's now borrowing half a trillion. I mean, loans of half a trillion by corporation. I mean, it's absolutely obscene. Everyone was thinking, you know, Amazon getting another 25 billion was a lot of money. And then Nvidia shows up and getting a, you know, all these partners together to borrow 500 billion, half a trillion. I mean, I don't think there's real economic value add in the splurge of just extreme number.

And quite clearly China's doing a lot more in a lot lesser number, and it's proving equally effective with you seeing cold wallets being drained with Kimmi, I think it is, whatever version that they're doing. So I don't think it's just about who spends the biggest money. You know, the Americans applied that to the military and defense complex, fine. I don't think in AI that all money is going to mean a bit the biggest spend.

But it is a way of making it a too big to fail industry because it's existential. We got to beat China, otherwise, you know, we might die as a country. Create the fear so that they can socialize and bailouts and do bailouts potentially and involve insurance companies and do damage to other industries that you and I have insured our car, health, our pets, or whatever. And now suddenly because their premium investments, they're front-loaded with premiums. They invest, they've been suckered into investing into private debt which they were sold a turkey. It's all part of a co-opted scam so that they then damage the insurance industry, then the insurance industry needs bailouts because they can't pay for your crashed car. So that's how you collateralize your particular industry into being too big to fail, and I'm pretty sure they're going to engineer that. And that means more fiat debasement, and that means more gold pumpamentals.

对"20K 黄金"预测的怀疑

So super bull market I just don't think we finished the year. A lot of people got really excited by the 20K calls. And I think that's, call option spreads that are probably going on. Because if you have unlimited risk, you have to have a lot of collateral. If you then buy a call higher up, even cheaply, but with a strike way out the money, you're allowed to get much higher percentage of your capital back to utilize elsewhere. The minute you sell options, you have to have a lot of margin if you've got unlimited risk. So spreads reduce that margin substantially.

So I think that most of that — it's, you know, I'm open to a conspiracy with the best of them. But does someone know that by the end of the year you'll be 20K? Technically, right now with what I'm seeing, I'm not seeing end of the year 20K. You know, let's just show you where 20K is. Ha, you know. Let's keep going. Okay? It's here. And we're mid-August. So, you've got September, October, November, and half of December, you know, Christmas Day, nothing's happening then. No, not in that time frame.

And some people are getting their time frames wrong and turning it into a little bit of "I'll be the biggest bull. I'll — a pissing match throwing out the bigger number." My suggestion is technical analysis should justify a geometric pattern. At the moment, I don't have one on gold for you. I do have on silver 330. And we've had our pause at our second interim, which was the $100 run and pullback in a similar falling wedge, which is silver.

白银的当前结构

And it's also responded, so I should show you silver before I hand back. There it is. And we saw also this was a little head and shoulder, by the way, where you had that secondary spill. Down into this. This is also just coming out for its break. And this is not unbelievable momentum. You can see a little selling wick down to there. It's not unbelievable volume. You know it, we do volume candles. That's up there. So it's not super fat. It's not like this guy over here, which was your blow-off top. Volume. So nothing about that says you're ripping to 300 before the end of summer, you know, by 1st September.

I would love it to be that way, by the way. I would say there's a 10% chance, there's not a 0% chance, but as someone who wants to trade the meat of the probabilities and are going to stay in that range rather than seek headlines, I'm going to say you're not going to run the 120 this side of New Year in my expectation. I would say it's a 50% likelihood you're going to finish in the range between the lows of 55 and the 121 probably around 60, 70s, possibly get into the 80s, somewhere in that range.

And there is also a possibility, it also has to be borne in mind that if we get that demand-destroying debt event, that we first dip below this falling wedge, you could go lower shortfall, much like CV19 crash, much like subprime crash. Straight away you reverse. So subprime we went from $1,003 to $698 in 08 and then we smashed up to 1927. So it's often a technical flush out to the downside to kill everybody at the weakest, most vulnerable moment and to get them all sold out before it then pumps and runs. So this doesn't feel like that moment. I'm still waiting for the possibility of another washout. You can go up and have a sharp stab that panics everybody where everybody thinks it's the end of the world. Highly emotional people jump out kind of like the CV19 as well. A lot of people were in immense fear, they didn't know if they were going to live the next three or four years. They thought they were going to fall dead like the guy they saw in China that just toppled over. You know, there was a lot of extreme angst. Let's just leave it there. That's when you want to be buying and if we get that opportunity, I'll truly load up the trucks with blue pots and even maybe some leverage trades.

白金：突破在前、结构独特

Mhm. And what about platinum then in that relationship as well to gold in specially?

I'll show you — I've actually taken some platinum longs right now. As I mentioned we really trade. This is the only one I was really comfortable with taking into the CPI. And we think there's a nice continuation pattern. So platinum went up and it broke out. It broke — the white metals actually broke first before silver and gold. Platinum and palladiums came out of the falling wedge first. I can show you that weekly if you want.

And then on the lower time frame as I'm mentioning let's just show you that. This had come out for some time. Over here it went sideways you were breaking out really early. And then on the lower time frame they didn't continue to go up like silver and gold they formed a little bit of a continuation pattern. So going into the CPI we think that's continuation. So you're broken out. We had a couple of entries. You can see the entries here. We've got our stops down there. It's a little bit more wiki and a little bit more bigger spreads. You have to be a lot more careful trading platinum. It can be more sketchish. You can pay a higher spreads. The juice has got to be worth the squeeze. I prefer to be in gold and silver generally but we'll take off some of those up top there for a tactical trade and some of them we'll leave on for a little bit of outperformance.

So that's where we are at the moment with platinum. It was the first to move and actually it took it — went sideways and squared up quite nicely to get the energy to break out.

白金的稀有性与"提前拿到剧本的人"

It's very unique very rare and I'll add to that — BlackRock, BlackRock, BlackRock has bought another 5% of Impala Plats which it has been accumulating at quite a rapid rate. And of course Zelensky and his billionaire backers owned a quarter controlling stake in Northam Platts, another South African platinum miner. So you've got two South African platinum miners that have got the interest of very interesting people that tend to have the script before you and I do. So I personally am — I see it as an endorsement of our view that platinum has a very, very bright future, and at some point on thin liquidity could scream up even faster than a silver or gold.

Once, you know, its uniqueness and its place is need. It's very rare. It's exceedingly rare. So just, you know, the relationship between finding good silver and gold, I think we got to seven or eight ounces of silver for every gold is mined, and then for every 16 oz of gold, you get 16.5, you get 1 oz of platinum. So you can multiply that out for yourself if you want a silver to platinum ratio, but it's an exceedingly rare metal.

And the one — Veltera, which is the old Amplats — Anglo American Oppenheimer and Co., the same people that bailed out of diamonds now that diamonds have been properly slammed into nothingness and gave someone else the bag to hold. Now known as Veltera, that's 38% — that single mining holdings of Veltera and the old Amplats is 38% of global. One mining group is 38% almost 40% of all platinum provided in the world. So it's quite a bit bigger than Northam and Amplats as well.

And that Southern African conurbation that include Zimbabwe into South Africa is 80% of global supply. And Russia weighs in at 11, and the rest — you Canada, America, little bits and bobs, fractals here and there.

南非政治与能源风险

And so, what would you assess on the risk of — I mean you in South Africa there's also the political risk, there's also the bit of instability sometimes also based on the energy grid and these kind of things. How would you assess that and based on being cautious maybe about investing in the mining company that is or just in derivatives concerning that?

When the big statist people are involved and it's their money, it's amazing how things work just fine. And that's what's happening. In fact, there hasn't been grid shutdowns or they used to call it load shedding where you would have a certain number of hours a day where they would just switch off.

What's tended to happen — and this is the effect of unintended consequences — is that the wealthy end of Southern Africa and, you know, in both my properties in Southern Africa, we have full solar and independence and batteries. And that just pushes you further towards self-reliance and I'm good with that. I want that everywhere I live. And what's tended to happen is the best quality electricity customer is leaving. And then the townships that rely on the grid and don't have the investment capital to put on top of the shanty town expensive solar panels end up being the customer that Eskom keeps.

So it's amazing how quickly since the solar uptake has ramped up and even shopping centers have generators, solar panels, you name it. Suddenly, they are — no no no no, they don't want to lose customers anymore and there's no more load shedding. We haven't had for a few years now. And that was at one point threatening the mining industry because obviously it's energy intensive. So those aren't matters anymore and I don't expect them to be whilst the big money is in there. And there was never was any reason why there should be. It was just incompetence, lack of maintenance from a ruling party that should really not be given the responsibility of managing a country. They're quite incompetent and very corrupt, but enough people have got involved to ensure that the key things remain functional.

白银：Gisele Bündchen 之美依然在场

And so, now quoting you on your — on your, let's say, on the way you characterize silver being the Gisele Bündchen of all assets, is it still something that you're really fully bullish on, has your spotlight, you have the same convictions as we talked last time?

Yes, and it helps to remind people of the big picture. I'd love to take you into the long-term picture with silver one more time because this will help explain not only what we expect, but what's already happened pretty well. It's doing everything it should be doing. We highlighted that it's in one of the largest technical structures. Most people are forcing it into what is known as a cup and handle.

Let's see your screen, Francis.

bring it up. I'm still getting it all nice and —

Yeah, that's okay.

So, we'll share and you can watch me do that. But it's typically characterized by traditional technical analysts as a cup and handle. This is the chart. I've done it by volume. You can see how fat the recent volume was. I'll just switch off my jaw.

But we have different framing and that is part and parcel of the volatility funnel-based focus that we have and it gives us a massive advantage in our opinion. We were getting involved a lot sooner because we were understanding the critical moment was coming a lot sooner while other people were waiting for major technical resistances to fall, we were already largely in, which is part and parcel as to why we were pretty lucky with the original move as well. Let me just see if that's going to come up. I need to get I just have to make one adjustment. 81428. So there's a slight data glitch on this high. You did in fact trade 50 on the Hunt Brothers high of 18. No relation, I promise.

So this is always been our model. This is a 6 month. So this is a huge time frame that we are actually trading. People have to understand that each candle is half a year. It's massive. And this is essentially a bull market from the depression era 30s all the way into 80. And then from 1980, I was wearing much younger clothes back then, I can tell you Alexi, all the way through to this period and that triggering events of January 24, that's 6 months in January 24 when we called for the triggering and there was a smaller time frame squeezing here. We were long at 25.

And that triggering event, we've so far benefited for the run up to there. We got out at 111s 117s to 111s on our silver longs. We are still investors. We've never sold silver. We only accumulate on blue pod. I'm talking about leverage trading. That is a quite a big rejection that essentially is the falling wedge structure. The first 6 months of it and this is part of a degree of recovery in this pattern. But that's where the 330 comes from.

$330 白银目标位的技术推导

And you are at 66. So you still have the bulk of this move to come. You know, 66 from 25 you've only really done around 30 dollars of the move so far. If I just de-log this for a second so that everyone can just understand how much more we expect to come. This is a very flat pattern now. 330 is up there. So if you can manage focusing on this pattern that is now looking very, very flat. A squeezed continuation pattern like that. You are here.

And we are saying to you at some time in the future, not so distant, but we're not putting a long stop on that. You're going to trade 330. That's one heck of a move going from 66 all the way back through 100, all the way to 150, 75, 200, 210, 250, 275, 300, 320, 330. It's a long, long, old way. And that's the gift you're still playing for. And this is what you've taken out the market so long, so far. So I mean, it's an unbelievable risk reward. 24 hours. The stop loss, the entry to the stop loss. As I've already mentioned, we squeeze that tighter on a primer.

Is there a more bullish macro chart? Not for me, anywhere in the world. So if you're asking me the question, are you still silver bullish? 100%. I just have no idea what pattern it will be doing, but I imagine it'll be doing something pretty interesting, too. And gold, wow.

金银比跌破 10 的"皮洛士式胜利"

And we've also said beyond the 333, we are expecting a four-digit and a single gold-silver ratio for at least one day. One moment in time, you will fall through the 10 for a 9.99 or lower on the gold-silver ratio for silver. And that will likely be at a moment when it is a four-digit number, and gold will be one extra zero on it, approximately, for a 10x on silver. So that will be a very high number, I'd imagine. A very high number indeed.

But that will rather than being a function of precious metals is entirely a function of the debt and fiat base collapse and the measuring stick of the dollar and the other westernized currencies all in a state of huge decline. And they would — that's why they go down together, as well.

So I don't think it's going to be a joyous moment for many. You know, it's going to be a quite a Pyrrhic victory for us as precious metals. We're going to have to bite our bottom lip and not scream too loud about our hoorays and everything because there's going to be pain and social unrest around on a grand old scale. So, as I say, it's it's that kind of prediction. You know, you just got to do it, but be humble about it.

时间框架与"长止损"

And the time frame here, like you pointed out to up to like to say 2040, is that random or is it not something that you can really say?

The long stop is ridiculously far away to not worth mention. We close, that means something's gone wrong if it hasn't made there. So we have something called a very long stop. Now, normally it's being applied on much shorter time frame charts. When you apply it to the duration here, it's very far out.

But if you look at what was achieved, we made second interim in literally three or four candles. You broke here two three four five six. Depending when we go back to the highly impulsive state. I wouldn't like to put a time on it, but I think sooner or rather than later, but it's actually a dollar story, not a silver story, as I keep saying. What you're really asking is when does the whole debt bomb blow up that currencies become a meaningless benchmark of measure, so that silver ends up at insane currency number. That's the question you're truly asking and I'm not sure that this particular doesn't give us enough to come for me to commit to that.

Although it's progressed incredibly well and has already done first interim and second interim and the remaining part is to finish to target which usually goes in melt up stage. So it is a crisis that's coming for this to be fulfilled and it could even be you know, you could have two three candles and then boom, one big surge right through there. That could take you into never mind 330 but in in a six-month period you could trade from 100 to 200, 300 and even end up at 700 in a single six-month period and who knows possibly beyond. So in that single candle that's when it happens but that's also the turmoil, the resets, the everything else.

收尾

Great. Thanks a lot Francis. Unfortunately, it's the end of our time. Just like precious metals, it's precious for you and me. I appreciate all the insights, the charts, the explanations and obviously being able to talk to you, pick your brain for an hour. So thanks a lot Francis.

Absolute pleasure. People who want to follow me on the market sniper, it's a reset season you're preparing for. Traditional financial advice does not look after you at all well for that and we're here to help you build wealth, protect that wealth and broaden out your optionality across multitudes of jurisdictions so that you are not tied to the Western collapse that is surely coming our way.

On this note, I have also linked up everything in the description. Thanks a lot Francis.

Absolute pleasure. Bye for now.

[music]

Mhm.

item.description:
## 一、日本不是"东方的孤岛"，而是美元帝国的隐藏心脏起搏器
大多数投资者把日本国债当作一个"太平洋另一端的地方新闻"，但 Francis 揭示的真相是反直觉的：**美国霸权的强度上限，是由日本能否维持其债券市场决定的**。这就像一个人的心脏节律器藏在陌生人的胸腔里——你的生命体征取决于一个你从不关心的人。
这里有一个让人意外的观察：**日本从二战后就从未完全恢复财政主权**（Prof Werner 的论点）。也就是说，我们今天看到的"日美金融联动"，本质上是 1945 年那份投降协议在 81 年后仍在收取的复利。Bessant 出面为日元"喊话"不是外交礼节，而是**债主对自家抵押品的紧急护理**——因为如果日元继续贬值、JGB 收益率继续冲高，日本将被迫抛售美债，Hotel California 的"永远无法真正退房"规则就会当场破产。
## 二、"加州旅馆效应"——市值幻觉是这个时代最大的定价谎言
Francis 讲了一个跨领域的绝妙类比：**美国国债市场 = Richard Hart 的 Hex 微币盘**。这个 Hex 代币用"锁仓 555 天"的话术让持币者变成永

item.title: [Lex Clips] France vs Brazil vs Spain: Greatest soccer team of all time | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三支"完美之队"背后的隐藏结构

一、"影子球员"才是完美的真正密码

对话里最容易被忽略的一句话是——"beyond those superstar names, they were also very strong players who kind of stayed in the shadow of those stars"。表面上我们在谈 2002 巴西的罗纳尔多、里瓦尔多、罗纳尔迪尼奥"3R"，但真正让这支队伍接近"完美"的，是那些甘愿站在阴影里的埃德米尔森、克莱伯森、卢西奥。一支"完美之队"的判定标准，不是它拥有多少太阳，而是它能容纳多少愿意做月亮的人。 这与硅谷创业圈"10x 工程师神话"恰好相反：真正稳态的高绩效系统，星光度分布必须是不均匀的，且低星光位必须由高能力者填充——这是一个反直觉的"能力浪费"，却是稳定性的来源。

二、1998、2002、2008–2012 —— 一个隐藏的"四年脉冲"

法国 1998、巴西 2002、西班牙 2008–2012，这三个时间点之间的间距不是巧合。足球国家队的"完美窗口"，本质上是一个国家青训体系约 8–12 年前投入的延迟兑现。 法国 98 的黄金一代来自 1980 年代末克莱枫丹青训学院的重建；巴西 02 的爆发来自 90 年代初俱乐部体系向欧洲输出球员的成熟；西班牙那一波则源于 2000 年前后 La Masia 与巴斯克青训哲学的融合。换句话说，你现在看到的"梦之队"，是十年前某个默默无闻的教练在给 12 岁孩子讲传球线路时种下的种子。 这跟经济学中的"资本折旧曲线"、跟半导体行业的"制程投资滞后"是同一个数学结构——只是我们习惯把它当成"天赋的偶然"。

三、"接近完美"这个措辞，泄露了一个哲学秘密

Lex 和 Khabib 都用了 "close to perfect"，而不是 "perfect"。这是一种非常重要的克制。 在复杂系统里，真正达到"完美"的系统反而是脆弱的——它意味着零冗余、零容错、零进化空间。2008–2012 的西班牙就是最好的反例：他们真的"过于完美"地掌握了 tiki-taka，以至于当对手（2014 荷兰、智利）找到破解方式时，整个体系瞬间崩塌。一个跨领域的连接：这与生物进化中的"过度特化"如出一辙——特化到极致的物种，环境一变就灭绝；而那些"够好但不完美"的通才，反而穿越了多个纪元。 法国 98 之所以在讨论中被排在最前，可能正因为它在天才与冗余之间保留了那一点点"不完美"——齐达内的艺术与德尚的粗粝并存，这种张力才是长寿的秘方。

啊哈时刻：我们讨论"史上最强"时，其实一直在讨论一个错误的问题。真正值得问的是：一支球队的"完美"，究竟是它某一刻的巅峰高度，还是它抵御崩塌的深度？ 前者属于博物馆，后者才属于历史。

📝 转录文本

讨论国家队层面的"史上最强"

as the national team level. Um, you could pick France in 1998.

1998 法国 与 2002 巴西

Yes, that 1998 France team is very close to a perfect team. And also, um, 2002 Brazil — in 2002 they were extremely strong.

Yes, you had Ronaldo, you had Ronaldo, Ronaldo, Roberto Carlos, Kafu, right? You had Emerson, you had, um, Clayverson, I think, Rookie Jr., Lucio, Edmilson.

Um, and beyond those superstar names, they were also very strong players who kind of stayed in the shadow of those stars.

阴影中的强者

Stayed in their shadow.

西班牙的黄金时代

So, Brazil 2002, France 1998, and then there was then later Spain from Euro 2008, the 2010 World Cup, and Euro 2012.

At period 2, Spain, the Spanish national team was close to perfect.

item.title: [Business of Sport] The €4.2bn Play: What do the Owners of F1 have Planned for MotoGP?
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的悖论：MotoGP 明明"更好看"，却卖不动

一个反直觉的事实：从纯粹的观赏性和肾上腺素维度看，MotoGP 客观上比 F1 更刺激——超车更多、身体暴露、物理对抗真实可见。但恰恰是这个"更 raw、更危险、更真实"的属性，反而成了它商业化的枷锁。

这里藏着一个媒介悖论：当代娱乐经济奖励的不是"真实的极限"，而是"可被叙事化的极限"。F1 车手戴上头盔坐进碳纤维壳里，看似把人"藏起来了"，但正因为赛道上看不见人，Netflix 才有空间在场外"造人"——《Drive to Survive》本质上是在填补 F1 的视觉空缺。MotoGP 反过来——车手在赛道上已经把自己交出去了，反而没留下"叙事真空"给内容团队去填。

跨领域连接：这和拳击 vs UFC 的品牌困境很像。UFC 在赛场上更暴力、更"真实"，但拳王梅威瑟单场收入长期碾压任何 MMA 选手——因为拳击的"缓慢"和"仪式感"给了叙事发酵的空间。过于饱和的感官体验，反而挤压了故事的生长缝隙。

二、Liberty 的真正赌注不是美国市场，而是"成本帽的政治博弈"

表面上大家都在谈 Drive to Survive 复制、谈美国扩张。但你仔细看 Charlie 那段近乎愤怒的独白——真正的战场是让制造商同意成本帽。

这里有个几乎没人点破的隐藏结构：MotoGP 的车队为什么只值 5000 万美元，而 F1 垫底车队值 15 亿？ 差价不是流量、不是明星、不是转播权——是"经营确定性"的资本化溢价。没有成本帽，任何投资人买车队都是在买一张"永远可能被军备竞赛拖垮"的期权，估值自然被砍到骨头。有了成本帽，车队瞬间从"烧钱黑洞"变成"可预测现金流资产"，估值倍数就能从 1x 跳到 20x。

出人意料的观察：Ezpeleta 在采访里说"多花 1000 万欧只能快 0.05 秒"——这句话看似在辩护"不需要成本帽"，Charlie 一针见血指出这是special pleading（自利式辩护）。真相是：成本帽的价值从来不在于省钱，而在于把不确定性从资产负债表上抹掉。这个原理在私募股权、SaaS 估值、甚至学术终身教职制度里都成立——可预测性本身就是一种被严重低估的资产类别。

三、私募的"20 年 8 倍"其实是失败——一个反常识的估值真相

Bridgepoint 从 5 亿卖到 40 亿，账面 8 倍回报，听上去很美。但 David 一句话就把这层皮撕开了：20 年 = 三个基金周期 = 通过"接续基金"内部倒手 = 事实上没退出。同期体育资产整体涨了 10 倍以上，这意味着 Bridgepoint 实际上是 underperform 了整个赛道。

这里有个所有做投资的人都该记住的洞察：在牛市里跑输 beta 的绝对收益，比熊市里亏钱更能说明问题。Bridgepoint 拿着一个全球第二大赛车 IP 20 年，做不出 CVC 用 F1 做出的东西——不是运气问题，是"金融资本 vs 运营资本"的能力边界问题。私募善于财务工程，但把一个"深度但不广度"的粉丝群变成全球娱乐 IP，需要的是媒体运营基因。

跨领域联想：这和 Kraft-Heinz 被 3G 资本掏空的故事惊人相似——当资产的价值创造需要"进攻性运营"而不是"防御性优化"时，PE 的工具箱就失效了。Liberty 的赌注本质是：MotoGP 不缺资本，缺的是被讲述的方式。

四、一个隐藏的时间炸弹：西班牙 / 意大利 / 法国占三分之一的赛事

大家都在说这是"地理集中的风险"或"扩张的机会"。但换个视角——这个结构本身就是被历史锁定的"文化型资产"，和红酒产区、时装周城市、宗教朝圣地是同一类东西。Liberty 想复制 F1 的全球化打法，会撞上一个 F1 从没面对过的问题：F1 的欧洲遗产是"贵族式的"（摩纳哥、银石、蒙扎），可以被包装成 luxury lifestyle 输出全球；MotoGP 的欧洲遗产是"民粹式的"（Mugello、Jerez 的看台文化更像足球死忠）——这种能量向外输出时会失真。

这可能是 Liberty 真正要解决的、比成本帽更难的问题：如何在不摧毁 tribal 归属感的前提下，把它翻译给不理解这种归属感的美国和亚洲市场。

📝 转录文本

引子：为什么现在聊 MotoGP

So, last weekend with the British MotoGP, the Grand Prix — that the motorcycling Grand Prix at Silverstone. Um, that's only one event on the MotoGP circuit. And Charlie and I thought this would be a good moment to do a deep dive into MotoGP, um, and where it's at, where it's come from, where it's going to.

Um, and yeah, this is just that time of the year when we — we've just had the French and the Italian and the British, um, and I think the Spanish — sort of big legacy Grand Prix's have now happened. So, we can take a health check on where they are. But also look at, um, the recent acquisition of MotoGP by Liberty Media, who of course acquired Formula 1 10 years ago or so.

Yeah. Um, I was just going to say that. Well done. Uh, yeah, look, I think the thing to say is this is a huge sport with a massive fan base and great history, and there's only certain amount that we'll be able to cover in in 15 or so minutes. So, you know, we can we can develop this going forward. I think it is a really interesting, um, story to explore.

42 亿欧元的收购与 Liberty 的判断

Now, not least because Liberty have bought it for 4.2 billion euros reportedly. Uh, when I say reportedly, Carlos Ezpeleta — who's the chief, uh, sporting officer, um, who I've spoken to — said that on a show that that we did with them. So, you know, we can take pretty accurately that Liberty paid 4.2 billion euros for, um, MotoGP.

There must be some significant value. You'd assume that a company riding the wave that Liberty are and the reputation they have through what they've done with Formula 1 — what they see significant value in this sport.

Now, like me, Charlie, when I first did a MotoGP show, I must admit I didn't know a huge amount about MotoGP other than Valentino Rossi and Marc Márquez and some crazy crashes that I'd seen online, and maybe, you know, when I was younger, uh, you know, a few glimpses of races. It never been something that had properly captured me. And I think that's probably down to just the wealth of sport that's available and — you know, if it was a motorsport, Formula 1 had been the thing I'd covered.

But when I did get into it, I really started to appreciate, you know, how big this sport was. And I don't necessarily just mean big from the breadth of fan base. I mean big from the depth of fan base.

深度 vs 广度：MotoGP 的粉丝结构

The audience for MotoGP globally — and, you know, we're always careful how you say these, but let's just say it's over 600 million people. Last year, I think, was it over 3.6 million spectators went into the 22 um races throughout the year.

There's a real geographical element to it. Spain, Italy, France host a third of the the events — the the the Grand Prixs — and they are a huge portion of that fan base. So, you've got depth in some areas, but you have little global breadth, if we want, for a sport.

Now, if you're looking at a value, that's a concern potentially, or it's a huge opportunity. You can see Liberty looking at that and going, "If there's great attention for this in those markets, fantastic. That's a core we can build off, but there's a massive opportunity for us to go and take this, um, into into new areas."

What does that remind you of? It reminds me — It reminds me of — It reminds me of Formula 1 15 years ago, where you had an enormous European audience, um, and where America basically wasn't interested at all, um, and where they'd lost the the threads a bit in in Latin America as well, and Liberty made the bet that they could crack the US, and in so doing, they would totally change the business dynamics of the sport.

所有权简史：从 CVC 到 Bridgepoint 到 Liberty

I think it's worth noting that, um, Liberty are not the first major financial institution to own, um, MotoGP. Um, it was actually originally bought, um, by CVC back in 1998, and that's before CVC owned Formula 1.

Um, and the only reason why CVC gave it up, which is quite interesting, is that when they then bought Formula 1, um, the European Commission said that they would have to divest themselves of MotoGP because only MotoGP and Formula 1 would give them too much dominance within motorsport space within the European Union. So, I'm not quite sure how those the same rules haven't applied this time, cuz obviously Liberty have been allowed to buy both MotoGP and Formula 1.

Anyhow, um, they bought it. CVC bought it for 80 million bucks back in in the 1990s. Um, and they sold it to Bridgepoint, another private equity firm, once they were forced to divest of it, for 500 million bucks. So, they made a good turn over 7 or 8 years. And then Bridgepoint have held onto it for the thick end of 20 years. They sold a bit of minority along the way to then exited at 4 billion bucks.

Right? Now, it might sound like 500 million to 4 billion is a great return, but actually it's — that's not how a private equity firm would see it over 20 years. 20 years is effectively three fund cycles. So, you're talking about what we call continuation vehicles effectively, where it would have been in a Bridgepoint fund. It wouldn't have been deemed ready for sale, so it would have been put into the next Bridgepoint fund at a certain slightly higher valuation and then into the next Bridgepoint fund.

So, I mean, it's not it's not a bad return for Bridgepoint over that period, but it certainly doesn't suggest that they were able to do anything with it that really changed the mold, particularly given that in general terms sports business valuations during that time went through the ceiling in many other um different areas.

So, effectively Liberty are betting that as kind of sports and media operators — which Bridgepoint aren't, they're a private equity firm — as sports and business specialists, that they are going to be able to achieve something that CVC and Bridgepoint were not able to do, which is to turn the the sort of latent, um, demand for motorcycling and motor — sort of sports, but two-wheeled variety — around the world, and coagulate it into MotoGP.

So, if you look, for instance, there's a lot of demand for motorcycle racing in the US. Um, I've seen motorcycle racing in the US. It's just not MotoGP.

品牌史与"明星缺席"的问题

Now, MotoGP itself, Charlie, is — as a brand name — has not been in existence for all that long. It was — It was around sort of 25-30 years ago that it was changed. Up until that point, there were various different championships of prestige frankly. Of which the top one, generally speaking, was 500 cc. The 500 cc world championship was reckoned to be the the marquee, the blue chip event.

And when I was a young whippersnapper in growing up in this country, in the UK, the biggest motorsport celebrity in the country, two wheels or four wheels, was a man called Barry Sheene, who was the 500 cc double world champion. He was an immensely charismatic Cockney who was, you know, used to smoke on the grid before starting the races, had beautiful girlfriends, was a real sort of high-living James Hunt style type figure.

Um, but that gives some idea that when Sheene was racing at Silverstone, you had crowds there that at the time were absolutely the same as for a Formula 1 Grand Prix, maybe even bigger. I mean, that he was a bigger — He was a more famous person than Nigel Mansell was in the UK at the time.

Um, so effectively, what I think the sport has lacked somewhat in the last 10 to 15 years are marketable stars outside of two — maybe Valentino Rossi, um, and Marc Márquez being two who even I would recognize and go, "Okay, yep, those are big names." But they haven't been able to develop, unlike Formula 1, those types of rivalries and charismatic people who do stuff outside of the track, and the whole thing becomes sort of great sort of um, uh, sort of show.

Um, it's very much carried on being something for the enthusiast. So, I'm going to be really interested to see the Liberty playbook. How much of the Formula 1 playbook are they going to apply to this, Charlie?

Drive to Survive 的启示与"客观更刺激"的悖论

Well, let me — and let's be honest, right? That that's what Formula 1 removed the helmet. Sorry, Liberty Media — Drive to Survive. They said Liberty Media decided that Drive to Survive is going to be a great tool for them to do a lot of this. They removed the helmet from the drivers. We got to know everything about them plus the people behind it. Interest grew because it was a human story. It was people, it was sport, it was everything packaged into one plus, you know, high intensity, incredibly dangerous, exciting — well, I say exciting, sometimes exciting — sport.

MotoGP is insane. You know, races can't really be longer than 45 minutes or an hour because the intensity on the body and the physicality that is required to race some of these is is so intense. You got guys that —

MotoGP is both objectively more exciting and more dangerous. There's much more overtaking because obviously the size of the motorcycles compared to a car makes it more feasible to overtake, and because the drivers are so obviously physically exposed to the track, it's extremely dangerous.

So, if you're into adrenaline and speed and real daredevils, etc., MotoGP really should be more your thing than Formula 1, which has become, you know, a driver enclosed within a car, as you say — once the helmet's on, there's not much you can see about that particular driver. I mean, motorcycle is a more physical sport where they have to wrestle the bikes around the place. It is unbelievably exciting.

I've been to Silverstone — I think maybe it was Donington, actually — to watch a MotoGP event or 500 cc, I can't remember which one it was, 20, 25 years ago. And I've never seen anything like it. I mean, it was — it was so adrenaline-fueled. I mean, the whole thing was, you know, you could see the the the the drivers fairly close up.

Yeah. So, it is an interesting sports mystery as to how it's never quite managed to crack — not never, but how outside of certain core markets, particularly Italy and Spain, it hasn't quite managed to crack the broader market.

车队估值：巨大的价差与投资机会

That that's got to be the belief of Liberty. I'm really excited to see who comes in as potential buyers of teams if they're up for sale, which I know a few —

Charlie. It's a good point. Right, so basically — just to summarize to people — there are 11 teams, five of which are what we call factory teams. So, that's where the manufacturer themselves has the team, just like in Formula 1 where you have Mercedes, um, and so on and so forth. In in motorcycling, you have Ducati, you have Aprilia, you have Honda, you have Yamaha who own their own teams. They then also supply engines and technology to six independent teams.

And those teams currently, which obviously are the ones that can trade — cuz the factory ones by definition —

Well, they could trade. We've seen that with Mercedes recently, but that not currently that so much the case. But, those teams are currently trading at about 50 million bucks. Now, we think that Formula 1 teams right now, Charlie, are being valued at — well, over a billion minimum up to 6 billion.

Right. So. Premier League — Probably the cheapest Formula 1 team you're probably getting is about 1 and 1/2 billion now, right? I think you'd say bottom of the grid. So. Right. So so so the delta — Mercedes — Mercedes valuation in our first show was 6 billion is what George Kurtz bought into it at. 6 billion. We just talked about Liverpool being valued at 4.5 billion. Yeah. [snorts] Right. Um, but we've also noted, Charlie, that prior to Liberty's takeover, the smaller Formula 1 teams were being valued at 100 to 150 million bucks. Well, yeah, I mean — and that's — and that's generous, Charlie, right? I mean, if we're being really honest, they were worth pretty much nothing if you're looking at the mid-2010s. I mean, they they could barely survive.

But, on that point, you know, that's — I mean, that's the key element, you know, that they were businesses and underperforming businesses. They'd been built into franchises. And if you're looking at what you've got — a MotoGP opportunity now, can you make these businesses — can you turn them into those similar franchises?

Now, that price — I always look at like the gap between total asset value and then the, you know, the key components of what makes a MotoGP, i.e. the teams. You got pretty much a 100 X difference between what some of the teams are trading for and what the total value is. Now, I remember when I first saw this, I was like, "Someone surely got this wrong. Someone's got this wrong. One's massively overpriced, one's massively underpriced."

The more I've got into it, you know, I think to be honest, yes, maybe — maybe for you know, plus billion was punching from from a buy price. Actually, the economics of — I don't think were — I mean, I can't — I actually don't have it right in front of me. I think it was about nine — eight nine times revenue at the top end of of sports valuations if we're looking purely at that metric, not ridiculous.

The teams, however, that makes them buyable. If they can put an ecosystem together where you get really smart and exciting investment coming in and deploying cash alongside what they can do as MotoGP Central, you've got the foundations for a for a good organization.

关键战场：成本帽与投资确定性

Now, they don't have cost caps. That's — So, we we also talk — we talk about Drive to Survive, but as we've also mentioned on many an occasion, what made Formula 1 really big and a lot of the business it is today was the implementation of a cost cap because it just meant that investors didn't have to come in lose bucket loads of cash to win things.

They don't have that in MotoGP, but they — it's kind of a subtle change and I spoke to Carlos about this on the show. I think he said a 10 million euro spend would get you 0.05 seconds gain. So, he said it's not — even if you spend ridiculous amounts of money trying to improve the speeds of these bikes, it's not actually going to give you a huge advantage. To get a second ahead, which would be a huge advantage, you would need to spend 200 plus million.

I think that's special pleading from Ezpeleta in — he knows that it would be much more attractive with a cost cap, but they haven't been able to get the manufacturers to sign up to it yet, which is just where Formula 1 was before. So, he sort of says, "Well, you know, yeah, okay, we don't have a cost cap, but it doesn't really make that much difference." It makes a huge difference.

And the reason it makes a difference, Charlie, is something that you mentioned in relation to buying football clubs, um, earlier — and is if you can have business certainty that over a 5-year period your entity is not going to lose money on an operational basis, you as the new owner of that team can plan your investment around marketing.

You can actually say, "Right, we know — we know we've got the operational side locked down cuz I think they actually receive from MotoGP each team receives about 8 million in TV revenue distribution, right?" So, let's just say that they had a cost cap of 10 million or 15 million and you say, "Right, okay, we're getting 8 million from central. We're then getting 5 or 6 — 7 million from sponsorship on a reliable basis. Okay, right. So, we are now operationally break even. So, any money that I now invest into my team is going to go into marketing my team and try to make it into the franchise, which then enables the valuation to rise."

And without the cost cap, you never quite know where the next frontier might lead if one of the other teams then gets a big new advantage where you might have to then follow it to be competitive — and without being competitive, you don't have your attractive franchise and so on and so forth.

So, for me, this is going to be one of the big battlefields for Liberty, in fact, over the next two to three to four years is persuading all of the teams, "Guys, all of your valuations are going to massively increase if you agree to a cost cap."

跨界比较：足球俱乐部老板不懂的道理

Totally like screws with my mind that people don't understand this — and we'll have to come on next week cuz we haven't had time this week to cover football cost caps where there's big news flow at the moment — is I speak to football club owners who simply cannot comprehend that losing less money would make that entity more valuable.

They literally can't understand it. They say, "Yeah, but if I lose less money, that means I'll be less good at football. If I'm less good at football, then I'll be worth less money." No, no, sorry. The cost cap applies to everybody. It doesn't just apply to you. It applies to everybody, and therefore, everybody becomes worth more money. "Yeah, but what happens if I want to beat this other team?" Forget it. Doesn't matter. You're going to become worth three to four times as much even without beating that team.

Now, if MotoGP can get that into the franchises, the franchises will rise in value or the teams will rise in value, and it will also mean a reallocation of capital away from spending on trying to get faster into actually becoming better marketed, better businesses, etc. They'll be able to hire better executives to run their commercial and marketing side and all this type of stuff.

So, I I think this is —

makes you more efficient, right, as well. It actually improves your technology investment to an extent because you're more refined in what you're doing. You're not just spaffing loads of money to try and do stuff.

And —

again, taking it back to football, Charlie, this is why I call sort of like the differential between like Brentford and Stoke, right? Whoever runs Stoke knows that they've got an owner in the Coates family who own Bet365, who are basically willing to spaff as much money as they possibly can find on Stoke City cuz they just don't care and it's their club and they want everyone in the town to think they're great people, right?

And then you've got Brentford where — where it's one person who is a wealthy person, but not a billionaire, um, who every pound counts, everything has to get measured, there has to be efficiency in every single thing they do.

Who wins at football compete between Brentford and Stoke? The ones with the billionaires spaffing money or the ones who are run on a tight rein? The ones who are run on a tight rein — which again is the other thing which is very hard for owners to understand within sport.

Anyhow, the long and the short of it is is I think both you and I are quite excited by MotoGP as a proposition. And with what Liberty — and with what Liberty can do for it.

银石站数据的解读：英国例外还是全球增长？

Yeah, I enjoyed it this morning as I was getting — I I know when you are excited by something cuz I get loads of messages and screenshots of articles and I think, "Oh, he's in a hole here. He's enjoying it."

Um, the MotoGP — So, so the event that we had at Silverstone at the weekend, you know, should we say statistically I've seen some some negative commentary around it, you know, UK and —

This is around the attendance. This is around the attendance. Around the attendances, [clears throat] yeah.

Yeah, the attendances were about 100,000 over 3 days with 45-odd thousand on the main day. Listen, by general standards that's bloody good. But it's true to say that in the case of the British Grand Prix that is somewhat down from its peak of about 150,000.

At the same time, not to be too Anglo-centric about it, the French Grand Prix's been breaking records — up to 300,000 now on a reliable basis every year is going there — and the Italians are up to almost 200,000 and the Spanish are up to almost 250,000.

So you are seeing massive attendances just with a little asterisk that says I think that Britain is suffering here from not having had a very preeminent motorcyclist for quite some time. Carl Fogarty, who was the World Superbike champion — which which is a different series — was the last big English British motorcycling champion, really, and that was 15-20 years ago. Now we've got Cal Crutchlow who rides and who is a good rider, but he hasn't managed to break into that upper echelon of British sporting celebrity.

Whereas if you look at Spain and Italy and France during that last 15-year period they've had competitive riders.

年轻观众与增长信号

Completely — and that was why I wanted to bring that up because I thought if, you know, for us and any listeners in the UK, if you've seen any articles on this in the last few days it could have had a negative spin on it. If we look at it — and as you said take away the English perspective, look at it as a whole — it's actually doing quite exciting stuff and the audience demographics are quite exciting as well, which I think Liberty would like.

Um, you know, over half of the global fan base remains under the age of 35 based on the data they've done, which is hugely appealing for a sport at the moment. The viewership grew on average by 9% across each Grand Prix last year and the social following is over 60 million followers.

So, you know, there's lots in there to like and hey look, Liberty have done great things previous years as we've said. Who's to say they won't do it again? I think that'll be really interesting to —

They've only just started. They they bought it a year ago. So, I I I — like watch this space. This this sport in the next 5 to 10 years could become something big.

💡 创造性洞见

一、"传球恐惧症"其实是一种普遍的组织病理

表面上，Khabib 在讲足球——那些拿到球就马上甩出去的球员。但你若把"球"换成"决定权"、"bug 修复权"、"会议上被点名的问题"、"论文的第一作者位置"、"新产品线的负责人"，你会发现 Zlatan 描述的正是所有高压组织中最普遍的一种反射："Not me, not me."

有意思的是，球在这里是一种"辐射物"——它承载的不是机会，而是被评判的风险。所以真正稀缺的不是"传球技术好"的人，而是那 3 个"愿意把辐射物接住"的人。Zlatan 说三个就够——这个数字恰好和社会运动学里的"临界质量"（约占群体 3.5%）以及创业团队里的"关键少数"惊人一致。一个百人组织，如果连三个"接球者"都凑不出来，它就会陷入慢性瘫痪。

二、Ronaldo 罚失后再罚，本质上是在对抗"损失厌恶"

Khabib 讲 Ronaldo 罚丢一个又主动去罚第二个——这段话如果放到 Kahneman 的行为经济学教科书里，是一个近乎完美的反例。人类默认的心理机制是"损失厌恶"：同一个人在刚刚遭遇损失后，会异常回避同类风险（心理学称之为"snake bite effect"，被蛇咬过之后怕井绳）。

Ronaldo 的举动之所以罕见，不是因为技术，而是因为他神经系统里的这个"snake bite"回路被压制掉了。 这里有一个跨领域的镜像：连续押错方向的交易员会缩手，连续被拒稿的科学家会自我审查题目，连续被拒的追求者会降低标准——所有这些"退缩"都是同一个损失厌恶的变体。所谓"大心脏"，本质是一种反进化的神经配置：在别人系统提示"危险"的时候，你的系统提示"机会"。

三、Maradona 的阴影是一种"路径依赖"，而 Messi 完成的是极稀有的"锁定破除"

Khabib 提到那不勒斯的现象非常锋利：谁去了都活在马拉多纳的阴影里，永远得不到"完整的承认"。这在经济学里有个专门的名字——path dependence（路径依赖）。同样的机制解释了为什么我们还在用 QWERTY 键盘、为什么铁路轨距是那个奇怪的数字、为什么某些公司一辈子活在创始人的影子里（想想库克之于乔布斯）。

而这里有一个让人意外的观察：Messi 走出马拉多纳阴影所需要的，不是"打破路径依赖"，而是"在同一条路径上走得更远"。 他没有反叛马拉多纳的模板，反而是把这个模板复现到极致（同样的国籍、同样的号码位置、同样的世界杯救赎叙事），然后在最后一步——2022 世界杯——完成了原型都没做到的事。这是一种极稀有的策略：不是掀翻神像，而是站到神像肩上再迈一步。硅谷里能这么做的只有一两个人（黄仁勋之于 Intel 的原型；马斯克之于航天工业的原型）。大多数试图走出阴影的人，都选择了错误的策略：另辟蹊径，反而让自己变得"不可比较"，从而也"不可被封神"。

四、隐藏的元洞见：这段对话根本不是关于足球

一个 MMA 冠军和一个 MIT 出身的播客主，在讨论踢球的人。但 Khabib 每一句话的底层结构都是领导力的动力学：谁承担风险、谁在阴影下、谁能承受连续失败。这暗示了一个所有精英领域共享的秘密语法——无论 MMA、足球、创业、学术，最顶尖的一层人在讨论的从来不是各自的技术，而是同一套关于"主动权和风险"的语法。所以当你听两个不同领域的顶级从业者对谈时，如果听不出他们在讲同一件事，你就还没到那一层。

📝 转录文本

On Style: Players Who Take Initiative

Lex: What style of football do you like? You prefer short passing, long balls, individual plays, you know, like Maradona carrying the ball or of course Cristiano Ronaldo taking the ball and scoring himself — mostly those who take the initiative. You like that?

Khabib: Yeah, definitely. I like players who are willing to take the initiative.

I was recently talking to Zlatan about this and he said, "It drives me crazy when I have players on my team who, when you pass them the ball, they immediately get rid of it. They don't want to take the initiative."

When you have three or more players on the team — if there are three people on the team who are not afraid to make mistakes, that's usually enough. They take the initiative, take control of the game, drive the team forward, make mistakes, but they keep trying.

And then there are others who hide. He says they get the ball and immediately pass it to someone else. Just don't give it to me. Not me. Not me. They just want to get rid of the ball.

"Give It to Zidane" — The Quality Not Every Player Has

It's like, you know, it's like something one of Zidane's coaches once said: "If you don't know what to do with the ball, give it to Zidane. [laughter] He'll figure it out."

So, you see, that's the thing. It's a quality not every player has. You're taking the ball. You're taking responsibility. You're taking the initiative. You are not afraid to fail. You're not afraid to make a mistake.

Cristiano had a moment like that. He missed a penalty. And later in the same match, he stepped up to take another one. Think about that. You take the first penalty, you miss it, then another penalty comes along and you still step up to take it. Because if you miss two penalties in the same game, you're under a lot of pressure, right?

But that's the point. You're not afraid to fail as a leader. You take the initiative and you're willing to take risks.

The Beauty of Risk

That's honestly the beauty of it. The beauty of sports in general. The bigger the risk, the bigger the potential for greatness. If there's no risk, then you can't put yourself in the category of athletes people will talk about as some of the best ever — especially when it's a high-level game like the World Cup. And yes, the more risk, the sweeter the victory. There must be risk.

Maradona and the Shadow at Napoli

That's why they often speak of Maradona as a great player. There are many great players. He's great.

Lex: One of them. Yeah.

Khabib: For many reasons. But one reason is that he kind of carried the team on his shoulders. He took the initiative and carried them. That's when he led Napoli. You know, when he led Napoli to the league title.

Who knew Napoli then? Maradona came from Barcelona to Napoli and made them champions, and the whole stadium was named after him. Many guys played in Napoli, but there was never anyone like Maradona.

And recently I saw somewhere — or I think someone pointed out — the pressure on the guys who are transferring to Napoli. Whoever you are, you will always be in Maradona's shadow. And you stay in the shadow because fans will never give you the credit you might deserve, because they will always compare you to him. Are you Maradona or not? And if you're not Maradona, you will never get full recognition.

Messi Emerging From the Shadow

Lex: I want to say that one of the things that makes Messi great, I think, is that he really had to live in such a shadow of Maradona, especially with the World Cup.

Khabib: Yes. It's not easy. And he came out of it.

Lex: Hard to emerge from that shadow.

Khabib: Yes. And he won the World Cup.

Lex: Yeah. In that sense, you have to give Messi his due. I'm addressing the Real Madrid fans now. [laughter] Ours's yours — both sides.

Khabib: You're explaining it to them.

Lex: Yeah. Yeah, I got you. Most of them, I think — even if they don't like Barcelona, they still recognize Messi's greatness.

On Zlatan's Confidence

Lex: I know that you met Zlatan and you talk to him. I think he's one of the most self-confident people in football, in the world in general. What do you think about this confidence? Of course, he's joking around a little bit, but I think he really believes in himself.

Khabib: Well, yeah, he does. He does. I've known Zlatan for years now. We get along well, and I know his kids, and I like his personality. I like his confidence.

I mean, he's a unique player. There are not many Zlatans in football. You know, wherever he played, he always scored. He's a goal scorer. He is that kind of center forward, and he always carried the team. He was a leader wherever he transferred. It doesn't matter — Milan, Inter, Juventus, when he moved to LA Galaxy or Paris Saint-Germain. He was a leader everywhere he went, with the national team, with his clubs. He was always the guy driving the team forward, taking the initiative, and honestly he cemented his place as one of the greatest players to ever play the game.

And yeah, maybe when it comes to trophies — not individual achievements, but team honors — Sweden wasn't exactly the greatest team, and some of the clubs he played for didn't always win the biggest trophies. But as an athlete, as an individual, as a person, he is a very strong athlete.

观看原视频 →

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"热水瓶启示录"：仪式感如何构建冠军心智

Habib 讲了整整一段关于 Fedor 保温杯的故事——很多人会当作趣闻掠过，但这里藏着一个反直觉的真相：顶级战士的仪式感，恰恰是他们把"战斗"降维成"日常"的技术手段。

Fedor 打完一场刚结束的搏击，走回场边，倒茶，配蜂蜜，喝完再走。这个动作序列在心理学上叫"锚定行为"（anchoring behavior）——它把杀戮般的对抗，嵌入一个"喝下午茶"的常态框架里。你不是在把战斗升格为神圣事件，而是把它降格为一杯茶之间的事情。这与禅宗茶道、日本剑士千利休"一期一会"的原理惊人一致：越是生死时刻，越用最平凡的动作把它拉回地面。

对比之下，那些赛前两天睡不着的选手在做相反的事——他们在心里把这场比赛"抬高"，于是被自己抬高的重量压垮。

二、Habib 无意间说破了一个跨领域的"元规则"

他说："主要的比赛是与自己比。你先打败自己，然后才真正开始与对手比。"

这句话表面像鸡汤，但如果拿它去对照三个毫不相关的领域，会发现它是一个通用律：

  • 交易员（金融）：亏损的不是市场，是自己没能压住手指的那一瞬间。
  • 写作者：真正的敌人不是白纸，是你脑内那个第一时间跳出来说"这句不够好"的审查官。
  • 外科医生：手术刀在颤，不是因为血管难切，是因为你允许自己害怕颤抖这件事。

惊人的意外之处在于：Habib 描述的"情绪同时命中你"（fear, nerves, watchers, "what if I fall"）——这不是运动员独有的，这是任何一个人在做他/她真正在乎的事情时的默认状态。绝大多数人一生都在避免踏进这个状态，所以他们从未体会 Habib 所说的"通过皮肤、肌肉、大脑让它穿透你"。

三、最反常识的洞见：Shogun 的"腿部软肋"其实是他的美学签名

Habib 在评价 Shogun 时说了一句很奇怪的话："是的，他的摔跤薄弱，但……"——然后立刻转向站立技的赞美。

一般人会把"摔跤薄弱"当作缺点。但 Habib 作为一个摔跤统治级选手，反而把 Shogun 供奉在与 Fedor、GSP 并列的位置。为什么？

因为完美会消灭风格。 Shogun 的"漏洞"迫使他每一次被摔倒都必须立刻站起来——这个"必须立刻站起"的约束，反过来锻造出了他独一无二的爬起-衔接-反打节奏，那正是 Habib 说"没人那样打"的东西。

这里有一个跨领域的映射：爵士乐里 Miles Davis 的小号技术并非最高的，但他的"缺陷"塑造了他冷峻留白的风格；乔布斯不会写代码，恰恰逼出了苹果对"工业设计-软件融合"的痴迷。冠军的辨识度，往往长在他们不完美的那一侧。

而 Habib 作为一个"零漏洞"的完美摔跤统治者，可能在心底最羡慕的，正是 Shogun 那种被缺陷雕刻出的美学。这或许解释了为什么他早早退役——当你没有漏洞，你也失去了继续被雕刻的空间。

📝 转录文本

开场：谈谈 MMA 的历史巨星

If we can, I want to talk about MMA and football in that same context. Let's start with MMA. Who do you think are the greatest fighters of all time? You said you have a few favorites.

Shogun, George St. Pierre, and Fedor Emelianenko.

Let's talk about those fighters and maybe others who interest you. They all had different distinct styles.

Shogun Rua：Pride 时代的黄金标杆

So tell me why Shogun. You've always said that he was important to you as a fighter and naturally he had legendary moments in Pride in 2005. His soccer kick.

Yes, that's right. Well, Shogun Rua, when I was 15, 16 years old, he was the Pride champion at that time. For me, it was the best organization in the world. The best fighters in the world competed there — Fedor, Cro Cop, Shogun, Wanderlei Silva, Anderson Silva, man, they had everybody. Overeem, Dan Henderson, the Nogueira brothers, the Emelianenko brothers. They were the best at that time for me and honestly for MMA as a whole.

And right there in second place in my opinion, shining right behind Fedor, was Shogun. And the way he fights — no matter how they took him down, he'd get right back up. They couldn't do a thing to him. Yeah, his wrestling was lacking, but his striking, tight clinch, punches, kicks, knees — when he landed those soccer kicks, well, he really appealed to me as a fighter. Very calm, careful, very emotionally restrained. And his fight style, his style was actually at a very high level. The way he fought, no other fighter ever did. At that time he really impressed me.

Then he crossed over to the UFC and became the UFC champion. And UFC fights and the Pride fights at that time — I didn't have a computer, internet, none of that. I remember there was this video rental place. We'd grab tapes and watch all these fights with my father. Mauricio Shogun Rua to me was like the gold standard of a fighter back then. I'd say right alongside Fedor and George St. Pierre.

与父亲一起"拆解"比赛

And by the way, when you watch the fights with your father, did you watch them for fun or analyze them too?

Mostly we analyzed them. My father always loved to analyze fights. We'd sit like this and he'd say: this, this, chokes, striking, wrestling. We were constantly analyzing.

There was a fight in 2006 or 2007 — I don't even remember the exact year, approximately around that time — when Georges St. Pierre fought Sean Sherk. We even rewatched that fight a couple of times. Then Georges St. Pierre fought BJ Penn — the second fight, I think — after the fourth round when there was a stoppage. Then, well, there were many, many fights and my father actually admired the fighting style, the fighting style of Georges St. Pierre. He really impressed us and my father always emphasized his timing of takedowns after striking, how he closed the distance.

And honestly my whole, you know, like teenage conscious years growing up, my formative years transitioning into an adult, it was all tied to Pride in its prime. And after the UFC bought Pride and those fighters crossed over, that whole boom in 2006, 7, 8 and 9, the rise of the UFC — I remember that era so vividly. My father and I rewatched so many of those UFC fights.

Fedor：来自俄罗斯的启示

Well, I have to ask about Fedor. What can you say about him? He had some legendary fights. He beat Cro Cop, Big Nog, Mark Coleman. Yeah. And Kevin Randleman. And then he had those legendary fights with the Japanese fighters who were big stars over there.

Man, I loved it. Honestly, he inspired me just by the fact that he was from Russia and he was a fighter. He was closer to our school of training — Combat Sambo.

2004 达吉斯坦的那一晚

And there was this moment back in 2004, the Dagestan Combat Championship. Can you imagine? 2004, the Dagestan Combat Sambo Championship. And Fedor showed up. He showed up. He came to compete in the Dagestan Open Combat Championship while being the reigning Pride champion. I was 15 years old at the time. I was right there in the venue. My father actually invited him. He was sending out invitations to different schools back then. It was Stary Oskol where he used to train. Fedor's coaches were sent an invitation. He came with his brother Alexander. They both made it to the finals back then. I just remember: $5,000, $3,000, $1,000 — first, second, third place. At heavyweight, they gave a car. When the two brothers arrived, they beat everyone to get to the finals. They didn't fight each other. One of them took first place — that was Fedor. Alexander took second place.

保温杯与茶

I remember back then when he was warming up, I was standing next to him while he warmed up. It was this building, you know, a venue that fits maybe 1,500 people. And over there was this partition, like a wall, and everyone was warming up behind that wall. At that time, practically very few people even knew who Fedor was. But I knew Fedor. I knew who he was. That he was the Pride champion at that time. He beat Nogueira, beat Mark Coleman, beat Randleman. This was before his championship fight against Cro Cop. I would come over and just sit there watching how he warmed up, what he did.

I just remember very well — I don't know, maybe Fedor will see this podcast — he had a thermos. [laughter] He had a thermos and he was just drinking tea.

And I remember he fought Ibragim Magomedov. He was also a legendary fighter of ours, a heavyweight who fought in Pride, too. He fought against him. It was either his first or second fight. And he was warming up incredibly well. I remember how he was warming up his nose and his ears. I watched him and it was unusual for me at that time. I never warmed up my nose and ears. I just remember how Fedor was really working on his nose, his ears, his whole face — and he went, fought, came back. This was in Makhachkala, 2004.

It's the same as a UFC champion now coming and fighting at the Dagestan Combat Sambo Championship. Can you imagine that? Back then it was the best heavyweight organization in the world. He comes there and fights. So he finished a fight, goes back and he had this big thermos with him. His team was sitting separately over there. [snorts and gasps] Uh [sighs] he was drinking tea. He just fought, walked back, poured some tea, and drank it. He had something to snack on with it. Maybe honey or something. I just don't remember.

And I was — "Wow, Fedor is right here." For me, that was just such a, you know, great source of motivation back then. It's really hard to put those emotions into words.

By the way, maybe you could ask him about that on the podcast. About the thermos? No, no. About the tea. What was in it? Time. What did he put in there?

Well, I would love to talk to him on this podcast, but I think he rarely does interviews. I think you can reach him. I can help you. Well, if you could put in a good word for me. Yeah, of course. I think it would be interesting for people to hear him. Absolutely.

冷血的气场：Fedor 与 Habib 的共同之处

Yeah. But psychologically, he's kind of like you in a way. You mean calm? Yeah.

Yes. That calmness. You see the Pride era, those huge fights, those really tough matchups, and still he always stayed calm. It's his aura. Yeah. I don't know about others, but for me that was his aura. The fact that he'd come out with such a calm, cool-headed look and knock out giants, strong fighters at that time, right?

Yeah. You know, we used to joke about his face — that he kind of looks like a kindergarten teacher, you know — and then he goes out there and knocks out absolute giants. And he was like that both before and after the fight. He never showed much emotion.

But I think we're a little different in that regard. I think Fedor by temperament is calmer than I am. That's my impression. But with that cold-blooded calmness of his, I think he got to a lot of people mentally.

内心沸腾，表面冰封

It's like something's happening inside both of you. Like something's boiling inside. So when we look at your face, of course it's boiling. What do you think?

You know what? It's one thing when it's boiling inside and you show it. But there are some who can't hide their feelings. But it's a different thing when it's boiling inside and on the surface you stay cold, cold-blooded, calm — and you can handle all these different emotions that hit you at the same time. There are a lot of them, and they all hit differently.

When you compete, what makes a fighter and athlete at the highest level so unique is that so many different emotions hit you at the same time. Fear, nerves, the fact that people are watching you, the thought that you might perform badly, that you might not show what you've trained for, that you might mess it up, that you might, I don't know, fall. So much enters your head and you can put each emotion where it belongs. So you know if all of that gets inside your head and turns into chaos, you won't be able to handle it emotionally.

But you stay cold-blooded. And you know that if you don't handle these emotions that are coming at you, if you don't handle this pressure, then it will be difficult for you to compete — because the main competition is against yourself first. You fight yourself, you beat yourself, and only then do you actually start competing with your opponent.

So I think it happens to everyone, not just him or me. The big difference here is how much you can control it. Fedor himself famously said: "The only person who can defeat me is me. The only person who can beat me is me." He was talking about that fight with yourself. I'm sure — because if you lose to yourself, then you'll lose to your opponent very easily.

直面恐惧：不能忽视，必须穿越

There's an interesting thing I came across. Adam Sativ said that high-level athletes often make a mistake — and what they do wrong is that when they feel fear, they tend to ignore it. He believes that you have to confront that fear and overcome it.

Yes, psychologists talk about how to work through those thoughts when they arise. You know, when fear comes up and you feel it, that's absolutely normal. It's what the Almighty put in us. People get scared, or people get cold. People feel pain. People get hungry. These are things that are inside all of us. The real question is how you deal with them. How you overcome them within yourself.

100%. You can't ignore it and you must work through it. You have to answer their questions. Why did this happen? Could I do it this way instead? And this comes only with experience. Only with experience. And the more you compete, you know, the more you train and the more you face it. Some people actually try to avoid that moment, but the more you face it, the better and better you'll become each time.

It's the same with athletes. They get nervous. That's what we call the jitters, right? At first, whenever someone competes, they get the jitters. But when you keep competing over and over again, you gradually learn how to channel those nerves in the right direction. Then it gets easier for you. And in order to get there, you have to compete. And what is competition? You meet this fear face to face. You don't avoid it.

A lot of guys are staying away from competitions when they're young. They have this tension, this self-consciousness, this fear, the jitters. They're nervous. They can't sleep at night. You have to go through all of that yourself. Nobody can do it for you. A coach can train you. A coach can teach you, but all he can say is: practice, practice, practice. Then there's you alone with your own feelings — when you lie down, when you wake up, when you walk, when you're by yourself, when you eat. There are so many moments when a person has to go through all of this on his own.

And when you have to go through this over and over again, some people back away. They don't want to face it. And what do you need for that? Patience. You have to come and endure it and go through all of it — through your skin, through your muscles, through your mind. You must let all of this pass through you and overcome it. And each time you'll get better at it.

GSP 的问候：连伟大的人也害怕

A good example of that is the third person you mentioned, George St. Pierre, who by the way sends his regards. I train with him a lot and he has a very deep respect for you. But he didn't give me much good advice, because when I told him I was going to train with you, he told me — what did he say? He texted me: "If you die, you die." That's what he said. [laughter]

Good advice. He's a wise man. Didn't support me. And said, "Say hi." Tell him I say hi, too.

As we were talking about, he himself has spoken about this — that he was afraid and always felt fear before every single fight. That's interesting. One of the greatest fighters in history. Yeah. And even he feels fear. He's not afraid to admit it.

Everybody has fear. Everybody gets afraid. But I don't know how big that fear was for him. I really don't know. We never discussed it. But I've watched a lot of his interviews, his fights, and his training camps — the way he analyzed his past fights and all that. The way I see it, he's a very sensitive person.

上帝赐予的冷静：赛前的四小时

There are people like that, too. Some guys take all of this very lightly, like: "Okay, we fight tomorrow. We'll see who my opponent is and how he shows up, right?" But there are others who find it very difficult to handle psychologically.

But the Almighty gave me this kind of calmness. Sometimes I'd get to the arena and they bring you in four hours before they fight. They have to weigh you. They have to do doping control and they have to tape you up. There are so many athletic commission procedures. Every state has different rules — how they bring you into the arena and all that.

Sometimes I'd get there four hours early and think: what am I supposed to do? So, I make myself a little bed and say, "Please keep it quiet." I would lie down. I could sleep there for an hour, maybe an hour and a half. That's it. Wake up, warm up, and then I could go out and fight.

And some guys, they don't sleep for two days before they fight. Believe me, there are fighters who don't sleep the night before a fight, and it's very hard on them. It's not really fear. It's hard to describe with just one emotion. It's too many emotions that come over a person and they can't fall asleep. It's panic, it's fear, it's worry, it's nervousness, it's the jitters. All of that builds up and the person just can't fall asleep.

So in that regard, the Almighty gave me a little more calmness than others. I had, you know, such a cool head and calmness before the fights.
