## 一、"保温杯里的冠军哲学"——被忽略的最强隐喻
大多数人听这段访谈会记住"Fedor击败巨人"的画面，但真正的信号藏在那个**保温杯**里。2004年，一个正在统治世界的Pride重量级冠军，跑到达吉斯坦地方赛去打比赛，打完一场，走回后台，**倒茶、就着蜂蜜、慢慢喝**——然后再上场。
这不是"放松"，这是一种**拒绝仪式化紧张**的姿态。绝大多数顶级运动员会在场边用音乐、跺脚、拍脸、嘶吼来"进入状态"，把自己的神经系统调到高频；Fedor 反其道而行——他用**日常动作稀释比赛的重量**，让"打Pride冠军战"和"在家喝茶"处于同一个能量层级。Khabib 15岁的记忆里最强烈的画面不是拳头，而是茶壶，这本身就说明：**真正的威慑力来自把非凡场景当作平常事的能力**。
## 二、跨领域连接：Fedor的"幼儿园老师脸"与日本能剧的"面"
Khabib提到俄罗斯圈子里开玩笑说 Fedor "长得像幼儿园老师"，然后他一拳KO巨人。这个对比让我想起**日本能剧的"中间面"（中間面）**——那种表面上无表情、微微下垂、看起来温和的木刻面具。能剧大师会告诉你：**越是"无表情

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib and Islam speak different languages - Dagestan has 30+ languages | Khabib Nurmagomedov
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、语言的"不可通约性"：一种被低估的文明基础设施

最令人意外的观察是：Khabib 和 Islam 作为师徒、兄弟、同乡，日常竟然"根本听不懂彼此的母语"。这不是方言差异，而是两套完全独立的语言系统（Avar 与 Kumyk/Lak 语族分属完全不同的语系）。他们能并肩训练二十多年、共同征服 UFC，靠的其实是第三方语言（俄语）作为"中立协议层"。

这颠覆了我们对"团队亲密度"的常识——通常我们认为"共享母语"是信任的前提，但达吉斯坦的案例揭示：当没有人能强迫他人使用自己的母语时，反而催生出一种更平等的沟通契约。这与硅谷早期工程师文化异曲同工——正因为大家母语各异，英语作为"降级过的通用协议"反而促成了更快的协作。

二、跨领域连接：达吉斯坦是"生物多样性"的语言学镜像

30+ 种语言挤在一个略大于苏格兰的地区——这个密度在全球仅有巴布亚新几内亚、亚马逊河上游可比。有趣的是，这三个地方有一个共同的物理特征：地形极度破碎（高加索山脉、热带雨林、山地部落）。

这里藏着一个跨学科的"啊哈时刻"：语言多样性遵循的是生态学中的"岛屿生物地理学"定律。每一个山谷就是一个"进化孤岛"，语言像加拉帕戈斯的雀鸟一样各自演化。Khabib 一句轻描淡写的"我们有 30 多种语言"，实际上在陈述一个地理学、进化生物学、认知科学交汇的深层规律。

更反直觉的是：格斗冠军的密集产出与语言的高度碎片化，可能共享同一个根源。当每个村庄都必须自我防御、每一次跨谷通婚都需要谈判与力量证明时，"身体语言"（摔跤、khash 摔法）就成了唯一超越语言隔阂的通用协议。MMA 冠军之乡的秘密，或许写在语言地图上，而不是训练馆里。

三、隐藏的系统真相：文化"消化力"决定文明韧性

Khabib 提到达吉斯坦"吸收了很多文化和信仰"——伊斯兰是主流，但饮食里同时能看到欧洲、亚洲、高加索的层叠痕迹。这是一个值得放大的系统性观察：

一个地区能在 1500 年里保留 30 多种语言而不被同化，同时又"消化"了无数外来元素——这需要一种极特殊的文化代谢机制：吸收营养但保留骨架。

与之形成鲜明对比的是许多"熔炉型"文明（比如美国的 Melting Pot 隐喻）——它们通过同质化换取效率。而达吉斯坦走的是另一条路：分布式冗余的文明架构。用软件工程的话说，这是"微服务架构"对"单体架构"——每个山谷是一个独立服务，故障不会蔓延，但系统整体依然能对外接口。

这或许解释了一个更深的悖论：为什么在全球化最凶猛的今天，这些"看似落后"的碎片化文化区反而展现出惊人的输出能力（顶级格斗手、独特音乐、独立的道德叙事）。碎片化不是弱点，而是一种反脆弱的战略储备。

📝 转录文本

语言的多样性

We have so many languages — more than 30 different languages — and people just don't understand each other.

Take Islam and me: we have different languages, come from different backgrounds. Islam is Lak and I'm an Avar. When we talk, it's not like it's a dialect — we don't understand each other at all. But since Islam has been with us for nearly 25 years, he actually picked up some Avar over time.

历史的印记

But anyway, the deep history of the region — it all left its mark. It created many different languages and traditions.

Basically, of course, Islam is our primary religion, but Dagestan has actually absorbed a lot of cultures and faiths. Even our food culture, it is incredibly rich: we have European, and Asian, and Caucasian — our own unique cuisine.

独一无二的达吉斯坦

So on the people themselves, the last 1,500 years of history have left a huge mark.

If you're into history and you start reading about Dagestan, I think you'll get completely immersed and be amazed by what a unique place it is.

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] How Nuclear Will Unlock Energy Abundance with Valar Atomics Founder Isaiah Taylor
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察一：核能行业的"模拟陷阱"——一个跨行业的隐蔽病理

Isaiah 说了一句非常锋利的话："大多数核能公司其实是建模仿真公司。" 这不只是对核工业的批评，而是揭示了一种普遍的组织病理——当一个行业因监管或恐惧而无法迭代真实硬件时，它会退化成一个"论文工业"。

有趣的跨领域连接：这与生物医药行业的"临床前动物模型工业"惊人相似。药企养了成千上万只小鼠，产出无数漂亮的机制论文，但真正让新药通过 FDA 的成功率却低于 10%。同样的病理也出现在自动驾驶——多年来 Waymo 之外的公司大都在"模拟里数亿英里"，但真实道路的边角案例才是决定性的。当反馈周期被切断，任何行业都会用"复杂性"替代"真实性"，因为复杂性可以被作者控制，而真实世界不能。

Valor 真正的哲学突破不是核物理，而是重新恢复"tick rate"作为组织的第一性度量——这个词借自游戏引擎，暗示了一件让人意外的事：Isaiah 把核反应堆公司当成了一个实时游戏系统在设计。

洞察二："事故概率" vs "事故后果"——一个被误用了半个世纪的心智模型

传统核能安全的整个哲学是降低事故发生概率（odds）；Valor 的哲学是降低事故后果（consequence）。这两者在数学上是等价的风险控制手段，但在组织行为学上完全不同。

出人意料的观察：追求"低概率"会让组织变慢，追求"低后果"会让组织变快。因为降低概率需要无穷的冗余、审查、模拟、防御性工程，每一层都会滋生官僚化和责任回避；而降低后果只需要在架构层做一次正确的物理选择（TRISO 燃料 + 石墨慢化 + 氦冷却 + 被动散热几何），之后组织可以自由地快速迭代。

这是一个非常深的元规律：你在设计上把"最坏情况"处理好了，你在流程上就可以放开了。 这个原则不仅适用于核能，它解释了： - SpaceX 为什么敢炸火箭（可回收 + 无人驾驶 = 最坏后果被架构消除） - Netflix 为什么敢在生产环境放 Chaos Monkey（微服务架构本身容忍失败） - 加密协议为什么可以开源审计（密码学保证最坏情况的安全边界）

"架构上的悲观主义"是"执行上的乐观主义"的前提。 这几乎是所有能高速迭代的高风险系统的共同秘密。

洞察三：能源是"一切成本的极限"——AI + 机器人正在把这个哲学论点变成会计事实

Isaiah 最后那个"麦克风思想实验"看似漫谈，但藏着一个可能重塑二十一世纪经济学的观察：当 AI 和机器人把"人力"这一输入项转换为"能源"时，能源就变成了所有物品成本的渐近极限。

传统经济学的三大生产要素——土地、劳动、资本——正在被悄悄地归约为一个单一变量：焦耳。土地是能量场的空间承载；劳动是热力学做功；资本是过去凝结的能量。当机器人可以替代几乎所有物理劳动时，边际成本函数会退化成一条纯能源曲线。

跨领域的意外连接：这与信息论中的朗道尔极限（Landauer's limit）在哲学上是同构的——擦除一比特信息的最小能量代价是 kT ln 2。物理学告诉我们，信息、计算、制造，最终都是能量的不同形态。Valor 押注的不是"更便宜的电"，而是"把整个文明的成本函数压缩到一个变量上"——一旦这件事发生，那么"能源便宜 10 倍"意味着 "GDP 便宜 10 倍"，这是一个远超普通商业机会的赌注。

最让人意外的暗示：如果 Isaiah 的世界观成立，那么"AI 竞赛"和"能源竞赛"其实是同一场竞赛，只是从对偶的两端逼近同一个瓶颈。谁先把"能源单位成本"打下一个数量级，谁就先获得了下一个文明台阶的入场券——而这个洞察，恰恰是大多数 AI 公司和大多数能源公司都还没真正内化的。

📝 转录文本

开场：一次历史性的启动

Welcome to War 250. First advanced reactor to ever make power by a startup.

We did something pretty awesome today. The first ever AI chip powered by a nuclear reactor.

First trico reactor to turn on in over 50 years in the United States.

How much of the premise of Valor is possible now comes from increasing demands for power in the United States largely driven by AI compute. Energy being a commodity, the demand is set by the price. If you can figure out how to make energy cheaper, you will have demand.

When SpaceX started going, people were like, there's no way they're going to hit the numbers that they're hitting today. Most of the nuclear industry is a modeling and simulation industry. They're not focused on hardware iteration, hardware execution, building the simplest and safest reactor that allows them to scale. And Valor just demonstrated that we are.

主持人开场

Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today I'm here with Isaiah Taylor, the founder and CEO of Valor Atomics. We're here in their Utah nuclear facility where we're going to do a tour, talk about why speed and scale are the only path to making nuclear reactors in the United States again. Um why energy is the only input to our hyper techchnoindustrial future and why there's an open regulatory environment for progress in energy R&D for the first time in years.

Welcome Isaiah. Thanks so much for doing this.

Of course. Welcome to Valor Atomics at San Rafll. Thanks for coming.

Valor 在做什么？

So what is what are you doing here at Valor?

We are making nuclear reactors built for planetary scale. So nuclear fision is kind of an old technology. It's around the 1940s that we really started working on it. Um and we've built a lot of nuclear reactors, but we've never built them from mass scale. Nuclear's never had its Ford moment or its Tesla moment, if you want to put it that way. And that's what Valor Atomics is working on doing. We have nuclear reactors that are more manufactured than constructed and uh they're extremely safe and we think the combination of these two things is going to allow us to scale nuclear fision and make energy 10 times cheaper for humanity. So that's what we're working on.

And that will be true about energy forever, right? From now until the end of time, we know that energy is is sort of the only scarce thing in the universe, right? It's the only irreversible thing in the universe in terms of a resource. And so if you can figure out how to make energy cheaper, you will have demand.

Um and and so I I view valor as having a fundamentally infinite market because if we can figure out how to make, you know, energy at 1 cent, you induce your own demand, right? We begin to imagine ways to do things better with cheaper energy. If you can make it a tenth of a cent, you've induced even more.

And so, yes, it's awesome that we have these, you know, tailwinds of customers who are really hungry for power. I think it's also great just from a um a public awareness perspective where suddenly everyone remembers that power is super important right? But I also know that uh fundamentally making energy cheaper is what induces demand for more energy and that's really going to be our strategy for the next century.

Nvidia 合作：第一块核能驱动的 AI 芯片

Can you talk about what you are doing with Nvidia?

Yes. So uh we did something pretty awesome today. Um we powered uh the first ever AI chip powered by a nuclear reactor. Um so we took an Nvidia Blackwell. um super grateful uh to them for providing the system to us and we connected it directly to our nuclear reactor. Um and we actually hosted uh the nuclear website. So depending on when this podcast drops you'll be able to see it. Uh if you go to nuclearbite.com that website is directly hosted on the nuclear reactor. Um it is entirely coming from that chip provided by

consume some nuclear power. Nice.

Actually, on the website, if you go on it right now, we tell you exactly how many atoms of uranium were split in order to deliver that web page to you. Um, we've uh we've always been asked if we're going to sell merch, and I've always said that we're not going to sell any merch until we've actually split an atom. Um, and so actually the nuclear website is the only place you can buy Valor merch. Uh, so you actually have to buy it hosted from the reactor. Uh, so we we take billing in the physical world um very seriously.

Uh the other thing is if you're watching this podcast too late, you're not going to be able to see it anymore because once the reactor turns off, uh the the website is directly hosted from there. So it won't be available anymore. Uh so there's some exclusivity to it as well.

So got to tune in while it's live.

That's right. You have to tune in while the reactor is running. We'll keep it running for a few days. Uh as we continue our final testing um and we'll go through various tests over the next few months.

与大买家的分歧：2031 vs 现在

When you go talk to the big buyers of compute and thus power today, they will say nobody can deliver at scale until like 31, 32 and until then it's going to be um diesel gen sets and maybe solar and batteries and you know we got to figure out how uh to to make it until that period of time. What what do you believe that they don't believe about the next 5 years?

Yeah, I think that they've looked at all of these u nuclear companies of the past and again most of the nuclear industry is a modeling and simulation industry. That's really what it is. If you you know companies are what they do, right? And so I actually did not allow Valer Atomics to call ourselves a nuclear startup until we

you're a concrete pouring in graphite.

We we are legitimately a nuclear company because we split atoms, right? Um but you know, I'm I'm serious. We didn't allow ourselves to call ourselves a nuclear startup until we'd split the first atom, right? because companies are what they do. Before that, we were a company that was planning to split an atom. Now, we're a company that has done it. Uh, you know, 10 to the 20 or so atoms so far. Um, that number will keep going up.

Um, but uh yeah, so I I think there's a just a big gap in mindset between are you serious about scale? And I would also point out that exponential curves are very counterintuitive, right? If you look at the predictions of how many satellites would be in orbit um when when SpaceX started going, people were like there's no way they're going to hit the numbers that they're hitting today. And exponentials are just really really hard for for humans to understand.

Um so I would say yeah, if you're looking at the nuclear space today, you don't expect people to have this problem solved in 2031. In fact, I would say even 2035, a lot of these companies are still not going to get there because they have the wrong mindset. They're not focused on hardware iteration, hardware execution, building the simplest and safest reactor that allows them to scale. And Valor just demonstrated that we are.

自研混凝土与"石头猎人"

We actually had to invent our own grade of concrete in order to do this. Um, and the reason is we need a high enough density to block camera rays. The concrete also needs to be very strong because these are self stacking blocks. And we also can't use rebar because if we use rebar, um, rebar becomes activated by neutrons. Uh so you'll actually be producing nuclear waste.

We took two uh two engineers on our team. One of them is a uh nuclear physics uh uh mechanical sorry one of mechanical engineer one of nuclear physics and we had them tag team this. who said, "Go invent a grade of concrete which has the density to block gamma rays, which has the strength to actually be a concrete block that's self-cast, that has no rebar, and that has the right atomic mix that it will not become u nuclear waste when it becomes irradiated."

And they literally flew all around the country collecting rock samples from all around the United States. Uh we called it the rock hunt. It was about a 3-week period from plane to plane, literally collecting bags of rocks and they would come back on a Friday night and they'd set up the conference room with a bunch of buckets of acid and they would dissolve the rocks and then they would take the rocks through a spectroscopy analysis to figure out the exact BBM and then they go back out the next week and collect the next sample.

Uh, by the way, the uh the two team members are 23 years old and 21 years old, respectively, and they've done things that the nuclear industry has been dreaming of for literally 30 years. When we unveiled the system for the first time, we got DMs from from people who have been in nuclear literally their entire career saying, "I've been writing about how someone should do something like this since the 1980s, and I've never seen anyone be able to actually pull it off."

And that's a really awesome thing about working valor at Valor. That's also why we get the best talent in the world is because if you are a really really talented person who cares about nuclear, you want to see things actually get built and and you need to go where where you can actually build things.

垂直整合：Valor 的"秘密武器"

You are not a paper and simulation company, you're a nuclear company, but you also seem to be a road building company and a building building company and a concrete pouring company and a rock finding company. So, how how do you think about you're very opinionated that you know if we must for speed we will verticalize. How do you think about like having those capabilities and why you make that decision?

Yeah, I mean this is the secret weapon of valor and I'm going to give you the secret weapon because I fully believe that no one will be able to copy us in this. Um we are willing to verticalize anything that is necessary on our path to scale. Um and we've proven that a couple times in this in this reactor so far uh in areas that we were told repeatedly was utterly impossible.

Um, and the fact is like when a problem is important enough, you can go solve it and you can verticalize it because when a problem is as important as making energy cheap, um, you can go get the most talented people in the world to come and help you solve that problem, right? You can assemble the brightest minds to tackle it. You can get the best capital formation who who helps you go and and acquire the resources necessary.

Um, and it's really a mindset thing. you know, we've talked to and and know many of the most talented nuclear engineers in the world. And what we keep finding over and over is yes, there are amazing designs, um, but not much has actually been physically built. And if you have the muscle as a company to build things in the physical world, if you know how to do fundamental clean sheet design all the way through to prototyping, testing, and manufacturing, um, you have an edge, right, that that nobody else has in nuclear today.

Um, and so we look at really anything in the stack. And it's not that we want to verticalize everything. We'd prefer that most of the plants commoditize. Right. In theory, it'd be great if we could just buy a kit, right? Like if I if anyone is selling a nuclear reactor kit, I'm a buyer, right? I'm going to go staple it together and I'm going to make energy and that's great.

You're just going to make lots of plants.

Exactly. But, you know, that's not how it works. In in actuality, um, there are a lot of these components that are wildly overpriced that have super constrained supplies. And a fundamental edge that Valor has is that we know we are competent to verticalize any individual piece of that that prevents scale. Um and once we identify that um we attack it ruthlessly.

And you don't think any piece of it is like you know intersecting with more regulatory pain too complicated for you to figure out like when I think about your fuel supply chain

it's definitely intersecting with regulatory pain. Um and like we run at that pain like we just run toward gunfire on the most complicated things every time. We're two and a half years, three and a, you know, three years into this company and we've done something that no other nuclear startup has ever done, which is make nuclear power.

Um, and it it it comes from this fundamental mindset that the team that the team has, which is yes, there are complexities and regulation. Yes, this is hard, you know, equipment to manufacture. Um, yes, it's difficult to do both of those at the same time where you have complex equipment and regulation and construction and rock hunting and pouring concrete and building buildings, but the company that figures out how to do all of that complexity at scale and at pace is going to win.

And, you know, we're sitting here right now, you know, less than 3 years from the founding of the company. And I think if you look back at 10 years uh in 10 years from now and you know Valor's worth 500 billion something like that um you will be able to see that throughine where we took the hardest parts of nuclear right which is the site right and the regulatory and the fuel supply chain and the instrumentation and the shielding and all these things that everyone tries to outsource. And we said actually we're going to become masters of that right and we're going to go hire the best people in the world to tackle that and that becomes our edge.

案例：$5M 的 RPS 变成 $400k

Um and in the actual manufacturing,

this is another really good example of makes what makes Valor unique. This is our control skid. Uh these three boxes right there are uh basically a analog to digital electronics box. Uh so if you know anything about uh electronic circuitry, it's pretty simple stuff. You've got some signal amplifiers. You got some basic rectifiers in there. uh and and basically we take some analog signals from our our detectors and we send them to the control room. Each one of those boxes costs $450,000.

This is when it when anyone talks to you about like cost and nuclear like oh nuclear is expensive. Uh they are talking about ridiculous things like this, right? And this is really where Valor's going to win. that we accepted the $450,000 cost on this one because we're moving really fast, you know, and spending a million and a half dollars for these three boxes was more worthwhile to us than taking a couple months of delay.

But this box over here, totally different story. This one, it was bid out at $5 million. They told us that it was going to cost $5 million to buy that box right there. That is our um what's called reactor protection system, RPS. This is basically the brain of the reactor. Uh this system right here is super unique. It has no human input. It's basically a selfdeterministic uh machine that decides whether or not the plant is in a safe state. So it has three different sections that vote against itself to say is the plant in a safe state or not. And if two of them vote that the plant is not in a safe state, it shuts down.

And we were quoted about $5 million. Uh, and we were told it would make it would take about two and a half years to build. Um, and so we said, "Well, all right. Maybe I'd be willing to pay $5 million, but I'm certainly not going to wait two and a half years."

And so after having haggled with this vendor for about two months trying to convince him to go faster, uh, we eventually got the team together and said, "Guys, we're going to have to build our own RPS." And, uh, we sat down with Joe who runs instrumentation and control. Awesome guy, Brown dropout. uh really really good with electronics and he brought together five team members and uh locked ourselves in the conference room and uh six weeks later we had a a working RPS and we spent about $400,000 on it.

Um everywhere in nuclear is like this. There are uh totally fake costs from an industry that is just totally anemic and doesn't know how to build anything anymore.

By the way, the conclusion to that story is kind of unfortunate, which is that when the vendor realized that we were going to do it ourselves because we just could not, you know, get our heads around a two-year timeline. Uh they freaked out and started telling everybody in the industry that were an unsafe company that's going to kill people. Uh because we would dare to to do something ourselves that, you know, is their special sauce that they're charging the market $5 million for.

Uh, and if you go to I don't know if you guys use any of these like investor search platforms where you can like go look up a company and people have done like expert calls. Um, they contacted all of those expert calls companies and volunteered to do an expert call on Valor where their CTO

shitty.

Yeah. Their CTO uh basically went and like ranted about how we're the worst company on earth. Uh, because this is a massive massive threat to them. the fact that their $5 million system we can just make for a couple hundred grand with a team of 5 in years.

Uh but the more that you look at a nuclear the more it's like this everywhere you look it's a fake industry that has not been building anything for 40 years and the little bit that they have been building they're charging a 100x margin on. But if you just take it from first principles and you have smart people in the room and you're willing to build it yourself you end up with this and the plant is running.

There is something very inspiring about the idea of like given the physics work.

Yeah.

It should be possible and if it is possible to do it faster here, the best people will come. Yes. And the capital will come.

Exactly.

融资哲学：股权风险 vs 项目融资

Um this is an expensive project as far as I can tell. Uh how do you think about the fact that the uh you're an equity financed venture-backed company today. How how do you think about the fact that the like debt vehicles, project financing, operational proof of this doesn't really exist in the ecosystem to you know perhaps support as much scale as you'd like as quickly as you'd like.

Yeah. So this is actually one of the things that I noticed um years before starting the company. the the sort of traditional plan for a nuclear startup is you try to do some engineering and some design and some customer loss and you try to assemble this package and it's a it's essentially paper right but it's a package that's attractive enough to get somebody to come and fund the project right that's the essential plan of all nuclear startups they want to uh convince a debt financer or project financer or something like that to fund their nice paper package of designs and partnerships

Um, I went into this company believing that, and by the way, I believe that that was possible like 10 years ago.

And after watching this fail over and over and over in other startups, um, I came into this company knowing we're not going to do that. Um, one of the unique advantages that the United States has is a risk on equity capital environment, right? And the type of risk that we are asking investors to take is um, we know the physics works. We know that there's infinite demand and how we go from here to there is technology execution.

And guess what? Venture capital in the United States is the best at underwriting tech risk of anywhere in the world. Right? That is how Silicon Valley has come to be what it is. That is how venture capital has come to, you know, eat as much of of finance as it has is that venture capitalists know how to underwrite technical risk. Um, and it's execution and it's, you know, when we say tech, we're not talking about physics. We're not talking about science. We're talking about mechanical engineering. We're talking about thermal hydraulics. We're talking about instrumentation, right? Manufacturing methods. These are um it's complicated. It's nuclear, but it's like significantly less complicated than a rocket engine for example.

Um so, you know, I think this is one of our our fundamental edges and advantages is that um we're risk about this and we have a cap table that's that's risk on about this. We are willing to go build reactors on equity balance sheet because that's going to allow us to prove it years ahead of anybody else, right? Where where our competitors are still trying to convince, you know, uh fundamentally riskaverse uh you know financers to to finance a project, we will be on our fifth reactor, right? And after five reactors, well actually now project finance is an option, right? Now debt is an option but it's only an option uh once those early backers have put the capital in the ground demonstrated it and that becomes an enormous moat that's frankly going to be impossible to beat.

Gigasite 战略：自建电厂，让负载来找你

Uh one of the more different things that you've decided to do here um is you know try to build your own plant independently. Yes. And bring customers to it as you know at much scale as possible in a gigite. Yes. Right. Um and you know part of the belief there is like well if I can provide power at scale and especially cheap power like the load will come to me for many things. Um you know can you describe like the rationale behind that strategy?

Yeah.

So it it comes from a very similar uh argument that I was making before where I'd watched these uh these startups try to get that deal right for a very long time and frankly there's just too many parties, right? There are like too many people and too many parties

touch your speed to be like well let's negotiate about this site and this permit

exactly like yes in theory could we go to you know a hyperscaler who wants a gigawatt of power in a place like yes and certainly we will at some point um but we could also just put a gigawatt on the ground right and we can do that on our own timing um at our own pace and that pace is going to be faster than anyone else in the world

Um and and then the question flips around which is

if I have you know a gigawatt of power with land and fiber is someone going to put a data center there? It's like yes, absolutely. Right.

Um and so yeah, I think like in the long term we'll maybe start to do some of these deals where a dedicated customer wants their own gigasite for their hypercluster or something like that. Um but it'll be driven by speed even in that case, right? We'll go to the customers who say um you know and we want it delivered in a year, right? Not the customers who say oh we're thinking about this in 3 to four years.

So really speed and scale. If you honestly if you ask me any question and you keep digging back you will find speed and scale like that really is what nuclear is missing. It's missing its its Ford moment it's Toyota moment it's SpaceX moment where you have a company that realizes that the actual thing that nuclear is missing is scale deployment and and that's really what we care about. And so the gigasite, you we've got a site here. We're going to build more reactors here. We have a a planned gigasite nearby. We get to go with conviction, build power. Um and yes, I'm absolutely confident that load will follow.

作为 CEO 如何推动速度与规模

How do you um if you just think of your primary objectives as speed and scale? Yes. Given safety, right? Um how do you like drive that personally as CEO? What do you wake up every day and like think about problems to solve or what to focus on?

Yeah, this is one of those things that I think is the probably the most irreplaceable attribute of a company is its internal pace. We call it tick rate.

That's a sort of a metric that we've designed around going critical in in new systems, but you could probably translate that to any uh industry. You know, in software, it's probably something like, you know, new uh continuous integration builds per hour or something like that. But um I think it's the hardest thing to replicate. You have to start it from the first day of the company. Um, it has to come from the CEO and the first five team members have to have it deep in their bones. The first 20 team members have to have it deep in their bones. They have to be trained that when they hire people, they're looking for that in their, you know, those people's bones.

Um, and that's also not enough. Also, once you're in that setup, I have to constantly, and I, this is really what I do, go around the organization and speed things up, right? you know, continuously ask u my chief of staff's laughing over here because she's seen this happen many times. Um, you know, I go I go war mode on things, right? So, like look around and like, okay, that's going slow. And we will we will set up a a literal war room and I guess not literal war room, but we'll set up a physical war room um and we will say, how do we turn a six-month timeline into a four-week timeline, right? And maybe we'll hit 8 weeks, right? But it's not six months.

Um, and I think I've realized like there is no autopilot for that. There's no automatic mode that makes a company faster inherently. There are lots of things you can do to set it up for success. Um, but

but you have to push.

You will always I will always have to push and I will always push and it's because um I know that the physics are here, right? I know that energy will be a thousand times cheaper than it is today. I know that nuclear fision will make energy a thousand times cheaper than it is today. somebody will do that and it's really up to us as a team whether or not that's going to be in the future decades or the future centuries because that time is up to us right it's up to us how quickly we go down that path how quickly we make energy more abundant um and that feeds into everything else so it's it's highly motivating for us um and we are are tackling it as fast as we can.

能源丰盛的未来图景

People in their daily lives thinking about what happens for them if this works and you get very cheap abundant nuclear energy like imagine that future for us.

Energy is the fundamental input to uh the quality of human life. U if you look backward into time and say how did humanity go from one standard of living to the next, it's always unlocked by cheaper energy, right? Right.

So when we went from essentially a solar powered world, which is what we were in agrarian age, um like literally human muscles were solar powered because you were either eating plants or eating animals and both of those things were essentially um chemical energy that is built up by the energy of the sun through photosynthesis. Um life was hard, right? Life was really, really hard.

Um when we got into underground hydrocarbons, you had this massive uh explosion of quality of life, right? where we have, you know, heat in the winter and we have AC in the summer. Um, where we're able to drive cars to get to the hospital. Um, even really simple things, you know, we're in an aluminum strut building right now. Um, every one of these these struts that you could see behind us are made of aluminum. There was a time when aluminum was considered a precious metal. Um, where kings would literally make jewelry out of aluminum because it was that rare. And the thing that changed it to a literally structural metal that we make buildings out of uh is energy becoming cheaper, right? We figured out, you know, Charles Hall here in the United States figured out aluminum electrolysis. Um and cheap enough energy means that you can actually just separate that oxide from the aluminum. Uh and you can have pure aluminum metal. Um and that is that is entirely downstream of of energy.

So I would say that the standard of living that we enjoy today is entirely downstream of the fact that we figured out you can make pretty cheap energy with hydrocarbons. Now our goal is not pretty cheap energy. It's insanely cheap energy and that's going to be unlocked by by nuclear.

Um what it will look like I think is fundamentally unpredictable but I I have a few ideas. Um first of all I'm very very excited about transportation. Um, like if you think about the fundamental limits of why is it that I can't go see grandma every week, you know, on a plane, like why is it just so hard to do? Why is it so expensive? Why is it so complicated? It really just comes down to the fact that we've kind of squeezed as much juice out of jet fuel as we can, right? It it's just hard to imagine jet fuel getting 10 times cheaper than it is today. Uh, and it's polluting the environment and all of these different things. Um, if you could make energy 10 times cheaper, um, then you probably could go visit grandma every other day. You know, just on a on a Saturday it takes 30 minutes and, you know, she lives across the country, but you you go and visit her on the weekend.

Hyper-technoindustrialism：思想实验

I'm very excited about what I would call uh hyper techchnoindustrialism. This is a term I invented for

Okay. Haven't heard it.

Yeah. Um, for basically everything becoming free. Uh it is this sounds like I'm I'm talking sci-fi here, but like an approximation of this will happen.

Um let me put out a thought experiment for you. So uh let's take a a a physical good that's manufactured today, right? Let's let's take this microphone. So this microphone came from a factory and the factory had um sort of three inputs, right? It had people in the factory that are working on it, assembling things. It had input materials, right? And I would include in those input materials, you know, the plastic on here and this foam thing. Also the machines, right, that you know, maybe injection molded that plastic. And then the last thing it consumed was energy, right? So energy is one of the three things that made this.

What's interesting is um with the introduction of AI, we're actually converting the human input element to energy, right? So instead of uh a person having to pick something up and put it onto the next tray, right? you're going to have a robot pick some up, put on onto the next tray and consume energy, right? Um, and instead that human will be able to coordinate hundreds of robots, right? So, their personal output will go from picking up an object and putting onto a tray to essentially picking up 100 objects and putting it onto 100 trays. And the trade-off we're making there is that we're increasing the consumption of energy.

Now, you could still say, okay, but you are consuming physical inputs. What's interesting about that, though, is let's dig into that. All right. So, there were some physical inputs and some machines that went into that factory. Well, where did those come from? Right? Those don't grow on trees. Those also came from factories. And you can ask the same question. What went into that factory? It was energy. It was machines and it was people, right? Apply the same rubric and you realize, okay, actually, it's really just machines and energy. Well, where did those machines come from?

If you keep asking this question, what you realize is energy is the fundamental input. When we figure out AI and robotics that allows us to do semi-aututonomous manufacturing, energy will become the cost of all things, right? The cost of buying a thing will become the cost of energy used to make it. And to the extent that we can make energy 10 times cheaper and then 10 times cheaper, uh that is the extent to which we will be able to make basically everything free.

Um and that's very exciting to me. Uh because if we're going to go explore the stars and we're going to set up, you know, a place for us to live on Mars and explore the universe, we're going to need a lot of stuff and it's going to be it's going to need to be a lot cheaper than it is right now. So that's very exciting to me.

Exciting to me, too. That's a great place to end. Thanks, Isaiah.

Thanks so much for having me.

结语

## 洞察一：核能行业的"模拟陷阱"——一个跨行业的隐蔽病理
Isaiah 说了一句非常锋利的话："大多数核能公司其实是建模仿真公司。" 这不只是对核工业的批评，而是揭示了一种普遍的组织病理——**当一个行业因监管或恐惧而无法迭代真实硬件时，它会退化成一个"论文工业"**。
有趣的跨领域连接：这与生物医药行业的"临床前动物模型工业"惊人相似。药企养了成千上万只小鼠，产出无数漂亮的机制论文，但真正让新药通过 FDA 的成功率却低于 10%。同样的病理也出现在自动驾驶——多年来 Waymo 之外的公司大都在"模拟里数亿英里"，但真实道路的边角案例才是决定性的。**当反馈周期被切断，任何行业都会用"复杂性"替代"真实性"**，因为复杂性可以被作者控制，而真实世界不能。
Valor 真正的哲学突破不是核物理，而是**重新恢复"tick rate"作为组织的第一性度量**——这个词借自游戏引擎，暗示了一件让人意外的事：Isaiah 把核反应堆公司当成了一个实时游戏系统在设计。
## 洞察二："事故概率" vs "事故后果"——一个被误用了半个世纪的心智模型
传统核能安全的整个哲学是**

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on Dana White: He is a cold-blooded businessman | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"冷血"不是缺陷，而是一种基础设施

多数人把 Dana White 的"cold-blooded"理解为性格特质，但 Khabib 在无意间揭示了一个更深的结构性真相：冷血本质上是一种"决策带宽"。当一个组织的领导者能够把"人际关系"从"业务判断"中彻底剥离，他实际上是把自己变成了一台不会因情感噪音而降频的处理器。这不是道德问题，而是信息论问题——情感耦合越多，决策熵越高，长期系统就越难维持一致性。

有意思的是，Khabib 引用了"黑帮电影里家族至上"的比喻，但这里出现了一个反直觉的置换：Dana 的"家族"不是人，而是品牌本身。UFC 这个抽象实体被拟人化为"家人"，而具体的血肉之躯（包括冠军、员工、朋友）反而被降级为"业务变量"。这是一种极其罕见的忠诚对象的抽象化转移——很多创业者做不大，恰恰是因为他们效忠的仍是具体的人。

二、被忽略的悖论：UFC 的"品牌免疫力"来自它敢于让单场比赛失败

Khabib 说了一句几乎所有人都会滑过去、但极其关键的话："即便某场比赛不成功，UFC 还是 UFC。"

这是一个隐藏的反脆弱结构。传统体育联盟（尤其是欧洲足球俱乐部、传统拳击推广公司）的品牌价值高度依赖"每一场都要精彩"，一旦砸了就动摇根基。而 UFC 反其道而行：它把"品牌"从"单一产品质量"中解耦出来，让品牌成为一种"入场券资格"而非"质量承诺"。

这里可以做一个跨领域的连接：这正是苹果 App Store 的逻辑，也是米其林指南的逻辑——策展平台的品牌力，来自"我在场"而不是"这一场很好"。UFC 30 年做到别的体育 100 年才达到的高度，秘诀可能不是"办了多少好比赛"，而是成功地让自己变成了 MMA 世界里的"操作系统"，而所有具体比赛只是运行其上的 App。你可以卸载某个 App，但你不会因此卸载 iOS。

三、真正让人意外的观察：Khabib 在赞美 Dana 的同时，也在为自己的"退出"辩护

这段访谈表面上是"退役传奇谈论老板"，但如果你把它放在 Khabib 自己的人生弧线里——他在职业巅峰急流勇退、拒绝金钱诱惑、回归家庭和信仰——你会发现一个镜像结构：

  • Dana：把"人"抽象为"品牌"，让 UFC 成为家人。
  • Khabib：把"品牌"抽象回"人"，让家人重新超越 UFC。

Khabib 说"我也运营过自己的联盟，我懂那种关系"——这句话看似谦逊补充，其实是在为自己当初 walk away 的选择提供了一个隐晦的合理化：正因为他理解 Dana 那种"必须冷血"的位置，他才更清楚自己不愿意成为那样的人。他对 Dana 的尊敬是真诚的，但也是一种保持距离的尊敬——像一个僧侣在赞美一位战功赫赫的将军。

跨领域连接：这与乔布斯之于 Wozniak、马斯克之于早期 PayPal 团队是同一模式——最出色的"人性化奉献者"往往主动让位给"冷血系统化者"，因为他们意识到：规模化的爱，需要有人愿意暂时放下爱。这是所有伟大组织背后一个几乎无人明说的、令人心碎的分工。

📝 转录文本

Dana White 是谁？——一个罕见的商业天才

Lex： From where you are now, you can see the entire fight business and you know Dana White very well. I'd say he's one of those rare geniuses in sports business. In business, period. I don't think the UFC would exist without Dana White. There are important people there, of course, but he's really at the center of it all. What can you say about him? What qualities, what traits have made him such a successful businessman?

双重视角：既是格斗者，也是联盟运营者

Khabib： First of all, I think if you look at it, I also—kind of, well, not kind of—I understand his position a little. I also ran my own league for a couple of years. I know what the relationship between a promoter—well, a league owner—and the fighters is like, not just as a fighter. Dealing with a league owner. I've been on both sides of it.

冷血的商业哲学：业务与情感的绝对分离

He's very good at separating business from personal relationships. For him, the two never, never overlap. He draws a clear line between them.

In business, he's extremely cold-blooded. He's made decisions, some major decisions, regardless of whether people like them or not. And those decisions, they were best for the league and for the UFC.

He always had that mentality, you know, like in those mafia movies where family comes first, right?

Lex： Mhm.

Khabib： Well, for him, the UFC always came first. That's the only way he was able to push their brand forward.

团队功不可没，但"樱桃"始终是 Dana

Of course, a lot of people contributed to that success. There were a lot of them. You have to give credit to Bruce Buffer, to Joe Rogan, to the commentators who were there. There were a lot of things that made the UFC unique, but the cherry on top was always Dana.

Dana did an incredible job promoting the UFC, and he still does. No matter what, the UFC is always there. You know, no matter how—no matter how unsuccessful a particular event might be, the UFC is still the UFC.

When they go into a new market outside the United States, even if a show doesn't go so well, people will still come back for the next event simply because it's the UFC. Over the last 30-plus years, they've established themselves as the premier MMA league in the world, and they put on the best fights.

So, in that respect, I think a huge part of the credit goes to Dana. The fact that the UFC has come this far is a major achievement.

建立这样的联盟有多难？

Lex： Building a league like that is incredibly difficult.

Khabib： Yeah, a lot of people have money, and a lot of people have tried. Many have come in, but building what the UFC has built is extremely hard.

And what they've achieved now with Paramount—that's something unique. It's a unique achievement. In just 30 years, they've grown to a level that some entire sports needed 100 or 150 years to reach.

归功于一人：Dana White

And you have to give credit where it's due, and that credit goes to one person: Dana White.

So, I think that his genius as a promoter—the way he promotes and pushes fights, and pushes his league as a whole—that is just remarkable. In my opinion, that's something a lot of people could learn from him.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Anthropic's $2T IPO, Zuck's AI Manifesto, Nvidia's $500B AI Bet, Grok's Comeback
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个反直觉的观察

1. Anthropic 的"两万亿定价"其实是一封投降书——败选投行故意泄露的"耻辱标签"

表面上大家在惊叹 2 万亿估值创纪录，但 Gavin 揭穿了一个华尔街的隐藏机制：这个数字几乎肯定是从"未拿到 Lead Left"的投行嘴里流出去的。当承销团里输掉主承销权的银行知道自己出局后，它们的第一动作不是庆祝，而是故意向 FT 泄露一个"看似高"的数字，逼中标的 Lead Left 陷入两难——定价低了显得无能，定价高了引发破发。

这里有个反直觉的推论：如果 Anthropic 真的以 2 万亿定价，恰恰说明路演反响炸裂，而不是"贵"。IPO 定价的博弈论几乎是反着读新闻的。这和你熟悉的产品发布的"预期管理"游戏是同一套代码——只不过这里的玩家是穿着定制西装的人。

2. Dario 的"Anthropic 可能是世界上唯一的私营公司"是一句结构性的自杀宣言

Gavin 点出了这句话时说"我建议 Dario 永远别再对任何人说这话"——这不只是公关失误。它触发了一个跨领域的镜像模式：SBF 说过类似的话（"有效利他 + 全世界的钱由我最优分配"）、Elizabeth Holmes、WeWork 的 Neumann——历史上所有说过"只有我们能拯救人类"的创始人，最后都倒在了同一堵墙前。

更深的洞察是：这句话不是傲慢，它是一种商业模式的自我暴露。Anthropic 的商业逻辑必须依赖"我们是唯一被允许存在的高智能"——这就是为什么他们同时游说政府监管、鼓吹开源危险、支持 Cartel 化。"世界上唯一的私营公司"不是幻想，是他们的收入模型的言下之意。Zuckerberg 那篇 6500 字檄文精准地打中了这一点："如果 AI 如此危险，你为什么急着造它？"——这不是伦理质问，这是商业模式的解构。

3. Nvidia 正在变成"AI 的美联储"——而 Anthropic 的 S-1 会是整个宏观周期的领先指标

这里有一个几乎没人在讲的跨领域连接：Jensen 的融资平台设计本质上和央行的公开市场操作一模一样。他提供 residual value guarantee（相当于折现窗口）、通过 Blackstone/KKR/Apollo 做通道（相当于一级交易商）、通过 telemetry 掌握全市场真实供需（相当于宏观数据）——Nvidia 已经不是芯片公司，它是 AI 经济的货币当局。

而真正让我震撼的推论是 Sax 那句话的言外之意：Anthropic 上市后的季度财报，将取代 CPI、非农就业成为 AI 时代最重要的宏观指标。因为整个 AI capex 链条是刚性传导的——Anthropic 一踩刹车，SpaceX 拿不到 500 亿，Nvidia 拿不到 300 亿，TSMC/Micron/SK Hynix 全线连环追尾。这是史上第一次，一家单一公司的季报会决定一个万亿美元产业的生死节奏。

隐藏的系统性真相：AI 时代的经济周期正在从"美联储主导"迁移到"anthropic S-1 + nvidia telemetry 主导"——而这场权力交接，几乎没有主流经济学家意识到正在发生。

一个额外的跨领域彩蛋：Zuckerberg 的这篇宣言不是写给公众的，它是开源版的《共产党宣言》的资本主义翻版——马克思用"生产资料私有化 vs 社会化"作为轴，Zuck 用"智能中心化 vs 分布化"作为新轴。AI 时代的意识形态战争，正在用完全对称的语法结构重演 19 世纪的辩论——只是这次，"资本家"变成了 EA，"无产阶级"变成了开源社区。

📝 转录文本

开场：本周阵容

All right, everybody. Welcome back to the All-In podcast, the number one podcast in the world. David Sacks and Gavin Baker are with us this week. We got a short crew, but a long docket and we are going to rock it.

How are you doing, Gavin? Nice to see you.

Fantastic.

You're still in that SpaceX afterglow. This is the biggest win of your career, correct?

You know, SpaceX was a magical moment. There's only one SpaceX but — to quote Bill Belichick, you know, it's on to Cincinnati.

Got it.

And there's a lot I think ahead for SpaceX. So the SpaceX story isn't over.

Yeah. And you're only as good as your last investment in our business. I guess everybody's like, "What now?" Sacks, you're back. How are you doing, brother? How's the summer wrapping up for you?

Good. I'm looking forward to talking to Gavin.

Oh, fantastic. Well, I'll try to stay with you and not step on you. You missed a really great discussion we had on the all-in interview show with your guy Rahm Emanuel. How did that go? I heard actually it got kind of spicy.

You know,

it got super spicy. Rahm came in like full guns blazing, but it's a really great interview and we'll take anybody who wants to do the interview show who's running in 2028. Did you catch it, Gavin, by chance?

I haven't watched it yet.

Okay, you got it in the queue. Beautiful.

Of course. And basically the verdict on Rahm is that he's kind of a throwback to the Clinton-Obama DNC.

I think if you were thinking —

has no chance whatsoever in the Mamdani DSA Democrat party.

This is the great irony. It's a very similar moment I think to what happened in your Republican party where you had this sort of civil war internally, and I'm hoping the moderates have a chance here but, you know, who knows what's going to happen with these lunatic democratic socialists. You have a take on that on that they're taking the Democrat party?

I'd say his — first of all he's got incredible amount of experience having worked for Obama, Clinton, been mayor of Chicago and ambassador to Japan. So he was awesome on foreign relations etc.

Yeah. And to your point, he thinks hard no on democratic socialists and the socialist policies are a road to nowhere. So he just went totally hard at it as hard as you would, Sacks. In fact, I hope he has — nothing would be greater than to have a moderate or more moderate candidates. I think we can all agree on that. So we'll see. It's worth checking out.

头条：Anthropic 传闻中的 2 万亿 IPO

All right, let's get to the docket. Breaking news. At the time of this recording — for those of you who don't know, we record on Thursdays, publish on Fridays — Anthropic targeting a $2 trillion IPO. According to the Financial Times, this would obviously break the record setting $1.75 trillion IPO by SpaceX.

FT reported Wednesday night that investors expect the company to go public in October, which is like six to eight weeks away. This lines up with the polymarket — the sharps at Polymarket saying 80% chance of Anthropic IPOing this year — and Brad Gerstner, fifth bestie, he also was signaling that this would happen sooner rather than later.

Annualized run rate — we talked about this, Sacks, a bunch — will end the year between $100 and $120 billion. This is an extraordinary ramp up of revenue that we have never seen in Silicon Valley at a $2 trillion valuation. Obviously, you all can do the math, but it's 16 to 20 times sales, which is a fraction of what SpaceX and Palantir and some of these highly valued stocks went out at.

So, pretty interesting revenue growth over the last year — 10x. Anthropic still has AI's top model, but Grok, and we're going to get into it today, is catching up quickly and OpenAI not too shabby as well. Polymarket says 67% chance that at the end of the year, Anthropic will have the top model.

Breaking on Thursday, Anthropic in talks to buy an AI startup called DART for six billion. Their software lowers the cost of AI training and inference by making chips more efficient.

I'll stop here, Gavin, if you could comment — and I don't know if you're a shareholder in Anthropic or not, so it'd be great to get that out of the way — but what's your take on just straight up the revenue ramp we're seeing here and then what to expect from an IPO?

Gavin: 我不是股东——SpaceX 优先于 Elon 的竞争对手

So, a few things. I'm not currently an Anthropic shareholder. I'd say the Anthropic / SpaceX datant probably came a little too late. I don't generally invest in Elon's competitors. I don't think it's a wise course of action.

That's right. And the détente was obviously Elon decided, when he had so much extra compute with Colossus, that he would rent it to Dario and Anthropic.

Absolutely. And I think he almost probably more importantly got comfortable with Dario's morals and that Dario is a good person and — like all humans, you know, to be human is to err. So maybe he's made some mistakes and the way he's handled government relations, but he got comfortable that his morals were in the good place. As Elon said, they don't set off my evil detector, and he has a pretty good evil detector. You know, he famously cut his conversation with SBF short.

So, a couple of things on Anthropic. You know, the rumored numbers are exceptional. We've really never seen anything like this. I still think those moments in April and May were some of the most extraordinary moments in the history of capitalism. And what's wild to me is that probably on the margin, Anthropic is losing share to OpenAI, to open source, and to Grok. And they're still growing so fast. The numbers are still exceptional. So I think, you know, that speaks to the —

And why is that? This is like an important thing for people to understand. The pie is getting ginormous. So even if on a percentage basis Anthropic is losing on a percentage basis, the real number — and we talked about open source being dark tokens that aren't tracked anywhere — you know, this is a major, major pie-growing moment. That's what you mean there.

That's the point. I think AI broadly accelerated in the month of July, which was kind of crazy to contrast with the public stock market action. Now we have a higher resolution view of what was happening.

投行博弈：为什么 2 万亿可能是"泄露的低价"

But a few things on the Anthropic IPO. Listen, it's an exceptional business. They've executed really well and they haven't just executed on the model. Their products are amazing. I always think about Erik Frischia — I don't think you've ever had on the pod, but I think he'd be a great guest. He's a good friend. He said — had a thought experiment nearly two years ago that he thought OpenAI and Anthropic would still have a lot of value even if they lost at the model layer because the product, the harness, the user familiarity, it's all so important. And I think there's an element of truth to that.

But as far as the IPO, listen, the first thing I would just say is the two trillion — I'm a little skeptical. We saw this with SpaceX. If you're — everybody's jockeying to be lead left in Anthropic, and if you lose, the first thing you want to do is make whoever's lead left look bad. So you leak to the press and you say, "Hey, we're in the room, you know, the bar is a $2 trillion IPO."

You said on a previous episode three to four trillion.

Absolutely. But I think that's probably where it might trade. I mean —

So they're sandbagging now.

Yeah, we haven't seen the S-1. You know, I do think if you're bringing a company out responsibly, you want to price it in such a way that you can absorb the lockup, because you don't want to price it really high, create a lot of volatility. That's very disconcerting for employees and you do not want anyone distracted at this moment. So, I think that they'll price it smartly. Maybe that is two trillion. Maybe it is two and it trades to three.

But you just got to remember these leaks are always coming from the bankers who probably lost lead left and they want to make lead left look bad. So if it comes out at two trillion, it probably means that the testing the waters and the road show just went incredibly well. And people do want to own this. We've never — you know, these numbers are unprecedented.

So are you saying the road show probably occurred already, or quietly occurred?

No, definitely not. I'm saying if they price it at two, it means the testing the waters went well, the road show went well, and they've got a lot of confidence about where it's going to trade.

Sacks：能否维持 10 倍增速的物理与市场约束

Sacks, in the history of Silicon Valley — you pointed out multiple times here during this podcast in 2026 — that we've never seen a revenue ramp like this. Can it continue? And if it does continue, what would that say about the value of AI to corporations and enterprises where Claude is the definitive leader?

Well, I think it can continue. Although it is a legitimate question, because if you're ending the year at, let's say, a hundred billion run rate up 10x plus year-over-year — and by the way, they've grown 10x year-over-year for the last 3 years, so it's growing exponentially — if that rate of growth were to continue, they'd hit a trillion dollars of ARR by the end of next year.

And then the question you have to ask is, well, is the TAM big enough for that? But also, is there enough compute? Is there enough energy? I think you start to get into physical constraints.

I do think the TAM is big enough. I think the demand is going to be there. There's so many new applications of AI. Agents are just taking off now. You saw that with the launch of Grokbot. All these other companies are going to keep extending the uses of AI into more and more contexts. So the demand for tokens is just going to keep growing exponentially. I think the question is whether they can physically meet that demand.

And then also Gavin's point about market share. Other companies are seeing what they're doing and they're competing more effectively to take share. Remember Anthropic made this huge bet on coding and that ended up being a very prescient bet. I don't know if it was because of ideology — they thought that was the way to get to recursive self-improvement first. I don't know if it was because they saw Cursor —

That's the reason — building on top of that —

understand. Yeah, they watched Cursor's utilization and they said we're going to take that business, and that's such an important note for you —

Vertically. Yeah, so they've started moving into verticals where they see their own users building successfully on top of their platform. So that was, you know, I think that definitely was a signal to them to get into coding. Nonetheless, they got into it first. They got into it very successfully. That led to a boom.

We hear that OpenAI now — they've basically pivoted to coding. They're doing a better job with that now with GPT-5.6. We've heard their growth rate is accelerating. They used to be growing at 3 to 4x a year. I've heard that over the past 2 months, that growth rate is now over 20% month over month, which if you extrapolate it out over 12 months would be a 10x growth rate.

Mm. So you're now seeing OpenAI growing as fast as Anthropic having made that pivot. We can talk about whether, you know, we think SpaceX AI may be able to get there as well.

But in any event, look, I think that regardless of whether Anthropic is able to grow 10x next year, I think they're going to grow very fast. And then the question is just what does the market share look like relative to their competitors?

供给侧：能源、涡轮机、以及"地上有 Billy Bob Thornton"

And I guess Gavin, it would be worth double clicking on two points there. The first point is: is there going to be a market for these tokens and can the growth keep up? In other words, is there a demand? I think all three of us agree — yeah, sure, of course there's demand. But the next two pieces, which Sacks mentioned, were energy and data centers, and that is a question I want you to answer.

Can they get to one trillion in revenue? And let's slow down here and actually try to, you know, do some back-of-the-envelope math — and this is your wheelhouse. What would it take in terms of infrastructure for them to go from a hundred billion dollars a year in revenue and 10x it, and is that humanly possible in the next year?

"Anthropic might be the only private company in the world"

So, a few thoughts. I think it's the right questions. First, internally Anthropic is very confident. I have been told by multiple people I trust that Dario has said that Anthropic might be the only private company in the world at some point. Think about that. And in this vision, in Anthropic maximalist vision, there's Anthropic and then there are governments and that's it.

So there's a lot of confidence. I'm sure they have more advanced checkpoints than Fable up their sleeve. They've executed really really well. I would probably take the under on them being the only private company in the world. I think it's going to be a long time before they lay a rocket or —

They deliver your lunch. I don't know. There might be other businesses in the world. Zipline might want to bring you a burrito. Uber might want to take you somewhere. Waymo might want to drive you home. But sure, Dario —

I might interpret that as a negative signal because it's so hubristic, you know.

Yeah.

This is getting into SBF land a little bit.

Yes.

I would certainly discourage Dario from saying that ever again to anyone.

So, you don't — So, AI Jesus should not claim that he is AI Jesus. Okay.

Pride cometh before the fall.

Uber actually has massive insurance exposure, massive lawsuits that they have to contend with for what those drivers do. So it's distinctly different and they've gone through this.

I'm not a proponent of socialism, but I do think that there's an opportunity for Amazon, which is going to be automating along the way, to just take a little bit of a haircut on their amazing business but then be on the right side of history and not take their employees' benefits, unemployment, food stamps, and health insurance and give that to the public to do. And these socialists are going to point this out in the next two election cycles to the point of absurdity. And it's going to play.

Socialism is playing. Socialism is making inroads and it's infecting people's brains. And it's up to capitalists to say, "You know what, we don't need to be as cutthroat and don't need to be as clever." So that's my message as a long-term shareholder in Amazon. I have a very big position in Amazon and I keep increasing it every year. They should do the right thing here and get ahead of this so that they can say, "Hey, we are an incredible employer" — as opposed to, "Hey, we really are trying to hide and move these expenses around."

That's my only point on it. Not a socialist, not a cuck, not, uh, you know, interested in messing with capitalism. I think they got a little too clever here. That's my only point. And I think they should do the right thing here and treat the most vulnerable employees in the lowest docket.

What's that?

Now I know why you put this on the docket so you can get on your soap box.

Well, no, no. I put it on the docket because it's one of the top news stories and I put it on the docket because we talk about socialism every week and we talk about all the virtues of capitalism and there are downsides to capitalism where we can get too clever and then try —

I think we spent too much time on this, but let me ask you a question. You said that you want Amazon to employ all these drivers. By the way, they all — I think they should employ —

I know you said you wanted a bunch to still remain with —

I think the DSPs can happen.

So, how do you decide which is which?

I think they could proactively do that. It's a great question. Andy Jassy could proactively decide — just like Schultz did — wants to get rid of the DSPs. He wants to make them all —

And I think there's a compromise here which is: there are DSPs to scale up when there's demand during the holidays. Seems like a great idea, but I think he should get ahead of it.

As soon as you acknowledge that the DSPs are better because there are more flexible working arrangements that people want, why are you meddling in this arrangement to begin with?

That's actually not true. The people who work in the DSPs, the DSPs themselves, the people who own those fragmented very small companies that go out of business the second they get in an accident to shield Amazon — those employees would very much like to have Amazon equity. They would love to get RSUs and they would love to get healthcare for them. Some of those drivers, they work for Uber a lot of the time.

And they toggle back and forth between being a driver for Amazon, being a driver for Uber. They like the flexible working arrangement.

You're actually misinformed here. You're incorrect. These are people who are working full shifts. They're working 8 to 12 hour shifts. I think it's actually 10 to 12 hour shifts.

I don't think you can speak for all these workers.

Uh, you can speak for them if you — they can speak for themselves and they are organizing. And Amazon has been trying to break the organization efforts when they try to unionize. And this is a tool for breaking that by forcing them to be part of the DSP. That's the game on the field, Sacks.

Well, you already acknowledged that you think the DSP should stick around, so I —

I think a portion of them should do that and I think Andy Jassy and the team at Amazon should get ahead of this because it's a bad look. It's not in the best interest of capitalism to be this cutthroat. I think he should do it proactively. I don't think he should be forced to do it. That's my personal belief.

The same way Schultz said there's an opportunity here to make baristas have a living wage and have benefits. And it was one of the best things Starbucks ever did. And it's really what capitalism should start thinking about. What is our role? What is our role in driving the move to socialism amongst young people? And this is an example of one of the reasons people are starting to believe in socialism is because they believe that companies like Amazon are cheating a little bit on the margins and maybe trying to take the expenses that they should incur and put them on the American taxpayer.

And you know what? Mamdani and New Jersey are going to win these lawsuits. I predicted now.

Well, look, J-Cal, that all sounds really nice and I want to save capitalism as much as you do. And if Amazon doing that would really save capitalism, then I guess I'm game for it. But I'm not sure it will. What we do know it will do is raise the cost of packages by about $5.20 per package. And it will cost families $664 more per year, and it puts something like 5,000 jobs at risk.

So there are real costs in terms of doing things the way that you're saying. When people are wearing their hat as voters, yeah, they fall for the socialism stuff, but then when they're consumers, when they're wearing their consumer hat, they just want to pay less for packages. They will hate the fact that packages cost $5 more. And like Gavin said, they should put the Mamdani surcharge on their orders. And it's not 25, it's $5. $5.20 per package. $664 per household per year in New York. That's crazy. That's a real cost. Talk about cost of living adjustment. That's a huge cost of living adjustment.

Grok 的强势归来：Elon 追平前沿

J-Cal has had internet issues and we're just moving on. Gavin, last issue. What did you think of Grokbot? What did you think of the releases that XAI made this week?

I guess it was Grokbot and then also it was Grok 4.6, right? And people were saying that it is close to the frontier or at the frontier but a lot cheaper. So, I've been maintaining as of even last week that we were down to a frontier lab duopoly with Anthropic and OpenAI. Was I wrong about that? Is this number three? Is it more flexible and fluid than I thought?

帕累托前沿：Grok 4.6 的破坏性定价

Yeah, I think it is. I mean, I think it's — can we show that graph of the Pareto Frontier?

This is pretty wild. Now on the left, what this shows is kind of like quality or intelligence on the y-axis and cost on the x-axis. So you want to be in the upper right quadrant. And you can see here you just want to be on the outside of this and you can just see how disruptive Grok 4.6 is pricing.

Right? So as you sorry just as you move — as if you move right on the x-axis it's getting cheaper —

and the y-axis is the capability and it's getting more and more capable as you move up. But they invert the x-axis so that —

as you move to the top right it's better right —

Exactly. And I mean this is now and this is on Cursor Bench. And XAI — you know, SpaceX is almost certain, you know, they have a right to acquire Cursor. They're working with Cursor. So maybe this is grading your own homework. Well, right here on the right, this is from Databricks, which just raised money at $190 billion. This is a very real company that is very sophisticated. And you can see even on this, you're well ahead of Fable 5, which, you know, I think most people would kind of agree is the gold standard. This is you're higher quality at a slightly lower price.

So I think Grok 4.6 — you know, the numbers are the numbers, you know, on X. I think we put it down — people, you know, we do have to wait and see the vibes. But I think it's pretty interesting. DHH, who I think created Ruby on Rails —

David Heinemeier Hansen.

Yeah, he posted something really positive. Basecamp. Basecamp David Heinemeier —

37 Signals, great, great —

37 Signals, Basecamp, yes. Um, he posted something really positive. You saw the Databricks evaluation, you saw our Mercor evaluation. And so I think the early vibes are really good in these benchmark scores are bearing out in the real world.

Elon has caught up, in other words. And if you were to attribute why he's caught up, it would really be two reasons. Number one, he bought Cursor. He's got that team. They're a dialed-in team. Number two, he reshuffled the management of XAI and brought in his killers from SpaceX. Yeah, Gavin, those are the two.

Absolutely. He brought in, you know, the SpaceX aces along with the Cursor aces and some new people.

And he did that in six short months. Gavin, never count Elon out. He's frequently late. He's never wrong. And he tends to overdeliver when it does come. And that's to his own admission. He's like, "I'm always late, but we get it right eventually."

Yeah, absolutely. And this is still a relatively small model. It's 1.5 trillion parameter models. A larger model, Grok 4.7, that should be significantly more capable is coming out, you know, in a few short weeks. Grokbot is also — seems just as important. It feels kind of like another OpenClaw moment for AI — for this kind of personalization of AI, of making it — democratizing AI, making —

The same thing that Zuckerberg said in his manifesto. He wants to create bots for everybody. And that's what Claude Code and Claude Tag both do exceptionally well, as well as Hermes, Perplexia, Computer.

And I'm just going to admit — for me some of those are — like, I try to be very technical — but I, um, like Bots —

Not too hard to use, but it feels much easier to use for — much easier to use. OpenClaw and Hermes. You need to be —

Hermes. Hermes.

Buying a scarf.

That's what I called them. They're Hermes. They're just like the —

P. If you've ever had that channel, it's like that. Sacks, like you, your — our wives order some channel once in a while and they brew birth us.

Elon 的双向期权：训练前沿 + 出租算力

Uh, it is pretty amazing that in six months they caught up. But Sacks, this creates a tension. This does create a little tension. He's hosting Anthropic. He's catching up to Anthropic. What do you think about that tension here that he's their Amazon Web Services — Elon Web Services — at the same time as competing with them increasingly?

What I love about it is that he's creating these huge compute clusters, right? And that gives him the ability to train a big model, a big potentially frontier model. So that you can think of that's like the call option is to catch up and become a true frontier lab. But if he fails at that, he's got the put option of just selling the compute at, you know, pretty attractive prices to the Frontier Labs.

And he has the right, Sacks, to take that compute back from Anthropic. He put that clause, according to reports, into the Anthropic deal so he could take back compute if he wants to.

Right. Both sides have a 90-day cancellation, which means that if the spot price of compute goes up, he benefits. If it goes down, by the way, it could hurt him because either side could renegotiate within 90 days, right? So, basically, Elon is able to charge spot minus 90.

So, that's the risk, but it all goes back to what we were talking about before, which is: do you think that compute will be supply constrained going into next year and the year after? And if so, that's a very advantageous dynamic for Elon because, again, he's very close to charging true spot for his compute, but he can also essentially reroute it to his own service if he's able to take the lead.

SpaceX 的多头看涨期权

Yeah. And just — can I say what's interesting? Sorry, sorry to interrupt, but no —

I talked to a lot of investors about SpaceX. Okay.

Yeah.

And what's just amazing to me is everyone will have a nuanced view on Starlink. Maybe they're skeptical. Maybe they're a skeptic on Starlink direct to cell. I think the plan to use kind of these distributed Starlink, effectively almost, you know — we'll call them small cells, femto cells — is interesting.

Everybody will have a nuanced view on orbital compute — whether they're bullish or bearish, they will have a view. They'll have a view on terrestrial compute. Very few of these investors talk about Grok at all. And it is Pareto dominant on a lot of measures.

And we have an existence proof that Anthropic went from — whatever it is — a billion to 50 billion really fast. And if Anthropic is worth, you know, with two — two trillion per the FT — you know, three or four trillion, you know, maybe settles on a previous —

Settle out.

I said I thought that was a market clearing price. I didn't say that's where I thought it was worth. Um, you know, maybe people should start to consider Grok when they think about SpaceX.

SpaceX has so many ways to win, and I think that's the higher bit here. And it's — we're obviously all talking our book here. The folks on this podcast are amongst the earliest investors in SpaceX.

I was part of leading — a small part of leading the second round of 10 billion.

突发：Silverlake 或收购 Workday

Hey, there is one thing that broke during the show that we should for sure talk about, and that's that Silverlake may be buying Workday. Workday is up 17%. And if this is true, this is I think a significant moment for the stock market.

Um, you know, software has been in a death spiral that really kind of has started, you know — that probably troughed maybe 3, 4 months ago, but it was in a tough spot for 12, 15, 18 months. And the return of a private equity bid for software really changes the investing landscape.

And I don't know what the potential buyers of Workday are thinking, but I do know that the rise of open source and the increasing competitiveness of open source is a godsend for the American software industry. It is an absolute godsend.

Yeah, if you want to throw up a chart of Workday, you know, like a five-year chart, you can just see it. But a world where you have one, two, or three dominant frontier models — I mean, you could just see the stock went from — yeah, we'll call it 300 straight down to a hundred, you know, in a really short period of time. And even with this bid, you've only recovered a little bit. But a world where Anthropic, OpenAI, and maybe even SpaceX are kind of the only model providers that dominate the model layer — that is a hard world for software.

If I were to guess why the private equity bid for software might be coming back, it's because they see what's happening with open source.

Pretty amazing. And that is the backstop, isn't it, Sacks? We've talked about this. If nobody in the public markets wants to own these companies, and private equity sees a way — we talked about Bending Spoons, I think, last week, a whole bunch. There is now, I think — I don't want to call them bottom feeders — but what would you call them, Gavin? Like, you know, sharp acquirers of money-printing businesses that want to extract even more revenue from it. Yeah, this is a good turn of events that there's a buyer for these companies.

Absolutely.

I mean, what what Silverlake is saying — they've been oversold.

They've been oversold. Yeah.

And so here they go. There must be some value in that. And if you use AI to run these — I think that was the thing Bending Spoons is doing really well. They get rid of 80% of the employees and then put the 20% who are left as AI-first employees, and they figure out how to get all of this incredible revenue.

There's your breaking news. Gavin Baker, amazing —

收尾：Bestie 排行榜与晚餐邀约

Tied right now. Just so you know, I looked at the metrics before we got on today. You're now tied with Brad Gerstner in terms of ratings. You and Brad Gerstner are neck-and-neck and tied for fifth bestie, which means one of you will drop to sixth bestie if this continues. And we'll see. Brad Gerstner may be on next week, so we'll see which bestie takes the fifth slot.

David Sacks, great to see you. Hey, maybe we get a — you around later. Maybe we can get a steak. You want to get a steak later? I'm — I got Thursday night off here. I got a hall tonight.

Yeah, maybe we can go get a steak.

This has been an amazing episode of the All-In podcast for August 14th. We'll see you next time. Bye-bye. We'll let your winners ride.

Rainman David and we open sourced it to the fans and they've just gone crazy with it.

Love you.

Queen of your besties are my dog taking your driveways. Oh man, my appetizer will meet the —

We should all just get a room and just have one big huge orgy 'cause they're all just useless. It's like this like sexual tension that we just need to release somehow.

Wet your feet.

That's going to be good. We need to get our —

I'm going all in.

item.description:
## 三个反直觉的观察
### 1. Anthropic 的"两万亿定价"其实是一封投降书——败选投行故意泄露的"耻辱标签" 表面上大家在惊叹 2 万亿估值创纪录，但 Gavin 揭穿了一个华尔街的隐藏机制：**这个数字几乎肯定是从"未拿到 Lead Left"的投行嘴里流出去的**。当承销团里输掉主承销权的银行知道自己出局后，它们的第一动作不是庆祝，而是**故意向 FT 泄露一个"看似高"的数字**，逼中标的 Lead Left 陷入两难——定价低了显得无能，定价高了引发破发。
这里有个反直觉的推论：**如果 Anthropic 真的以 2 万亿定价，恰恰说明路演反响炸裂，而不是"贵"**。IPO 定价的博弈论几乎是反着读新闻的。这和你熟悉的产品发布的"预期管理"游戏是同一套代码——只不过这里的玩家是穿着定制西装的人。
### 2. Dario 的"Anthropic 可能是世界上唯一的私营公司"是一句**结构性的自杀宣言** Gavin 点出了这句话时说"我建议 Dario 永远别再对任何人说这话"——这不只是公关失误。**它触发了一个跨领域的镜像模式**：SBF 说过类似的

item.title: [Alan Chen加州生活号] 美股圆桌：美股又创新高！AI硬件+软件开始一起涨，但现在最危险的是追高？
item.dc:creator: Alan Chen加州生活号
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反常识的观察：这周真正的信号不是"新高"，而是"齐涨"

多数人盯着大盘创新高，但真正稀缺的信号被埋在结构里——硬件与软件同时上涨。过去几个月，AI 板块像一个跷跷板：软件涨则半导体跌，半导体强则软件回吐，资金在同一个叙事里做零和搬运。而这周 Palantir、NBIS、光模块（AOI/GLW）、Dell、HPE 几乎同频起飞，意味着资金不再"内部循环"，而是有新的增量资金从体系外注入 AI 叙事。

这其实是物理学里"相变"的味道——水在 99°C 之前只是变热，到了 100°C 突然变成蒸汽。跷跷板结构 → 齐涨结构，是市场从"分蛋糕"切换到"做大蛋糕"的临界点。这个信号比任何新高数字都更值得敲黑板。

二、一个跨领域连接：SpaceX 与 Michael Burry 是同一种"叙事燃料"

视频里把 NBIS 从 150 拉到 270 的动力归因于 Michael Burry 的曝光，把 SpaceX 概念股的暴走归因于空头被逼平——表面上一个是"英雄背书"，一个是"逼空机制"，其实都是同一件事：市场稀缺的不是资金，而是"可以说出口的理由"。

这跟社会学里的"米姆传播（meme diffusion）"模型完全同构：一个观点能扩散多远，取决于它能否被普通人 15 秒转述给下一个人。Burry 的名字就是"15 秒可复述的信任凭证"，SpaceX ETF 是"15 秒可下注的确定性叙事"。未来判断哪只票会突然启动，与其看财报，不如看它的故事能不能被压缩成一句话——这是 2026 年这轮 AI 牛市和 1999 年互联网泡沫最像的一个基因。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：投资者的最大对手不是市场，是"隔壁老王"

嘉宾那句半玩笑话——"宁可自己不赚钱，也不能忍受朋友赚钱"——听起来是段子，其实是这轮追高最危险的引爆装置。行为金融学里叫 relative wealth concern（相对财富焦虑）：人对绝对收益的敏感度远低于对参照系的敏感度。

有意思的是，这条心理机制解释了一个技术面之外的现象：为什么每一轮牛市的最后一波都是"逼良为娼"式的斜率变陡？ 因为顶部时段的边际买家不再是基于估值决策，而是基于"再不进我就是全场唯一没赚到的人"这一社交痛感决策。所以真正应该盯的顶部信号可能不是 RSI 也不是量能背离，而是你身边多少个从不聊股票的朋友开始主动跟你聊 Palantir 和 NBIS——这是一个比 VIX 更早、更准的领先指标。

顺带一提：Intel 从"周期股"重估为"成长股"，本质也是一次叙事重写。估值倍数从来不是被数字驱动的，是被形容词驱动的。谁能重新命名一只股票，谁就重新定义了它的市盈率。

Previously, these were basically related to the software stock, that is, one rose, and the other one was a bit of a knock-and-call response. Now they seem to have returned to the AI trend and started to rise together. I think this is a relatively important observation. Everyone can pay attention to it.

Dell 与 HPE：新的领涨强势股

There are two more stocks that are growing more significantly in hardware. Compared to semiconductors, light, Dell and HPE. Yes, we have a focus on this.
